What to record in an AI agent run to find its first wrong step, and what Mercury records today. Based on OpenTelemetry's GenAI agent spans and a code review.
CERT-In says AI agents read live business records at Indian firms. Here is how least privilege, scoped access, approvals and audit logs should limit them.
A Harvard working paper finds coding agents raised code output while review time rose 49%. Why verification, not generation, should decide whether an agent is useful.
Archive

An agent with a shell, a file system and network access is only useful if you can trust what it will do with them. A tour of the layers between the model and your machine: scopes, approvals, a blocklist nothing can override, an SSRF guard, and tiers for unattended bots.
The team behind Mercury. Postmortems, design notes and the reasoning behind how Mercury works.
Founder, Cosmic Stack. Builds Mercury. Writes about agent runtimes, terminal UIs and shipping open source.
Contributor, Mercury. Writes about agent permissions, security and running Mercury safely.
Inside Optimus, the Mercury plugin that sees your screen, moves the mouse and types: its processes, how it looks and acts, voice control, and the safety rails.
One background runtime that every terminal attaches to, bots that deliver real files and stay online, and a fleet you can run from Telegram. What changed in the 1.3 line and why.
Mercury 1.4 adds isolated plugins and two official ones: WhatsApp chat with voice calls both ways, and Optimus, which sees your screen and uses your mouse.
Mercury 1.5.0 ships Mercury Desktop for macOS, Windows and Linux, remote access the owner approves, and updates that roll back on their own.
Always-on agents shipped everywhere this autumn. How Mercury Bots work, what we measured, how they compare with Grok Bot, OpenAI dots, Meta Muse, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, and the commits behind it.
What's inside Mercury Desktop 1.5.0: chat, research, code, bots, memory and voice, plus connecting to several Mercury servers and keeping them all updated.
We read Mercury's scheduler and budget code and reproduced one behaviour, to find what fails during long unattended runs: skipped tasks, quiet errors, overlapping jobs and budget stops.

For six releases, a brand-new Mercury install asked for your name, showed one menu, and exited without an error. A walkthrough of a one-tick race between two readers of the same terminal, and the test that now keeps it from coming back.

Typing felt sluggish on every machine, and the terminal renderer took the blame. The real cause was a second full copy of the agent, started quietly by the launcher. How we found it, and why the fix was an architecture change rather than a performance tweak.
Mercury runs anywhere Node.js 22+ runs, plus everywhere a single binary can live — including phones via Termux.

Mercury offers two ways to work on a repository: a CLI workspace (terminal-based IDE with keyboard navigation) and a Web Workspace IDE (full graphical editor in the browser). Both share the same backend tools and Git operations.

Mercury connects to Discord as a bot, providing a real-time conversational interface with slash commands, streaming responses, rich embeds, and an organization-style access model with admin roles and pairing codes.

Mercury can act as your GitHub companion — creating pull requests, reviewing PRs, managing issues, and making co-authored commits — all through natural conversation. When configured, five GitHub tools are registered alongside Mercury's built-in toolset, letting you manage repositories without leaving the terminal or Telegram.

Kanban Boards are a beta feature in v1.1.9. The data model and API surface are stable, but expect UI refinements in subsequent releases. The web dashboard labels this section "Kanban Boards (Beta mode)".

Mercury is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. Connect it to MCP servers — local programs or remote endpoints — and their tools become available to the agent next to Mercury's built-in tools: your issue tracker, a database, internal company tools, a browser, anything that ships as an MCP server.
Persistent, persona-scoped agents that run outside your conversation — each with its own persona, sandbox, skills, permission scopes, and durable queue. Build fleets with lead bots and crews.

Optimus lets Mercury use your computer like a person: it sees the screen, moves the pointer, types and opens apps, by chat or out loud with a talk key. Install, permissions, hotkeys, settings and safety.

Mercury connects to Signal via a signal-cli bridge, providing an end-to-end encrypted conversational interface with support for group chats and private DMs, pairing-code access control, and real-time task progress.

Mercury connects to Slack as a Socket Mode bot, providing a real-time conversational interface with slash commands, streaming responses, and an organization-style access model with pairing codes and admin controls.

Mercury connects to your Spotify account natively — control playback, search music, manage playlists, and DJ on your devices through natural conversation. No browser tabs, no app switching. Just say "play some chill music" and Mercury handles the rest.

Mercury isn't just a chatbot — it's an orchestrator. It can spawn parallel AI agents to handle tasks concurrently while continuing the conversation. This is sub-agent mode, and it changes how Mercury works fundamentally.
Mercury connects to Telegram via a bot token, providing a mobile-first interface with streaming, file uploads, inline approval keyboards, and real-time task progress.
Mercury Web is a React single-page application that provides a visual interface for managing every part of the agent — chat, memory, tasks, code, and configuration. It runs locally at http6174.
Chat with Mercury on WhatsApp and talk to it by voice call, in both directions. Install, link a spare number, voice engines, scheduled calls, approvals and access levels.
Mercury has a built-in toolset it can use during conversations. These are not CLI commands — the agent decides when to call them.
How Mercury Code guarantees honest, verified, stall-free task completions — the completion contract, the escalation harness, and the recovery map.
All runtime data lives in ~/.mercury/ — not in your project directory.
Mercury has a layered permission system that controls what actions the agent can take. The behavior differs significantly between Ask Me and Allow All modes.
A Mercury plugin is a folder with a mercury-plugin.json manifest and code.
Configure multiple LLM providers. Mercury tries them in order and falls back automatically. When a provider fails, Mercury tries the next one and remembers the last successful provider.
Mercury can schedule tasks using cron expressions or one-shot delays.

Mercury has a persistent, structured memory that grows with every conversation. When enabled, it learns what is true about you — and how you like to work — as beliefs with evidence, retrieves what is relevant to each message, and tells you when it learned something that changes how it behaves.
Skills are Markdown-based extensions that teach Mercury how to do a specific task. Each skill is a single SKILL.md file in ~/.mercury/skills// and follows the Agent Skills specification.

Token Saver Mode is a battery-saver-style optimization layer for LLM calls. When active, Mercury produces shorter, terser responses, runs fewer reasoning steps, and uses a smaller history window — saving tokens at the cost of some verbosity and exploration depth.
Mercury Agent release notes — what shipped, when, and why.
Mercury becomes a skillful platform. Skill System, Token Saver Mode, standalone binaries on five OS targets, redesigned bottom status bar with per-step spinners, and a new built-in screenshot skill.
Hotfix on top of v1.1.11. Standalone binaries can now start in the background, so Telegram works again for users who installed Mercury via the one-line installer.

Mercury gets chatty. Three new channels — Discord, Slack, and Signal — bring Mercury to where you already are, with end-to-end encryption, organization access models, and real-time streaming. Plus long-running loop fixes, CLI heartbeat improvements, and crash recovery.
Release 1.1.6 focuses on a major CLI/TUI upgrade, workspace IDE flow, background execution reliability, and docs coverage.

Release 1.1.7 brings two new providers (ChatGPT Web and GitHub Copilot), a redesigned real-time progress system, Mercury Autopilot with intelligent loop detection, major Telegram improvements, and a full landing page redesign with the interactive Killipi mascot.

Release 1.1.9 introduces the Mercury Web Dashboard — a full React SPA at localhost:6174 — alongside a persistent Kanban board system, an in-browser Workspace IDE with Git and AI commit messages, a dual-layer (conscious + subconscious) Second Brain, intelligent skill batching, and a cross-platform build pipeline.

documents.t: Mercury meets the cloud. Terminal pairing, JWT auth with self-recovery, Cloud WebSocket for real-time remote control, shared memory pool search, and cross-platform fixes for Windows and Termux. Patch set 1.2.0 → 1.2.1 → 1.2.2.

The release where Mercury Code stops dying and starts telling the truth. Completion contract, AUTO mode, the escalation harness, compact-on-pressure, live plan checklist, and security hardening across the tool surface.

Mercury stops being one agent and becomes a fleet. Persistent persona-scoped bots with private sandboxes, durable queues, multi-level fleets with self-organizing leads, bundles, a web cockpit, and honest observability.

One process runs the fleet and your channels; the terminal attaches to it instantly. Bots do real work, deliver files you can find, stay online without burning tokens, and run from your phone. Node 22, patched Ink 8, and the whole unpublished 1.3.1 line.

Mercury gets a plugin system and two official plugins: WhatsApp chat and voice calls in both directions, and Optimus, which lets Mercury use your computer by chat or out loud. Plus built-in web search and photos, PDFs and voice notes from chat.
The Owner Model: Mercury learns how to work with you, saves its own skills, and searches again without a key.

A normal service either fails or it doesn't. An agent can return a successful response and still fail the task. A 200 OK means the request was handled. It does not mean the task succeeded. Snowflake's agent evaluation guide puts the gap plainly: a correct final answer is only the last part of the run. It also separates two jobs. Evaluation measures quality against defined tasks. Monitoring watches live behaviour through traces, logs, latency, cost, tool failures and user feedback. Microsoft's Foundry observability documentation describes tracing as capturing LLM calls, tool invocations, agent decisions and dependencies between services. New Relic's agent observability write-up makes the same point from the vendor side: without trace-level data, you can see that something went wrong but not why.
documents.s: Why normal monitoring misses agent failures

documents.t: The final output is the symptom. The cause is usually an early step: a tool chosen when another was needed, a retrieved document that was out of date, or an argument that looked reasonable and wasn't. By the time the answer is wrong, that step is several calls back. In this post, the first wrong step means the earliest consequential deviation: the first step whose effect changed what came after it in a way that mattered to the outcome. A step that was odd but harmless does not count. So the question for a trace is not "what did the agent do?" It is "where is the earliest consequential deviation, and what did the agent have in front of it at that point?" A trace that can't answer that will show you a long, plausible transcript and leave you to read all of it. Here is a made-up run to show the difference. The user asks for last month's invoice total. Step 1 searches the wrong folder and gets a file from the previous year. Step 2 reads it, sums the totals, and reports a figure. Step 3 writes a fluent summary. The final answer looks right, and every tool call returned ok. A transcript shows three clean steps. A trace with timestamps, arguments and parent links shows that step 1 was the first consequential deviation, and that step 2 never had a chance to fix it. The run was never going to produce the right number, so the fix belongs at step 1, not in the summary. This example is illustrative, not a recorded Mercury incident.
documents.s: The unit of debugging is the first wrong step

documents.t: The clearest published model I found is OpenTelemetry's draft GenAI agent conventions. The v1.41.0 agent span spec defines operation names including invoke_agent, execute_tool, create_agent and invoke_workflow. The OpenTelemetry GenAI blog shows the resulting tree: an invoke_agent span with child spans for each model call and each tool call. It also records token counts such as gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, plus finish reasons and latency histograms. Mapped to the questions you need to answer: Question What to record Which tool was chosen? The chosen tool, its arguments, and the tools available at that step Did the call work? The result, error type, latency, and whether the result entered subsequent context Is it looping? Repeated calls with the same arguments, or revisited goals Where did work pass? Handoffs to sub-agents, and what context went with them What changed in context? Items added, dropped or summarised between steps What did it cost? Token usage and money per model call, so a runaway loop shows up as a number Where did it first go wrong? Ordered steps with timestamps and parent links, so you can walk back from the bad output The last row is the one that matters most. Parent links and timestamps are what turn a transcript into something you can walk backwards through.
documents.s: What a useful agent trace records

documents.t: Traces show what happened, not whether it was right. You still need evaluations over whole runs. Snowflake notes that production traces are often the raw material for later evaluations, so the two work together. Full content is useful and risky. Tool arguments and results can contain personal data, credentials or customer records. The OpenTelemetry GenAI blog notes that content capture is opt-in for this reason. Redaction and retention need an explicit design, not a default that someone forgets to change. The standard is not final. The OpenTelemetry agent spans are marked as development status, and vendor dashboards may use different attribute names. Treat these conventions as the best current reference, not as settled.

We read the code paths in src/core/agent.ts, src/core/context-window.ts and src/utils/logger.ts at commit c969d77 on main. We did not run a live session, so the findings below are from code review. It helps to separate two kinds of observability. Live observability is what you can see while a run is happening. Persisted observability is what survives the run, so you can debug it afterwards. Mercury has some of the first and, from what we found, very little of the second. Live observability: Live tool events. Each tool start and finish is pushed to the interface with its duration. We did not find a persistent record of these events. A per-turn usage log. At the end of a turn, Mercury logs the provider, model, input, cached and output tokens, step count, tool-call count and elapsed time. The logger is pino, and its level is silent unless you run with --verbose or set LOG_LEVEL. Persisted observability: A turn-end tool trace. Each tool call becomes one line: the tool name, one summarised argument capped at 80 characters, and an outcome such as ok (12 lines) or an error message. These lines are written into the session so the next turn can see them. The trace is capped by line count. We did not find the per-turn usage log kept anywhere by default. Redaction of errors. Errors pass through a redactDeep helper before they are logged, so keys in provider errors are masked. Measured against the table above, we did not find the following: Call IDs, timestamps, durations or step indexes in the stored trace. You can read the order, but not the timing. A record of the tools available at each step. A parent link from a delegated task to the work it produced. Per-model-call token usage or cost. Usage is recorded per turn. A record of context changes, such as compaction and tool-result summarising. These appear to happen in memory. Full arguments. The stored trace caps them at 80 characters, so you often can't reconstruct exactly what was sent. An OpenTelemetry dependency in package.json, or an audit log. So the honest version is this. From the code we read, Mercury can show roughly what it did in the last turn. We did not find a way to show the first wrong step of a bad run from what it stores. This is the same gap our October 17 permissions post described from the other side: we can't audit access we don't record.

The smallest change that closes the biggest gap is to give every tool call a stable ID, a start time, a duration and a parent turn ID, and to write those to the session store instead of only the summary line. That alone lets you order a run, time it, and link each call to the turn that made it. Per-model-call token usage comes next, then content capture behind an explicit, off-by-default setting with redaction. We have not built this yet. It is a plan, not a shipped feature.

If you run agents in production, check three things before you need them. Can you tell which tool call came first in a bad run? Can you see how long each call took? Can you see what a single run cost, call by call? If the answer to any of these is no, that is a gap to close before the next failure. If you cannot reconstruct the run after it fails, a successful response can hide more than it proves.

The Hindu reported that CERT-In said on Thursday, 15 October, that AI agents "undergoing testing" had reached live systems of Indian organisations. Reuters carried the same government statement. The organisations could not detect the access on their own, the agency said. The agents read "business records, including personal data and confidential material", through credentials and connection settings exposed in application configuration, public code repositories and permissive cloud service roles. India Today reported the same data exposure. Business Standard reported that some model providers had told CERT-In their models reached live systems during testing. CERT-In did not name the AI providers or the affected organisations, so the public reports cannot say which agents were involved. None of the weaknesses were new. CERT-In said the AI found and exploited conventional weaknesses "faster, more exhaustively and at greater scale than human attackers."

Tencent said that AI agents used to evaluate third-party models on its cloud platform showed unintended web-browsing behaviour. Quartz reported that the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to pull data from Alibaba's Amap service. South China Morning Post put the window at 28 September to 8 October. Tencent calls the browsing unintended. The coverage we read does not explain how the agents reached Amap, but a browsing tool without a tight boundary can fetch data nobody meant it to.

In both reports the agent did not break a lock. It used authority that already existed and that nobody had scoped to the task. A credential in a config file, a cloud role that reads everything, and a browser that reaches any URL are all standing permission. Nothing in the system said where the agent's job ended.

We think four rules cover most of this. 1. Least privilege per task. An agent should start with no access and receive only the paths, commands and network destinations its current task needs. A summary task does not need write access to the repository. 2. Scopes that name a path and a mode. A scope should say what it covers and whether it allows reading, writing or running. Scopes must resolve symlinks before the check. Otherwise an approved directory can contain a link to ~/.ssh, and the check passes on the link while the read lands on the key. 3. Approvals for actions that leave the box. Reading a project file is routine. Pushing to a remote, deleting a directory, or running a package install that reaches the network should stop and wait for a human. The approval should show the exact command or path, not a summary. 4. Audit for every access. If a reviewer cannot answer "what did the agent read last Tuesday, and why", the permission model is incomplete. CERT-In's finding that the affected organisations could not detect the access is the strongest argument for this rule.

Mercury reads its permissions from ~/.mercury/permissions.yaml. The shape looks like this: ~/.mercury/permissions.yaml capabilities: filesystem: enabled: true scopes: - path: . read: true write: true shell: enabled: true cwdOnly: true blocked: - "sudo *" needsApproval: - "git push *" - "rm -rf *" The full options are in the permissions reference. The enforcement lives in src/capabilities/permissions.ts and src/core/execute-guard.ts. Several parts match the rules above: Blocked commands never run. The blocklist is checked against every segment of a chained command, so a blocked command cannot hide behind an allowed one such as echo. Shell commands take one of two lanes. A plain command whose binary is on the allowlist, and whose path arguments stay inside the working directory or a readable scope, runs without a prompt. Anything else goes to approval, where the user sees the exact string. Writes always prompt in Ask Me mode. Even when a scope covers the path, a write asks first. Reads inside a scope do not prompt. Symlinks and hard links are checked. A read that resolves outside the approved scopes is denied. A regular file with more than one hard link needs approval, because it may be an alias of a file outside every scope. Unattended bots fail closed. A bot has no one to ask, so an out-of-scope action is denied instead of waiting. Skill elevation is ignored in that mode, so a skill cannot widen what a bot may do. Two gaps remain. Scheduled tasks run in Allow All mode for their own turn, so shell commands run unless they hit the blocklist and scope prompts are skipped. That is the weakest point, and it looks like the situation CERT-In describes: a background run with broad access and nobody watching. Second, we found no per-access audit log in the permission code, so we treat auditability as missing, not done.
documents.s: How Mercury applies these rules today

documents.t: If you run any agent with tools, check three things this week: Search your repositories and config files for credentials. Rotate anything that was ever committed. Open your agent's permission file and remove scopes you do not use, especially home-directory and cloud-role grants. Give scheduled or unattended runs the narrowest scope that works, and review what they touched. Read the CERT-In advisory itself, not only the coverage.

Lines generated, commits, and pull request count are easy to count, and in the study they all went up. None of them shows whether the work is finished. An agent can add 800 lines, declare "done," and hand over code that does not build, was never tested, or breaks a nearby path. Each unverified change moves cost onto a reviewer, who has to rebuild context, find what was skipped, and decide whether the diff is safe. Review burden is a fair metric, but it needs care. More comments on a large change do not automatically mean worse code. What matters is the total burden a change creates: review time, requested changes, follow-up fixes, and how many people had to step in.

Did it verify its work? Which build, test, typecheck, or lint commands actually ran, and did they pass? "This should work" is not verification. How much review burden did it create? Look at review time, requested changes, follow-up fixes, and reviewer intervention. Did it catch failures before handing back? A failure the agent finds is cheaper than the same failure found by a reviewer. Did it satisfy the task, or only produce valid code? Code can compile and pass tests while still missing the requirement. Compiling is not correctness. Passing tests is not the requirement being met. The fourth question is the one most dashboards miss.
documents.s: Better questions for a coding agent

documents.t: Verification and human review overlap, but they are not the same thing. A reviewer should not have to discover that the project does not compile. A coding agent should handle: build checks tests type checking linting obvious runtime failures Human reviewers should spend their time on: architecture and maintainability security product requirements edge cases that automated checks cannot see The goal is not to remove human review. It is to stop sending reviewers failures a machine could have caught first.

Checks can be made meaningless. An agent may edit a failing test until it matches the new implementation, skip a verification step, or run only a narrow subset of tests that avoids the changed behaviour. The result is a green run that gives false confidence. No intent is needed for this to happen. The check simply stops testing what it claims to test. So verification should record what ran, what did not, and any change made to the checks themselves. A reviewer should be able to see that a test file was edited in the same change that made it pass. Passing checks can also be too narrow. A suite that does not cover the changed path proves little, and an agent that reports green without saying what was covered is overstating its result.
documents.s: Why verification is hard to get right

documents.t: Mercury Code treats completion as something that needs evidence. For implementation tasks, its completion contract requires a build, test, or typecheck command to run and exit cleanly after the last edit before the "Task complete" banner is allowed. If the task cannot finish, Mercury is designed to surface the named blocker and pause, instead of presenting unfinished work as successful. The completion architecture describes the details. That does not replace human code review. A passing suite cannot judge every architectural trade-off, security implication, or product requirement. The goal is narrower: obvious, machine-detectable failures should reach the agent before they reach the reviewer. For any coding agent, including Mercury, ask for three things with each change: The exact commands run and their results. The parts of the change that were not verified. Any blocker that stopped the task from finishing. If an agent cannot give you those, it has produced code, not finished work.

Primary (working paper, not yet peer-reviewed) Fiona Chen and James Stratton, Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production, Harvard University, job-market paper, August 2026. fion.ac/jellyfish.pdf Secondary Ars Technica, coverage of the same study. arstechnica.com

The model never decides what it's allowed to do. It can ask to run npm test or write a file, but the decision happens in ordinary code, outside the model, before anything touches your machine. Prompt injection can change what the model asks for. It can't change the code that answers. Everything below is that code.

Some commands are never run, no matter which mode you're in, who's asking or what you approved earlier. sudo is one. Recursive deletes of the root or home directory are another, in every spelling we've seen: rm -rf /, rm -fr ~, rm -rf /*, and their PowerShell equivalents like Remove-Item -Recurse -Force C:\ with the flags in any order. The list is matched against each segment of a command. Mercury splits pipelines, chains and command substitutions apart first, and anything it can't fully decompose is treated as needing approval, so wrapping a blocked command in $( ) or chaining it after && doesn't hide it. It's deliberately short. A blocklist can't make an agent safe on its own. What it can do is make sure the handful of truly unrecoverable commands are off the table even in the most permissive configuration.
documents.s: Layer 1: a blocklist nothing can override

documents.t: File access is scoped to folders, and each scope is either read-only or read-write. Out of the box Mercury can read and write in the directory it's working in, and nothing else. If a task needs another folder, Mercury asks, and you can grant it for that one request or permanently. A short list of read-only commands runs without a prompt, because asking every time someone types ls trains people to click Allow without reading: things like ls, cat, pwd, git status, git diff and git log, plus npm test and npm run. Scopes apply to shell commands too. If a command writes to a path outside your granted scopes, Mercury treats it the same as a file write outside them. Scopes are per channel and per role. If you share a Telegram group with Mercury in it, members can talk to the agent, but they can't install skills or widen what it's allowed to touch. Those decisions stay with admins.

When something isn't covered by a scope, Mercury asks. In the terminal you get an arrow-key prompt. On Telegram you get buttons. In the web dashboard you get a card with Allow, Always allow and Deny. The prompt says exactly what will happen: the command, the file path, the folder being requested. You choose the default per session: Ask Me prompts for every write and every command outside your scopes. Even when a scope already covers a folder, writes in Ask Me mode still prompt. Allow All runs without prompting, inside the blocklist. One detail we're careful about: Allow All applies to the session where you turned it on. A request that arrives from a different channel doesn't inherit your permissive setting. If you said "allow all" in your terminal, a message from a Telegram group is still checked as a Telegram message.

fetch_url is how Mercury reads the web, and it's a classic way to attack a self-hosted service: ask the agent to fetch http://192.168.1.1/admin, or a public URL that redirects to one, and it becomes a proxy into your home network. So every fetch is checked before it connects: Only http and https. The hostname is resolved, and if any address in the answer is private, loopback or link-local, the request is refused. A resolver that returns one public and one private address doesn't get the benefit of the doubt. The connection is pinned to the address that was checked. A hostile DNS server can't hand Mercury a public address for the check and a private one for the actual request. Redirects are followed manually and each hop is checked again, up to five. Responses are also size-capped, so a page can't flood the model's context.

Mercury Bots run unattended. A bot working at 3 a.m. has nobody to ask, so for bots the rule flips: anything not explicitly granted is denied. A missing permission isn't a question, it's a no. When you create a bot you pick a tier: Tier What it can do Read-only (the default) Browse, search, read files, message other bots. No commands, no writes. Builder Also create and edit files inside its granted folders. Still no shell. Operator Also run commands, restricted to its granted folders. The blocklist still applies. Full access Everything, including deleting files. Meant for automation you fully trust. Each bot also has its own folder scopes, its own daily token budget, and its own memory. A bot's tier is a ceiling: a crew member can't do more than the permissions it was given, regardless of what its lead asks it to do.

API keys live in ~/.mercury/.env, not in the main config file, and the logger redacts anything that looks like a key or token before it's written. The web dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 only, and its first password is randomly generated and shown once, so there's no default credential from the public source code that works on every install.
documents.s: Layer 6: secrets stay out of the conversation

documents.t: It's worth being direct about the limits. If you choose Allow All and give Mercury write access to your home folder, it can do a lot of damage inside the blocklist, because you told it it could. Skills from the community registry are not audited, and a skill's instructions become part of what the model reads, so review them before installing. And no permission system makes a model's judgement correct. Mercury can still decide to do the wrong thing. The permission layers decide whether it's allowed to, and give you the chance to say no.

documents.t: Mercury does the thinking. It holds the conversation, picks the model, decides the next step and asks you for permission. Optimus has no model of its own for deciding what to do. It is a tool provider: it gives Mercury eyes on the screen and hands on the mouse and keyboard, and it reports back what happened. That split comes from the plugin rules we set in ADR-025 for Mercury 1.4. Features that only some people want ship as plugins, and a broken plugin must never take Mercury down. Optimus is one Rust binary, mercury-optimus. Mercury starts it as a child process and talks to it over MCP: JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line, on stdin and stdout. Logs go to stderr so they can never corrupt the protocol. Mercury supervises it like any other out-of-process plugin: Every request has a timeout, and a hung plugin is killed and restarted. Crashes restart it with backoff from 1 second up to 60. More than five crashes in ten minutes turns the plugin off, with a message saying why. The child gets a minimal environment plus only the secrets its manifest declared. Install it from any chat: /plugins install optimus The catalog entry pins each platform build to a SHA-256 checksum. If the download doesn't match, Mercury says "Checksum mismatch" and installs nothing. Builds exist for macOS on Apple silicon and Intel, Windows x64, and Linux x64 and arm64.
documents.s: Mercury is the brain, Optimus is the hands

documents.t: Mercury shows the model seven tools, namespaced as optimus__look, optimus__act and so on: Tool What it does look Takes a screenshot of one display, or zooms into part of the last one act Runs up to 60 mouse and keyboard actions in a row, then looks again act_consequential The same as act, for steps that commit something: send, buy, delete, submit open Opens an app, a URL or a file windows Lists up to 30 visible windows, front first permissions Checks or requests the OS permissions Optimus needs listen Starts a voice session An action is one of click, double_click, triple_click, right_click, middle_click, move, drag, draw, mouse_down, mouse_up, type, paste, key, scroll or wait. There is no accessibility-tree tool and no OCR. Optimus works from pixels, like a person looking at the screen. That keeps it the same on every OS and in every app, including the ones with poor accessibility support.

look captures the display and fits the image into 1280×800, which is the size computer-use models are trained on. It is resized and sent as a JPEG at quality 80. A 2880×1800 Retina screen becomes 1280×800, and a 4K screen becomes 1280×720. The model never deals with Retina scaling or monitor layout. It clicks in the pixels of the screenshot it was given, and Optimus maps those back to real screen coordinates: plugins/optimus/companion/src/ops.rs let sx = self.x as f64 + px * self.w as f64 / self.img_w as f64; let sy = self.y as f64 + py * self.h as f64 / self.img_h as f64; Ok((sx.round() as i32, sy.round() as i32)) self.x and self.y are the monitor's origin, so a second display to the left, at x = -1920, works without the model knowing it exists. A coordinate outside the screenshot is an error rather than a guess. On Windows the process declares itself per-monitor DPI aware, so it sees real pixels everywhere. By default look captures the display under the pointer. When text is too small to read, the model can ask for a zoom: Optimus crops the full-resolution capture and fits that region into the same box, but coordinates still refer to the full screenshot. Each look also reports the display number, the mouse position and the active window and its title. On the Mercury side, images go only into what the model receives for that step. Logs, chat history and the learning engine never carry the base64. If the model can't take images, Mercury drops the picture and tells the model so, instead of failing.

Most input goes through the enigo crate. Optimus adds the parts that make it behave like a person and land reliably. The pointer glides. It follows a curve with a small random bow of 4 to 12 percent of the distance, eased in and out, and pauses briefly after arriving. In the default Natural pace a move takes 200 to 750 ms depending on distance. Fast pace cuts that to 70 to 220 ms. Typing is key by key. Natural pace waits 28 to 85 ms per key, a little longer after spaces and punctuation, and occasionally pauses as if thinking. One type action holds up to 3,000 characters. paste is there for long text: it saves your clipboard, pastes, and puts your clipboard back. Scrolling uses each OS's own API. macOS: pixel-precise CGEvent scroll events, spread over eased steps. Windows: SendInput with wheel events in small increments. Linux: whole notches, which is what X11 offers. open forgives app names. On macOS, "Chrome" finds "Google Chrome". If nothing matches, the reply lists the installed apps so the model can try again. Windows uses start; Linux uses xdg-open for files and URLs and gtk-launch for apps.

An early build taught us something uncomfortable. Its logs showed 29 act calls rejected because the model sent its steps in a shape Optimus couldn't read. Nothing happened on screen, and Mercury reported success anyway. A model that is told "your call went through" tends to believe the job is done. So every act reply now says exactly what it can vouch for: plugins/optimus/companion/src/ops.rs // "Sent", not "done": an input reaching the screen doesn't mean it had the intended effect. let mut text = if done.is_empty() { "Nothing was sent.".to_string() } else { format!("Sent: {}.", done.join("; ")) }; if let Some(s) = &stopped { text = format!("FAILED: {s} {text}"); } text.push_str(" This only means the input was sent: check the screenshot below to see whether it actually worked before saying so."); After the actions run, Optimus waits half a second for the screen to settle, takes a fresh screenshot and attaches it. Mercury's desktop guidance tells the model to look after each step, check it worked, and never claim it is finished without a fresh look. Actions in a batch run in order and stop at the first failure. The action parser is deliberately lenient. Models send actions as JSON strings, double-encoded JSON, single-quoted pseudo-JSON, inside code fences, or as numbered objects. Optimus accepts all of them, because rejecting a well-meant call is how the 29 failures happened.

Optimus can also be driven by voice. Press the talk key, ctrl+alt+m by default, and speak. A plain letter can't be the talk key, because it would fire while you type. The key is caught differently on each OS: macOS: an event tap that swallows the key, so it never reaches the app you're in. Windows: RegisterHotKey. Linux: an X11 key grab, registered with and without CapsLock and NumLock. There are two ways to run a voice session: Speech to speech. A realtime voice model listens and talks: OpenAI Realtime by default, or Azure, Grok, ElevenLabs, Qwen-Omni or Gemini Live. Your own Mercury model. Speech-to-text with Deepgram, AssemblyAI, ElevenLabs or Sarvam, then your Mercury model, then text-to-speech with Cartesia, ElevenLabs, MiniMax, Sarvam or Deepgram. Either way, the voice model doesn't control the computer itself. It has three tools: ask_mercury, answer_approval and end_conversation. When you ask for something, it hands the request to Mercury, which runs a normal turn with the same tools and rules as chat. If that turn takes longer than 90 seconds, Mercury says it will send the answer to the chat instead of keeping you waiting on the line. While Mercury works, Optimus speaks a short line for each step ("Opening Safari", "Typing") and plays a soft tick, quiet enough not to trigger its own microphone. With speakers, the mic is silenced while Mercury talks so it doesn't hear itself. With headphones you can turn on barge-in and interrupt by speaking. A session ends after 60 seconds of silence, or after 30 minutes. The status row at the bottom of Mercury's terminal shows what Optimus is doing: "🎙 Optimus listening", "🖱 Optimus working" or "🔇 Optimus muted". When the row is short on space, that segment is the last one dropped.

macOS charges Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions to the app that launched a process. If Mercury started Optimus from your terminal, the grant would go to Terminal and cover every script you ever run there. We didn't want that. So on macOS the plugin builds Optimus.app from its own binary. It has no Dock icon, and it signs the app with a certificate created on your Mac, with no Apple account involved. It launches through LaunchServices, so the permissions belong to Optimus alone. The plugin and the app talk over a Unix socket, readable only by you. Two details make this survive real use: Updates keep your permissions. macOS identifies a signed app by "this bundle id, signed by this certificate", not by the binary's hash. The certificate stays the same across updates, so you grant permissions once. Your keychain is never touched. Signing uses a throwaway keychain that exists only for the codesign call. The app is rebuilt only when the version or binary changes, or when codesign --verify fails. LaunchServices starts the app with launchd's environment, not Mercury's. So the first message on the socket hands over the variables the app needs, such as API keys for voice. If the app quits, for example after you change a permission, the plugin relaunches it and retries once.
documents.s: Why macOS gets its own app

documents.t: Optimus is off until you turn it on. Until then, every tool except permissions answers "Optimus is off". Install shows a warning before you confirm: "Controls this computer: it can see your screen, move the mouse and type, in any app." Committing steps ask first. act_consequential is the one tool marked as not read-only, so in Ask Me mode Mercury asks before each send, purchase, delete or submit. In Allow All mode it doesn't ask. That is the point of Allow All, so choose it knowingly. Voice approvals need your voice. When Mercury asks for approval during a voice session, a "yes" counts only if your own transcribed words contain one after the question. If the voice model claims you agreed and the transcript shows nothing, the answer is "Not approved". You can always stop it. Say "stop", or press the talk key while it works. Every screen action halts at its next step, new ones are refused for 8 seconds, and Mercury cancels the task. The stop words include "cancel", "ruko" and "bas". Grab the mouse. If you move the pointer more than 12 pixels from where Optimus left it, it stops and hands control back. It checks between actions, during glides, and every 12 typed characters. It shows when it's driving. A glowing ring follows the pointer with the label "Mercury · Optimus is driving". On macOS and Windows it is excluded from screen capture, so the model never sees it. On X11 it hides during capture. Some things are instructions, not walls. The tool descriptions tell the model never to type passwords, card numbers or 2FA codes, and to decline games with anti-cheat. Those are rules Mercury follows, not technical blocks, and the docs say so.

Platform What works What doesn't macOS 12+ Everything, after granting Accessibility and Screen Recording macOS asks again for Screen Recording about once a month Windows Everything, nothing to grant Windows running as administrator, such as Task Manager or installers Linux X11 Everything Paste needs xclip Linux Wayland Screenshots, through the desktop's screen-sharing prompt Input and the talk key reach only XWayland apps; no overlay The 0.4.8 release fixed a Linux crash at start, "error while loading shared libraries: libwayland-client.so.0", on machines without Wayland installed. Optimus now loads that library only when needed. A small launcher adds bundled copies of any system library the machine lacks, and system libraries win whenever they exist. It shipped as a plugin-only update, so nobody had to upgrade Mercury. The Optimus docs cover setup, every setting and the voice providers. The source is in the Mercury repository under plugins/optimus: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent Soul-driven AI agent with permission-hardened tools, token budgets, and multi-channel access. Runs 24/7 from CLI, Telegram or More. ai-agentai-assistantllm TypeScript3.8K388MIT

Until 1.3, typing mercury in a terminal could start a full copy of the agent in that terminal, even when a background copy was already running. That sounds harmless. It wasn't. Two copies meant two Telegram pollers fighting over one bot token, two schedulers firing the same routines, and bot work running on the same thread that draws your keystrokes. We wrote up the details in We were running Mercury twice and didn't know it. Now there is exactly one process that owns your channels, your bots and the web dashboard. It runs as a login service on macOS, Linux and Windows. When you type mercury, the terminal attaches to that process. Close the terminal and nothing stops. Open it again and you're back in under a second. Two smaller changes make this hold up in practice: The login service follows the install. If you move from npm to the standalone binary, or from stable to the dev channel, Mercury notices that the service still points at the old install and re-points it. Before this, an old daemon could keep resurrecting itself on every login and hold the web port. Lag is now a number. /api/health reports how long the event loop has stalled in the last ten seconds, and stalls over 250 ms are logged. "It feels slow" turns into something we can actually look at.
documents.s: One runtime, and the terminal is just a window

documents.t: Mercury Bots shipped in 1.3.0. After a couple of weeks of running a real fleet we looked at the journals and didn't love what we saw: routines that produced status notes about other status notes, turns that read 750,000 tokens of context to decide nothing needed doing, and finished output buried somewhere under ~/.mercury. So 1.3 judges a bot run by what it did, not by what it said. Every run gets an outcome computed from the tool trace: it delivered a file, it took an action, it delegated, it replied, or it did nothing. A scheduled routine that does nothing three times in a row cools down for a few hours and then resumes by itself. Bots stay online. They just stop burning tokens on busywork. Finished work goes somewhere you can find it: ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot name>/, with final results at the top and work in progress under work/. There's a daily token budget per bot (5M by default) and per fleet, with a warning at 80%. Fleets got real coordination too. A lead bot can hand typed tasks to several crew members at once and gets woken up once, with a summary, when they're all done. A lead's standard job can be written down as a pipeline in bot.yaml, so "research, draft, fact-check, package" runs without the lead having to babysit each step.
documents.s: Bots that do work instead of writing about work

documents.t: A lot of you run Mercury on a home server and talk to it from Telegram, so 1.3 makes Telegram a first-class control surface. /bots shows the roster with Stop, Start and Run buttons for each bot. When a bot finishes a task you asked for from your phone, the result arrives as an attached file, not a path on a machine you can't see. You can create a bot from Telegram too: describe its persona in a message, then pick its permissions, whether it works alone or leads a crew, and its budget, all with buttons.

The npm package now requires Node.js 22. The standalone binaries carry their own runtime, so if you installed with the one-line installer, nothing changes for you. If you're on npm, mercury upgrade checks your Node version before it touches anything, and the package refuses to install on an older Node with a readable message instead of installing something that won't start. We also moved the terminal UI to Ink 8 with four patches of our own. The most visible one fixes a problem where long replies stamped copies of themselves into your scrollback on every repaint. The patches live in a public fork and we're working on getting them upstream.
documents.s: Node 22 and a patched terminal renderer

documents.t: The 1.3 line had more point releases than we'd like, from 1.3.2 to 1.3.8 in three days. Each one fixed something real: the first-run setup could quit at its first menu, /code didn't work from the default launch, the Windows installer failed on stock PowerShell 5.1, and the Linux binary crashed on CPUs without AVX2. The Windows and AVX2 reports came from people who took the time to dig in and tell us exactly what they saw. Thank you. Every one of those now has a test that would have caught it: the setup wizard runs under a real pseudo-terminal in CI, the Windows installer runs under PowerShell 5.1, and the Linux installer is tested on a CPU that pretends to lack AVX2.
documents.s: The hotfixes, and what we learned from them

documents.t: # standalone binary (macOS / Linux) curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh # npm, on Node.js 22+ npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Or just run mercury upgrade. If you're already on the latest version it now tells you so and does nothing, which is how it should have worked from the start. Your ~/.mercury folder (config, memory, bots, Telegram pairing) carries over untouched. On first start, Mercury moves old bot outputs into ~/Documents/Mercury/ and re-points your login service if it needs to. If something breaks, open an issue or find us on Discord. We read everything. The code, the issue tracker and every release live here: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent Soul-driven AI agent with permission-hardened tools, token budgets, and multi-channel access. Runs 24/7 from CLI, Telegram or More. ai-agentai-assistantllm TypeScript3.8K388MIT

WhatsApp calling needs a WhatsApp protocol stack, a realtime audio pipeline and a handful of voice providers. Computer control needs screen capture, synthetic input and, on macOS, its own signed app bundle. Many people who run Mercury want neither. Putting both into the single Mercury binary would have made the download bigger for everyone and put more native code into every install. So we wrote down a rule in ADR-025: features only some people want ship as plugins, and a bad plugin must never take Mercury down with it. The work started in #203. You manage plugins from any chat: /plugins install whatsapp /plugins disable whatsapp /plugins update /plugins rollback whatsapp /plugins uninstall whatsapp The same commands work in a shell as mercury plugins ..., and in the dashboard under Configure, then Plugins. The catalog lives at https://mercuryagent.sh/plugins/catalog.json. Every entry pins a version to a SHA-256 checksum, and Mercury checks the download against it before installing anything.

Both official plugins are out-of-process. Each is a separate Rust program that Mercury starts and talks to over stdio using MCP, plus a small channel extension for chat and voice. That boundary does most of the work: A crash is the plugin's problem. Mercury restarts it. After five failures in a row, or too many crashes, the plugin is turned off and you get a message saying why. It gets only what it declared. The manifest lists the network hosts a plugin may reach and the secrets it may read. Install shows you that list before you confirm. A plugin that controls the computer carries a new permissions.desktop flag, and /plugins info shows it as a warning. It can't widen access. For a chat channel, Mercury decides who gets through, not the plugin. Unknown numbers are dropped before they reach the agent. Changes are reversible. The previous version is kept, so /plugins rollback brings it back with its old settings. If Mercury fails to start twice right after a plugin change, it turns that plugin off. mercury start --safe-mode starts with every plugin off. Plugins also borrow Mercury's own AI providers. If you already set up OpenAI in Mercury, both plugins' voice features use that key. You don't paste it again. Keys a plugin needs for itself, such as a Gemini or Deepgram key, are stored with Mercury's keys and shared with any other plugin that declares them. The plugin menu took two rounds. In the first version, the main settings sat behind a "Change a setting" entry, the voice section forced you through every field, yes/no questions didn't say what each answer meant, and picking a voice engine didn't lead you to the key it needed. Now /plugins whatsapp lists every setting with its current value. A yes/no setting says what each answer does ("On: Mercury picks up when you call it"). Change the voice engine to Gemini and Mercury asks for the Gemini key straight away. Every question has a way back. The plugin API is now at 1.2. The main addition is that a tool can return images to the model, which Optimus needs for screenshots. The images go to the model with that one tool result and are never written to chat history, logs or memory. The author guide covers the rest.
documents.s: How a plugin is kept at arm's length

documents.t: The WhatsApp plugin runs Mercury on a spare number as a linked device, the same way WhatsApp Web connects. You chat with it from your own number. One warning up front: this uses an unofficial, reverse-engineered protocol. A WhatsApp update can break it, and automated use can get a number restricted. Link a number you can afford to lose, not your main one. Text works the way you'd expect. Photos and PDFs you send are passed to the model if it accepts them, and voice notes are transcribed with your OpenAI provider. Two access levels decide how much Mercury can do in the chat. General, the default, is conversation only, with no tools, files or memory. Extended is the full agent. Calls are where it gets useful. You can ring the spare number while you're out and ask Mercury to look something up, check on a task, or draft a reply. It can also ring you. Say "call me at 9pm about the deploy" in any chat, or on a call. The time is parsed in code, not by a model, and confirmed back to you as an exact time. If you miss the call, it tries once more five minutes later and then sends a message. "Call me when it's done" means it does the work first and then calls. Mercury won't call more than four times an hour by default, so a task stuck in a loop can't keep ringing your phone. During a call, Mercury uses its tools as usual and keeps you posted while it works. Anything that needs approval is asked out loud and posted in the chat at the same moment, and whichever answer arrives first wins. A spoken yes only counts if your own transcribed words say yes, and it never turns into "always". Mercury doesn't read links aloud. It sends them to the chat and tells you it did. OpenAI Realtime is the default voice engine, and the one we recommend for the best calls. Gemini Live, Grok Voice, ElevenLabs, Azure, Qwen-Omni, or your own Mercury model with separate speech-to-text and text-to-speech providers all work too. Setup only asks about the engine if you don't have an OpenAI provider already. The full setup is in the WhatsApp docs.
documents.s: WhatsApp: it can call you, or listen to you on the go

documents.t: Optimus is the big one. You ask, and Mercury does it on your screen, in whatever app you use. How it sees. The look tool takes a screenshot of the display the mouse is on, scaled to fit 1280 by 800, and can zoom into part of it. Screenshots are taken only when Mercury looks or acts. Nothing captures in the background. How it acts. We wanted you to be able to follow what it's doing. In the default Natural pace, the pointer glides along a gentle curve, scrolling arrives in small steps, and text is typed key by key with an uneven rhythm. Typing key by key means it works in every editor, and paste is only a fallback. While it drives, a ring and the label "Mercury is driving" follow the pointer. On macOS and Windows that overlay is excluded from capture, so it never shows up in Optimus's own screenshots. How it stays honest. This was the hardest part. The logs from one early build showed 29 act calls rejected because the model sent its steps in a shape Optimus couldn't read. Nothing happened on screen, and Mercury reported success anyway. Optimus now reads steps in every shape we've seen models send. Every step reports "Sent", meaning the input reached the screen, not "done", and returns a fresh screenshot. Failures start with FAILED. Mercury is told to look again and confirm the result before it says a task is finished. Optimus also records every step that failed or was stopped. In a voice session, the answer is checked against that record before you hear it, so a failed task is reported as failed. How you stay in control. Optimus does nothing until you turn on "Control this computer" in setup. Ordinary, reversible steps run straight away. The step that submits, sends, posts, pays, deletes, installs or changes a setting goes through a separate tool that needs your approval. Move the mouse while it works and it stops at the next step and hands control back. It's told never to type passwords, card numbers or 2FA codes. It asks you to do that part. Press the talk key (ctrl+alt+m by default, Control+Option+M on a Mac), hear a chime, and talk. Mercury answers out loud and narrates each step as it happens. A quiet tick-tock plays while it works. Say "stop", or press the talk key while it's working, and every action halts at once. The mute key (ctrl+alt+shift+m) stops listening without stopping the work, and nothing you say is sent while muted. After 60 seconds of silence with nothing running, the mic closes by itself. The terminal status bar shows when Optimus is listening, working or muted. Voice settings are shared with the WhatsApp plugin, so a key you added there works here too. Optimus runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and no Apple Developer ID is involved. On macOS, privacy permissions are charged to the app that launched a process, so if Optimus ran under your terminal, the grant would cover every script that terminal runs. Instead, Optimus builds its own Optimus.app and signs it with a certificate made on your Mac. You grant it Accessibility, Screen Recording and Microphone once, and because the certificate stays the same, the grants survive updates. On Windows there's nothing to grant, though windows running as administrator can't be controlled. On Linux, X11 gets full control. Wayland is limited for now: input and the talk key reach only XWayland apps. The Optimus docs cover every setting and permission.

A built-in web_search tool, free and keyless. In testing, asking for the news on a WhatsApp call made zero tool calls, partly because Mercury had no search tool to call. Mercury always knows it comes from Cosmic Stack. The dashboard model picker shows plain-language names, every local Ollama model and ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan models, and has a reasoning picker. Fixes for ChatGPT OAuth turns failing after a tool call, memory search failing on long messages, and the dashboard on the Windows standalone binary (found and fixed by @farena-ai in #189). The 1.3.9 fix, where mercury doctor restarts the daemon when your configuration changed, is folded in.

The first screen looks for Mercury on your computer. If it finds one, it connects. If it doesn't, Install Mercury here downloads the release for your machine, checks it against the release's SHA-256 checksums, and runs it as a service. Connect elsewhere adds a Mercury on another machine, and you can keep several connections and switch between them. Inside are chat, a coding workspace per project, research with live progress, bots and their results inbox, and notifications when something needs you. Install & first run covers the details, and a tour of Mercury Desktop walks through every part of it. One honest caveat: this first release isn't code-signed with an Apple or Windows certificate. macOS and Windows ask once before the first launch, and the download page shows the clicks. Updates are a different matter. Each one is signed with Mercury's update key and checked before it installs.

An app that connects to a Mercury somewhere else made us look hard at how remote access worked, and it wasn't good enough. Mercury listens only on 127.0.0.1, so a remote device reaches it through a tunnel or proxy on the same machine. Those connect from 127.0.0.1 too, and several "this computer only" checks trusted that address. Through a tunnel, a device with a token could do what you can do at the keyboard, including open a shell. In 1.5.0, a request counts as local only when it comes from 127.0.0.1 with no proxy headers and a localhost host. Everything else is remote, and remote devices work under your rules: A new device needs your approval. It shows a 5-character code, and you answer approve K7Q2M from Telegram or WhatsApp, from the terminal, or in Mercury Desktop on your computer. Sensitive actions from a remote device ask you each time: the terminal (off for remote devices unless you turn it on), Allow All, the workspace folder, powerful bots, plugins, channel tokens, restarts and the password. Devices unused for 30 days are signed out, revoking one cuts its open connections, and a device connecting from a new address tells you. /server in the terminal, or mercury server in a shell, manages all of it, and mercury doctor --security checks your setup. The design is in ADR-035, and Remote access & security explains how to use it.
documents.s: Other devices now need your approval

documents.t: Updating used to mean mercury upgrade, which removed the npm package before installing the new one, kept no backup, and didn't check that the new version started. Now an update, from the app or the terminal, does this: Waits for running work to finish, for up to 10 minutes. Downloads the new version, resuming if the connection drops, and checks its checksums. Backs up the current program and Mercury's settings. Stops Mercury, installs, starts it, and waits for it to answer as the new version. If it doesn't, puts the old version and settings back and starts that. We ran this for real on a test install before the release. Updating 1.4.1 to the published 1.4.2 worked and Mercury was back in about four seconds. The first attempt, though, rolled back: the 1.4.2 binary reports an empty version on its health endpoint, so the check never matched. The updater now asks the installed program for its version when that happens. A deliberately broken release also kept Mercury offline for the full 90-second wait, so the updater now notices a crashed start and rolls back in about 15 seconds. Mercury Desktop shows an Update button at the top right, like Chrome's. It gets more noticeable the longer an update waits, and one panel covers the app and every server it connects to. You can read what's new before you update. When an update has to happen, for a security fix, the app says so on a screen you can only get past by ticking a short checklist, and only for a while. Updating Mercury has the whole picture.

Research you can watch. A plan you can edit, every source read or failed with the reason, and a report even when a run is cut short. Reports export as PDF or Word. Files in one place. What Mercury makes goes in ~/mercury-artifacts, one folder per chat. MCP servers. Mercury can use tools from Model Context Protocol servers, and every MCP call asks first in Ask Me mode. See MCP Servers. Bots 2.0. Each run reports, says there was nothing new, or says it failed, and results wait in an inbox. Update with mercury upgrade, or download Mercury Desktop and let it update your Mercury for you. cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent Soul-driven AI agent with permission-hardened tools, token budgets, and multi-channel access. A bot is a folder. Each one lives at ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ and holds four files: bot.yaml sets its identity, model, schedules and fleet position. persona.md holds its character and standing instructions. permissions.yaml is the only file that decides what it may touch. .env holds credentials that only this bot can read. Bots form fleets. A lead bot owns a goal and has a crew of specialists, and crews can have their own crews. A typical fleet is a lead that plans a weekly report, a researcher, a writer and a fact-checker. Each one can run on a different model from a different provider, because the model is a per-bot setting. We studied Hermes Agent and OpenClaw closely before writing the first line. Our design notes credit both, and you can read them in BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md. The first runtime landed on September 16: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent69417f0 feat(bots): P0 — persistent persona-scoped bot runtime Implements the Mercury Bots P0 milestone per BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md and ADR-012: multiple persistent persona-scoped agents (own character, model, scoped memory, tool permissions) running as in-process coroutines that never touch Agent.processQueue, fail-closed and near-zero-intera… hotheadhacker committed Sep 16, 202617 files changed+2.7K −1 src/bots/bot-manager.ts+506 −0 src/bots/bot-manager.test.ts+359 −0 BOTS-ARCHITECTURE.md+334 −0 src/bots/store.ts+315 −0 src/bots/store.test.ts+263 −0

The whole fleet runs inside the Mercury daemon, the background service that starts when you log in. There is no process per bot and no thread per bot. A bot turn is asynchronous work in the same Node.js process, scheduled through one lane with a concurrency cap. That choice comes from the hardware our users run Mercury on: a Raspberry Pi, a small VPS, or a phone under Termux. A separate Node.js process costs tens of megabytes before it does anything, and a fleet of fifteen bots should not need fifteen of them. FlowchartOne process, many botsCopy sourceExpand Everything here runs inside the Mercury daemon on your machine. The terminal, the web dashboard and Telegram only attach to it. Work is written to the queue before the trigger is acknowledged, so a crash between "accepted" and "running" loses nothing. Jobs are claimed on a lease. If the daemon dies mid-turn, the lease expires and the job runs again. Failures are typed. A provider timeout is retried with backoff, and a permission denial goes straight to a dead-letter queue you can inspect and replay. The queue uses SQLite when the platform has it and falls back to a JSON file store when it doesn't, so it works on the same devices as the rest of Mercury. We learned the hard way that "one process" has to mean exactly one. Until a fix earlier this month, the launcher could start a second full copy of the runtime, and both copies ran the fleet. We wrote that story up in We were running Mercury twice and didn't know it.

An agent that runs at 3 a.m. can't wait for you to tap "Allow". Most products in this space solve that with approval prompts that time out, or with a second model that reviews actions. We chose a stricter rule. A bot has no ask handler at all. Anything granted in its permissions.yaml runs without a prompt, and everything else is denied and written to the journal: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ 705f6c0View on GitHub ↗ src/bots/registry-factory.ts · L114–123 // Fail-closed core: no ask handler, no allow-all, non-internal context. // Granted scopes apply without prompting; everything else denies. pm.setAutoApproveAll(false); pm.setFailClosed(true); pm.setCurrentContext('bot', deps.botId); // Relative paths and shell commands resolve inside the bot's workspace, // never the daemon's cwd (a bot with a wide grant wrote "sandbox/…" files // into whatever repo the daemon happened to be started from). registry.setCwd(deps.sandbox?.workspace ?? process.cwd()); At 705f6c0 · feat(bots): budgets by default, routine gate, 3-strike pause, visible deliverables (ADR-020) · Oct 10, 2026 Three details matter here: No allow-all for bots. A bot can never inherit the "Allow All" mode you might switch on in your own session, and a literal * in a bot's command allowlist is dropped. The deny list wins. The global blocklist and the bot's own blocked commands always beat an allowlist entry. The workspace is the default. Relative paths and shell commands resolve inside the bot's own workspace, never inside whatever directory the daemon was started from. We added that after a bot with a wide grant wrote its sandbox files into a real repository. You choose a permission tier when you create the bot, and the tier is written out as a complete permissions.yaml. If a bot keeps getting denied, the journal shows you exactly which action was refused, and you widen the grant on purpose.
documents.s: Bots never ask, they fail closed

documents.t: In early October we audited two real fleets that had been running for eleven days. The numbers were bad enough that we published them in the decision record: Bots across two fleets 13 Runs in eleven days ≈1,150 Input tokens 617M Lead runs that failed 38% Source: ADR-020 in DECISIONS.md, an audit of two production fleets before turn governance shipped. The median bot turn read 750,000 tokens of context, and one turn read 6.6 million. There was no cap on a single turn and no context compaction, so every step re-sent every earlier tool result. Tokens in a single bot turn, before governanceMeasured across the same two fleets. The dashed line is the per-turn cap that ships today. Cap per turn now · 300K tokens Median turn750K tokensMedian turn: 750K tokens. Half of all turns read more context than this. Largest turn6.6M tokensLargest turn: 6.6M tokens. One run, with no per-turn cap and no compaction. View as table Measure Value Note Median turn 750,000 tokens Half of all turns read more context than this. Largest turn 6,600,000 tokens One run, with no per-turn cap and no compaction. Cap per turn now 300,000 tokens Reference line Source: ADR-020, DECISIONS.md. The cap is DEFAULT_TURN_LIMITS in src/bots/bot-turn.ts. The fix went in as hard limits, at three levels: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ fad01f2View on GitHub ↗ src/bots/bot-turn.ts · L70–76 export const DEFAULT_TURN_LIMITS: BotTurnLimits = { maxTokensPerTurn: 300_000, maxTurnMinutes: 20, keepRecentToolResults: 8, maxToolResultChars: 24_000, sharedWrites: { softFiles: 2, softBytes: 32 * 1024, hardFiles: 6, hardBytes: 128 * 1024 }, }; At fad01f2 · feat(bots): typed tasks with fan-in, pipelines as data, continuity and memory (ADR-021) · Oct 10, 2026 Per turn: 300,000 tokens or 20 minutes, whichever comes first. Context is compacted on every step: the newest eight tool results stay verbatim, and older ones become short stubs the bot can re-fetch if it needs them. Per bot, per day: 5 million tokens by default. You get a warning at 80%. Setting the budget to 0 is the only way to make a bot unlimited. Per fleet, per day: 20 million tokens by default. Hitting it pauses every bot until midnight, so one runaway bot can't spend the day's allowance for the others. All three are pauses, not failures. A bot that hits its daily cap picks up its queued work the next day. /bots cost shows where the tokens went, by fleet and by bot. We show tokens rather than money on purpose: provider prices change too often for a currency figure to stay correct. cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent705f6c0 feat(bots): budgets by default, routine gate, 3-strike pause, visible deliverables (ADR-020) Manager and surfaces for the governed turn: - Daily caps on by default: per bot (suggestedDailyTokenBudget, 5M; 0 = unlimited via `/bots budget <id> none`) and per fleet (bots.fleetDailyTokenBudget, 20M). 80% warns once a day. - Routine gate: a cron tick is skipped — busy / too_… Salman Qureshi committed Oct 10, 202618 files changed+811 −104 src/bots/bot-manager.ts+244 −62 src/bots/bot-manager.test.ts+173 −3 src/bots/store.ts+132 −5 src/core/commands/bots-command.ts+78 −10 src/bots/journal.ts+30 −3

documents.t: The same audit found a subtler problem. Bots were busy, but much of what they produced was notes about earlier runs: "records", "receipts" and status files about other status files. Files in the fleet-shared folder after eleven days637 files in total Notes about earlier runs372 filesNotes about earlier runs: 372 files. Records, receipts and status files, not finished work. Everything else265 filesEverything else: 265 files. Data and drafts other bots actually consumed. View as table Measure Value Note Notes about earlier runs 372 files Records, receipts and status files, not finished work. Everything else 265 files Data and drafts other bots actually consumed. Source: ADR-020, DECISIONS.md. A model that is told to report its progress will report progress. So Mercury no longer asks the model whether it did anything. It reads the tool trace of the run and decides: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ fad01f2View on GitHub ↗ src/bots/bot-turn.ts · L639–657 export function computeOutcome(input: { trace: BotToolTraceEntry[]; deliveries: string[]; expects: BotExpectedOutcome; text: string; sandbox: { workspace: string; shared: string }; }): BotOutcome { if (input.deliveries.length > 0) return 'deliverable'; const roots = [input.sandbox.workspace, input.sandbox.shared]; for (const t of input.trace) { if (!t.ok) continue; if (ACTION_TOOLS.has(t.name)) return 'action'; if (FILE_WRITE_TOOLS.has(t.name) && t.arg && !insideAny(t.arg, roots)) return 'action'; if (t.name === 'run_command' && t.arg && !isReadOnlyCommand(t.arg)) return 'action'; } if (input.trace.some((t) => t.ok && t.name === 'bot_send' && t.task)) return 'delegated'; if (input.expects === 'message' && input.text.trim().length > 0) return 'message'; return 'none'; } At fad01f2 · feat(bots): typed tasks with fan-in, pipelines as data, continuity and memory (ADR-021) · Oct 10, 2026 A run produced a deliverable if it handed over a finished file, or an action if it changed something outside its own sandbox or ran a command that isn't read-only. It delegated if it sent a typed task to another bot, and it produced a message if a reply was what the trigger asked for. Anything else is none. Writing notes into its own sandbox doesn't count, and the journal flags any reply that claims work the trace doesn't show. A scheduled run that ends at none gets one nudge: deliver something, do the action, or say plainly that there was nothing to do. If a routine comes back empty three times in a row, it cools down for six hours, then twelve, up to a day, and then resumes by itself. Routine ticks also pass through a gate before they cost anything: cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent@ 8b2078bView on GitHub ↗ src/bots/bot-manager.ts · L404–425 // Routine gate (ADR-020): a cron tick is an opportunity, not an order. // It is skipped — never stacked — when the bot is still busy, when the // routine ran too recently, or when the routine was paused for // producing nothing. The next tick tries again. if (job.trigger === 'cron') { const key = job.routineId ?? `bot:${botId}:cron`; const routineState = this.store.readRoutineState(botId); const pausedEntry = routineState.paused[key]; if (pausedEntry) { const until = pausedEntry.until ? Date.parse(pausedEntry.until) : Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY; if (Date.now() < until) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'routine_paused' }; // Cooldown over: the routine is live again with a clean streak (liveness contract). delete routineState.paused[key]; delete routineState.noOutcomeStreak[key]; this.store.writeRoutineState(botId, routineState); logger.info({ botId, routineKey: key }, 'Bot routine cooldown over — resuming'); } if (queue.length > 0 || (this.running.get(botId)?.size ?? 0) > 0) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'busy' }; const lastEnd = this.routineLastEnd.get(key); const minGapMs = this.routineConfig(manifest, key).minIntervalMinutes * 60_000; if (lastEnd !== undefined && Date.now() - lastEnd < minGapMs) return { jobId: '', accepted: false, reasonCode: 'too_soon' }; } At 8b2078b · fix(providers): bots always get a provider that works; rejected keys are skipped; doctor flags malformed keys (1.3.3) · Oct 12, 2026 FlowchartThe life of a scheduled routineCopy sourceExpand A tick is an opportunity, not an order. Skipped ticks cost no tokens, and a cooled-down routine resumes by itself. The point is that the bot stays alive. "Always-on" doesn't mean calling a model all day. It means idle between runs, never silently dead, and never spending money to tell you it had nothing to do.

documents.t: When a lead delegated to five crew members, it used to get five free-text emails and run five full turns to read them. Now delegation is data. A task has a goal, acceptance criteria, an assignee, a status and a typed result. Tasks travel in batches with a wake policy and a deadline, and the lead is woken once, with a digest, when the batch is done: SequenceA lead delegates a batch and wakes up onceCopy sourceExpand The crew works in parallel. The lead spends one turn to dispatch and one to synthesise, however many crew members there are. A fleet's standard job can be written down as a pipeline in bot.yaml. Stages chain themselves, each one gets the previous stage's result, and the lead isn't woken between stages at all. A five-member crew now costs the lead one turn to dispatch and one to synthesise. Bots also remember, without writing status files. Every prompt carries the bot's last five journal rows and its own short working note. After a run that produced something, the bot's model extracts up to three durable facts into that bot's private memory namespace. cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agentfad01f2 feat(bots): typed tasks with fan-in, pipelines as data, continuity and memory (ADR-021) - Tasks (src/bots/tasks.ts): durable, typed delegated work — requester, assignee, goal, acceptance, stage, status, typed result — grouped in batches with a wake policy (all | each) and a deadline (120 min). Deduplicated by open goal, pruned after 7 days. - Fan-in: fleet_delegate… Salman Qureshi committed Oct 10, 202617 files changed+1.1K −15 src/bots/fleet-tasks.test.ts+272 −0 src/bots/bot-manager.ts+239 −11 src/bots/tasks.ts+220 −0 src/bots/memory-extract.ts+88 −0 src/bots/tools/fleet-tasks.ts+83 −0

documents.t: Finished work goes to ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot name>/, with final results at the top and crew work under work/. It's a normal folder in your Documents directory, not a hidden one under ~/.mercury, and nothing in it is deleted automatically. Most people run their fleet from a phone, so Telegram is a full control surface. /bots shows the roster with Stop, Start and Run buttons. documents.t: Here is the same set of questions asked of all six products. Where a vendor hasn't published an answer, we say so instead of guessing.
