Slack for Team Bots ChatGPT apps; Slack and Teams when an admin enables them Muse app, web and WhatsApp 33 listed in the docs 20+ listed in the gateway docs Price Free; you pay your model provider Included in SuperGrok and Cursor plans One dot included with Pro or Business Premium Free tier, $20 or $100 a month Free; no paid tier Free; optional Nous Portal subscription GitHub stars 3,421 Not open source Not open source Not open source 392,171 254,339 ✓ Yes◐ Partly or opt-in✕ No? Not documented Checked October 16, 2026. Closed products change quickly; follow the sources for current terms.

Honesty cuts both ways, so here is where each of them beats us today. A computer of their own. Grok Bot, dots and Muse give your agents a cloud computer with a real browser they can drive, which you can watch and take over. The work continues with your laptop closed. A Mercury fleet runs where you install it. If that machine sleeps, the fleet sleeps, which is why many of our users run it on a home server or a small VPS. Reach. OpenClaw lists 33 chat channels and Hermes lists more than 20. Our tappable fleet controls exist on Telegram today. Discord and Slack get the same commands as text. Scale. OpenClaw and Hermes have far larger communities, a larger skills ecosystem and many more people finding their edge cases. Consumer polish. Muse pays for things with single-use cards and asks before each purchase. dots connects to a much larger catalogue of apps than we do. Every project in this table is candid about the same unsolved problem. Meta writes that "prompt injection remains an open problem in the industry." The system card for GPT-6 Astra, the model behind dots, reports test runs in which the agent overstepped its authorisation. Hermes Agent's own security policy says that "the only security boundary against an adversarial LLM is the operating system." OpenClaw's skills registry had a wave of malicious uploads in February. Our answer isn't that Mercury is immune. It's that a bot can only do what one file says it may, that it spends inside a budget it can't raise, and that every run leaves a record you can read.

Mercury is MIT-licensed, and all of this is in the open. On first launch the app looks for Mercury on this computer. If one is running, it connects with the machine's local token and you're in. If there isn't one, Install Mercury here downloads the release for your CPU, checks it against the release's SHA-256 checksums, and runs it as a login service, so it's there after a restart. There's no terminal and no Node.js to install. Connect elsewhere takes the address of a Mercury on another machine. The app asks that Mercury for a device token, and the request waits for the owner: a 5-character code arrives on your Telegram or WhatsApp, or shows in /server on that machine, and you approve it there. The app never sees a password, and you can revoke it from either side. Remote access & security explains the rules.
documents.s: The first screen: install here, or connect elsewhere

documents.t: Every connection you add stays in the app. The top bar shows which Mercury this window is talking to and its version. Click it to switch, between your laptop's Mercury and the one on the VPS, for example. Tokens for remote connections live in the operating system's keychain, not in a settings file. Each connection is checked for updates on its own. If the server in the cupboard is a version behind, the Update button in the top right says so, and the updates panel has a row for the app and one per server. Update server starts the update on that machine. From a remote device the owner approves it first, like any other sensitive action. The server waits for running work to finish, backs up, installs, and checks the new version starts. If it doesn't, the old one comes back on its own. Settings → About has Check for updates, which asks the app and every server at once, and Update everything when there's more than one to do. Updating Mercury has the details.

Chat is where most time goes, so it got the most work. Commands and skills in the composer. Type / for commands and # for skills, from the same catalog the terminal uses, filtered to the ones that make sense in the app. A picked command becomes a chip you can see before you send. Attachments. Photos and PDFs go straight into the conversation. Ask Me or Allow All, shown the same way everywhere, so you always know whether Mercury will stop and ask before it acts. Saved chats open from a bookmark beside search. Honest waiting. A server runs one turn at a time. If another chat is mid-reply, yours says Waiting and names the chat it's waiting for, instead of pretending to think. You can open that chat or ask for yours to go first.

Ask for research and you get one visible run instead of a long silence. Mercury proposes a plan you can approve or edit. While it works, a checklist shows each step, every source it read, and the ones that failed with the reason, such as a timeout or a page that refused it. You can say Write the report now at any point. If a run is cut short, you still get a report built from what it found, with what's missing listed at the end. Reports open in the app, export as PDF or Word, and show each source's site icon. Like everything Mercury makes, the files land in ~/mercury-artifacts, one folder per chat, not loose in your home folder. The Artifacts view lists them.

Code is a workspace per project. Pick a folder and the chat in that project works in programming mode, with a panel beside it for the file tree, the git status of your changes, and the diff of any file you click. It's for reading along while Mercury works, not a replacement for your editor.

Bots are Mercury instances with their own persona, tools and sandbox that run on a schedule or on demand. The app is now where you manage them: An inbox of results. Every run closes with a report: what it did, what it made, and what it needs from you. Create and edit bots in words. Describe the job and the persona builder drafts it, or let Mercury decide the whole setup. Fleets. Design the crew for a lead bot yourself, or let Mercury propose one. Questions mid-run. When a bot needs permission, the question appears with Allow once, Always allow and Deny, instead of the run failing.

Brain shows what Mercury knows. Memories lists what it has learned about you and how you work, and you can correct anything that's wrong. People shows the people it knows from your conversations. Map groups your notes into topics, and Graph shows how people and notes connect.

Plugins install from Plugins, with their setup on one page. With the Optimus plugin, Mercury can use your computer, by chat or out loud. When Optimus is listening or speaking, a small capsule drops from the top centre of the screen, from the notch on Macs that have one. It stays above full-screen apps without stealing focus. The microphone picker, the permission checks and a live test sit at the top of the plugin page on every OS.

This first release isn't code-signed with an Apple or Windows certificate, so a downloaded installer asks once before the first launch. The download page shows the clicks. On a Mac you can skip that: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install-desktop.sh | sh checks the download and installs the app, and it opens straight away. Updates are signed with Mercury's update key and checked before they install, so after that first launch you're covered. A Mercury server still answers one chat at a time. Running several turns side by side is the next change to the runtime. The app is open source like the rest of Mercury, in apps/desktop. If something in it gets in your way, open an issue. cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent Soul-driven AI agent with permission-hardened tools, token budgets, and multi-channel access. Runs 24/7 from CLI, Telegram or More. ai-agentai-assistantllm TypeScript3.8K388MIT

Delayed tasks are saved to schedules.yaml in Mercury's home directory, with an executeAt time. On startup, restorePersistedTasks in src/core/scheduler.ts checks each one. If executeAt has already passed, it logs Delayed task already expired, skipping and does not run it. For example, a delayed task due at 02:40, during a restart at 02:50, will not fire. A task due at 03:00 during the same restart will. Cron tasks are re-registered on startup. We found no catch-up logic in the scheduler, so firings that fall inside a downtime window are not replayed. Different features behave differently; bot routines go through their own governor, described below. What to do: Use cron for recurring work. For one-off work that must run, check the log for already expired after every restart.
documents.s: Delayed tasks due during downtime are skipped [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: This claim is narrow. The scheduler's own error handlers only log: In addTask, a throwing handler logs Scheduled task error. Nothing else happens. In startHeartbeat, a failing heartbeat logs Heartbeat error. In addDelayedTask, a failing delayed task logs Delayed task error. Ordinary scheduled prompts take a different route. handleScheduledTask in src/core/agent.ts catches its own errors and logs Scheduled task execution failed. So for ordinary tasks, the scheduler's Scheduled task error path is usually not the one that fires. It fires for bot routines, where an error from enqueueing is not caught. Successful output is separate. A scheduled task's result goes back through its source channel like any other reply. We did not check whether a failure inside the agent loop is sent to the channel, so treat a missing result as unknown, not as success. What to do: Don't rely on error logs for overnight work. Have each task send a short end-of-run message. If it doesn't arrive, assume the run did not finish.
documents.s: Some scheduler errors are logged but not sent to you [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: In addDelayedTask, a finally block removes the task from schedules.yaml when its handler returns, even if the handler threw. For ordinary tasks, handleScheduledTask does not throw, so the removal happens once the prompt has been queued. The queued prompt is not lost on that basis alone. Accepted jobs are persisted in the work ledger, and on startup recoverInterrupted() re-queues the ones that were queued or interrupted (src/core/agent.ts). We have not tested a restart in the middle of a run.
documents.s: A delayed task leaves the schedule file once its prompt is handed off [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: Each cron task is registered with cron.schedule and an async handler. The scheduler keeps no in-flight flag per task ID. We reproduced this pattern with node-cron 3.0.3, the version Mercury pins: a job firing every second, with a handler that takes 3.5 seconds, reached four concurrent runs within eight seconds. Inside Mercury, the effect is different. Scheduled prompts go onto the agent's message queue, which processes one message at a time. Overlapping firings for a main-agent task therefore wait in line rather than running in parallel. [Confirmed from code; not run end to end.] Each queued firing still costs budget when it runs. Bot routines are different. The bot governor skips a tick when the bot is busy or the last run was too recent (busy, too_soon). [Confirmed from code.] What to do: Until overlap is tested on your own setup, avoid non-idempotent jobs (ones that write files, send messages, or spend money) with intervals shorter than their expected run time.
documents.s: Long runs may overlap [Reproduced at the scheduler level; queued inside the agent]

documents.t: Mercury tracks daily token use in src/utils/tokens.ts. The total is saved to token-usage.json and resets when the date changes, so a restart does not reset it. isOverBudget() is checked in handleMessage in src/core/agent.ts, before the agent loop runs. Scheduled prompts are not exempt. They enter the same queue and reach the same check, so a scheduled job is stopped by the same daily budget as chat. What differs is who hears about it: A chat message gets a budget notice. On the CLI, it gets an override prompt. A scheduled job with a source channel gets the same notice on that channel. A scheduled job with no source channel (internal) gets nothing. The check returns without sending a message. We traced this in the code but did not run it: we did not set a one-request budget and fire a job. To confirm on your install, set a low budget, fire one scheduled job with a source channel and one without, and check what each sends and logs. What to do: Keep daily headroom for the overnight run. Give unattended jobs a source channel so the notice reaches you. Check /budget in the morning.
documents.s: Budget stops can be silent for unattended jobs [Confirmed from code]

documents.t: Recurring work is on cron, not one-off delays. Each overnight task sends an end-of-run message. No message means unknown. Non-idempotent jobs don't run on intervals shorter than their expected run time. The daily budget covers the overnight run with headroom. Unattended jobs have a source channel, so budget notices reach you. You've checked the log for already expired after the last restart. You know what the agent does when a tool call hangs, and you've tested it.
documents.s: A checklist before you leave it running

documents.t: Mercury can recover after a restart. Accepted jobs that were queued or interrupted are re-queued from the work ledger. That does not mean every scheduled run is replayed. Firings during downtime are skipped, and expired delayed tasks are not run. Recovery covers work that was accepted. It does not cover work that never reached the ledger.

Scheduler reliability tells you a job ran. It doesn't tell you the job did the right thing. A tool that returns success with bad data, or a task that does the wrong thing correctly, passes every check above. An overnight run needs both: a schedule that fires, and a task that is correct when it does. We'll report the open tests here as we run them.

Mercury's setup wizard uses two kinds of input. The name questions use Node's readline interface: you type a line, press Enter, and get a string back. The mode menu reads individual key presses, so it can move the highlight with the arrow keys. That needs the terminal in raw mode and a keypress listener on process.stdin. Both read from the same stream, so they have to take turns. The question reader has to let go of stdin before the menu takes over.
documents.s: Two ways to read a terminal

documents.t: In October we fixed an older bug where pressing Ctrl+D during setup made the wizard exit silently. Part of that fix was to share one readline interface across all the consecutive questions, so an end-of-input during any of them would be caught and reported. Sharing the interface raised a question: when do you close it? You don't want to close and reopen it between two questions that follow each other immediately. So after each answer, the code scheduled the close for the next turn of the event loop: iface.question(prompt, (answer) => { pending = null; scheduleRelease(); // setImmediate(() => close()) resolve(answer.trim()); }); If another question came along before then, it cancelled the scheduled close and reused the interface. That's a sensible design for a sequence of questions. The problem is what happens when the next consumer isn't a question.

Here is the exact order of events after you type your agent's name: The answer resolves. A close is scheduled for the next tick. The wizard moves on and opens the arrow-key menu. The menu puts the terminal in raw mode, calls stdin.resume(), and attaches its key listener. The next tick arrives and the scheduled close runs. readline's close() pauses its input stream, which is process.stdin. Step 3 undid step 2. The menu was waiting for key presses on a stream that was no longer flowing. Nothing else was keeping Node's event loop busy at that moment: no timers, no open sockets, no pending promises tied to I/O. When the event loop has no work left, Node exits. Cleanly. With status 0. That's why there was no error. Nothing failed. The process just ran out of things to do.

Every test we had passed, and that's the uncomfortable part. The unit tests for the question reader passed because, in isolation, it did exactly what it should. The wizard's tests mocked the menu. The binary smoke test in CI ran mercury --version, which never reaches the wizard. And anyone on the team who already had a config file never saw the first-run path at all. None of those tests had a real terminal in them, and this bug only exists when two readers share one.

The fix is one line. The menu releases the shared reader synchronously, before it takes over stdin: export async function selectWithArrowKeys(title, options, config = {}) { // Release the question reader now: its deferred close would otherwise // pause stdin after we resume it. closeAsk(); readline.emitKeypressEvents(process.stdin); // ...raw mode, resume, keypress listener } closeAsk() cancels the scheduled close and closes the interface immediately. By the time the menu calls resume(), nothing is left that could pause the stream behind its back.

The part worth copying is the test. CI now runs the compiled binary through the real first-run wizard inside a pseudo-terminal. It types a name, answers the agent name prompt, waits for the mode menu, and then checks one thing: is the process still alive? Then it presses the down arrow and Enter and expects the provider question. Run against 1.3.6, it fails at the menu. Run against 1.3.7, it passes. It runs on every pull request on Linux and macOS. There's also a regression test at the unit level that fails if a deferred release can pause the input after an explicit close.
documents.s: The test that would have caught it

documents.t: If two parts of your CLI read stdin, decide the hand-off explicitly. Don't rely on whoever closes last. "Exited with code 0" can be a bug. In Node, a process that runs out of work exits quietly. When an interactive program exits without being asked to, look for a stream that stopped flowing. Test interactive paths with a real terminal. Mocks hide the exact class of bug where two components step on each other. A pseudo-terminal test is maybe forty lines of Python and it's the only thing that would have caught this. We're sorry to everyone whose first impression of Mercury was a menu that vanished. If you bounced off it, the current release gets you through setup, and we'd love for you to try again.

The first thing I did was take the renderer out of the argument. I wrote a benchmark that mounts the real terminal UI in a virtual terminal, loads a 100-message conversation and a 14-bot roster, and types 60 characters, timing each one from key press to the frame that shows it. The median was about 3 ms per keystroke. The worst was around 20 ms. Each frame wrote roughly 74 bytes to the terminal. Then I ran it again with a bot streaming its reasoning into the UI a hundred times a second, and it barely moved: about 6 ms. That's not a renderer you can feel. Whatever was eating the latency, it wasn't drawing the screen.

So I stopped benchmarking and looked at what was actually running. There were two Mercury processes doing real work. One was the background daemon I expected. The other was the terminal session itself, and it had used about four times as much CPU as the daemon. A terminal client should use almost nothing. This one was doing a lot. The daemon's error log had the second clue: nine copies of the same Telegram error in a single day. 409 Conflict: terminated by other getUpdates request Telegram returns that when two programs poll the same bot token at once. There is no way to get it with one process.
documents.s: The process list told the story

documents.t: The launcher had a branch that looked reasonable in isolation. When you typed mercury and no background daemon was running, it did two things in a row: start the daemon, then start the agent in the foreground. autoDaemonize(); await runAgent(); The intent was to make sure Mercury kept running after you closed the terminal, while still giving you a chat right away. The effect was two complete runtimes. Both built a bot manager on the same queue. Both connected to Telegram. Both registered the same scheduled routines. And the foreground copy ran every bot turn, every tool call and every context compaction on the same thread that renders your keystrokes. For months this didn't matter much, because bots were mostly idle. Then we made them always-on. The foreground copy suddenly had real work to do, on the worst possible thread, and typing started to lag on every machine that took that path. Which was every machine, because it ran on the first mercury after any reboot. On my own laptop it was worse. An old install from npm was still registered as the login service and held the web port. Every launch failed to connect to the new daemon, decided the runtime was unhealthy, and took the "start everything" path again.
documents.s: How we ended up with two

documents.t: You can imagine a smaller fix: keep the second copy but stop it from polling Telegram, or move bot work to a worker thread. Each of those would have removed one symptom and left the actual problem in place, which is that two programs both believed they were Mercury. The fix we shipped is a rule instead: one process owns the runtime, and the terminal attaches to it. Launching mercury starts the daemon if needed and then attaches to it. The terminal never becomes a second runtime unless no daemon can run on that platform (Android under Termux is the one case). If a foreground process does start beside a live daemon, for example to open Mercury Code, it runs as a terminal for the main agent only. It doesn't register channels, doesn't create a bot manager, doesn't bind the web port, and doesn't replay scheduled work. Attaching is instant. The daemon now binds its web listener first, before channels and bots finish starting, and answers a lightweight health check with its process ID. If something else owns the port, you get one sentence saying which process it is instead of a 30-second wait followed by a pointless restart.
documents.s: Why we didn't just make it faster

documents.t: The part I'm happiest with is small. Mercury now measures its own event loop. /api/health reports the 99th-percentile and worst stall over the last ten seconds, and any stall longer than 250 ms is logged with a warning. We spent days on this bug partly because "it feels slow" isn't evidence. Now it is. If a bot turn ever does something synchronous that holds the main thread, the daemon's log will say so, with a number.

The honest version: the double runtime existed for a long time and we never noticed, because nothing measured it and the symptom only appeared once the workload changed. The tests passed because each runtime, on its own, worked. So the fix came with a few guards that would have caught it: A contract test asserts the launcher never starts the daemon and then a second runtime. The login service is checked against the running install on every launch and re-pointed if it drifted. Merges now wait for the entire CI run, not just the checks that happen to have reported so far. If you're building something that runs in the background and has a terminal front end, the takeaway is the same one we learned: decide which process is the program, and make everything else a client. It's much easier than working out, later, which of two programs is the real one.
documents.s: What we got wrong, and what we changed

documents.t: Mercury runs anywhere Node.js 22+ runs, plus everywhere a single binary can live — including phones via Termux.

On a Mac, Windows or Linux computer, download Mercury Desktop. It installs Mercury for you, with no terminal, and keeps it updated. It can also connect to a Mercury on another machine. See Install & first run. The rest of this page installs the Mercury runtime from the command line: for servers, headless machines, Termux, or if you prefer the terminal.

macOS — curl | sh installer, Homebrew-style PATH setup, Apple Silicon & Intel binaries. Linux — works on any glibc distro; static x64/arm64 binaries. Windows — PowerShell installer, native .exe, optional WSL path. Termux & lightweight devices — Android (Termux), iSH, Alpine containers, Raspberry Pi. Cloud Instance — hosted Mercury Code via Atomic Bot. No install needed.
Every platform supports two routes — pick whichever fits.

A one-line installer downloads the latest pre-built binary, verifies its SHA-256, and puts it on your PATH. # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh # Windows irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex The installer: Detects your OS and CPU architecture (macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64/arm64, Windows x64). Resolves the latest GitHub release. Verifies the SHA-256 checksum against checksums.txt. Installs to ~/.mercury/bin/mercury (or %USERPROFILE%\.mercury\bin\mercury.exe) and updates your shell PATH. Environment variables​ Variable Default Purpose MERCURY_VERSION latest Pin to a specific version, e.g. MERCURY_VERSION=1.1.9 MERCURY_INSTALL $HOME/.mercury Install prefix (binary lands at $MERCURY_INSTALL/bin/mercury) MERCURY_NO_PATH (unset) Set to 1 to skip modifying your shell rc / user PATH

If you already have Node.js, the npm route is the simplest: npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Other package managers: bun add -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent pnpm add -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent yarn global add @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Or run without installing: npx @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

Mercury includes a built-in upgrade command for npm installs: mercury upgrade It stops the daemon if running, removes the old package to avoid ENOTEMPTY, installs the latest version, and reports the version diff. Binary installs mercury upgrade is npm-aware. If you installed via the shell installer, re-run it to get the latest binary: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh
After installation, run the doctor or edit your config: mercury doctor # ~/.mercury/mercury.yaml web: enabled: true The dashboard will be available at http://127.0.0.1:6174 when Mercury is running.

Command Description mercury up Recommended. Install service + start daemon + ensure running mercury Start the agent (same as mercury start) mercury start Start as background daemon (default) mercury start --foreground Start in foreground (interactive) mode. Shorthand: -f mercury restart Restart a background Mercury process mercury stop Stop a background Mercury process mercury logs Show last 100 lines of daemon logs mercury status Show config, providers, daemon PID, and budget mercury doctor Reconfigure settings — press Enter to keep current values mercury doctor --platform Show cross-platform terminal/daemon compatibility diagnostics mercury doctor --mcp Connect to every enabled MCP server and report its status mercury doctor --security Check remote access and security: password, devices, file permissions, the tunnel mercury setup Re-run the setup wizard (same as doctor) mercury help Show the full manual (tools, commands, config paths) mercury service install Install as system service (auto-start on boot) mercury service uninstall Uninstall the system service mercury service status Show system service status mercury --verbose Start with debug logging on stderr

Mercury updates itself safely: it waits for running work, downloads the new version and checks it, backs up, installs, and checks the new version starts. If it doesn't, the old version and your settings come back on their own. See Updating Mercury. Command Description mercury upgrade Update to the latest version (rolls back on its own if the new one fails) mercury upgrade --check Only show whether a newer version exists and what's in it mercury upgrade --now Don't wait for running work to finish mercury upgrade --force Reinstall even when already on the latest version mercury update Is there a newer Mercury, and what's in it mercury update check Ask again now instead of using the last check

mercury server (and /server in a chat on this computer) controls who can reach this Mercury from other devices. See Remote access & security. Command Description mercury server Open the menu mercury server status What can connect, and how mercury server on / off Allow or refuse other devices mercury server approve <code> Let a waiting device or action through (deny <code> refuses) mercury server devices Paired devices; revoke <id or name>, revoke-all mercury server token <name> Make a token for a device by hand (shown once) mercury server allow-ip <ip or range> Allow only these addresses; remove-ip, allow-any mercury server shell on / off The terminal for remote devices (each command still asks you) mercury server expire <days> / never Sign out devices unused this long (default 30 days) mercury server limit <n> The most devices that can be paired (default 10) mercury server check The security check (same as mercury doctor --security) mercury server log The security log

The mercury skills command tree talks to skills.mercuryagent.sh directly. See the dedicated Skills page for the full surface, examples, and the in-chat / dashboard / Telegram equivalents. Command Description mercury skills info Registry stats and reachability mercury skills list Show locally installed skills (from ~/.mercury/skills/.index.json) mercury skills categories List all registry categories mercury skills browse [category] [--page N --limit N] Paginated catalog browse mercury skills search <query> [--limit N] Full-text search mercury skills view <id> [--web] [--raw] Render SKILL.md; --web opens the registry page mercury skills install <ids...> [--force] Install one or many; --force reinstalls same version mercury skills install --from <urlOrPath> Install from a local file or arbitrary URL mercury skills update [id] Update all installed skills, or just one mercury skills remove <id> Uninstall a skill mercury skills doctor Check install root, registry connectivity, cache Shared flags: --json, --registry <url>, -q, -y. Environment overrides: MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY, MERCURY_SKILLS_INSTALL_ROOT.

The mercury mcp commands manage the MCP servers whose tools Mercury can use. Changes are saved to ~/.mercury/mercury.yaml and the background daemon is restarted to apply them. Command Description mercury mcp list Show configured servers, tool filters and env/header settings (secrets masked) mercury mcp add <id> --stdio <command> [-- args...] Add a local server; shows the command and asks before saving mercury mcp add <id> --http <url> Add a remote Streamable HTTP server mercury mcp test <id> Connect once and list every tool as allowed, hidden or skipped mercury mcp allow <id> <tools...> Show these tools to the agent ('*' for all) mercury mcp disallow <id> <tools...> Hide these tools again mercury mcp enable <id> Enable a server (asks before starting a stdio command) mercury mcp disable <id> Disable a server without removing it mercury mcp remove <id> Remove a server add options: --env KEY=VALUE, --header 'Name: value', --cwd <dir>, --allow <tools>, --auto-approve <tools>, --allow-private, --disabled, -y. Use ${env:NAME} (in single quotes) for secrets kept in ~/.mercury/.env.

mercury doctor re-runs the setup wizard with your current values pre-filled. Press Enter on any field to keep it unchanged, or type a new value to replace it. API keys are shown masked: sk-x••••4f2a Providers and models can be reselected; Mercury fetches models again for changed credentials Telegram token — type none to disable Telegram, or paste a token to start the pairing-code flow Daily budget — change the token budget limit mercury doctor

Use --platform to run a non-destructive compatibility check for your current environment: mercury doctor --platform This prints: OS + architecture Node.js version Terminal + TTY/raw-mode capability SSH/CI detection Daemon status Spotify inline-art support status Keybinding fallbacks (/view, /ws exit, etc.)

Use --mcp to connect to every enabled MCP server and report its health: mercury doctor --mcp Each server is listed as connected (with its tool count and how many tools are allowed), failed (with the reason and the end of the server's stderr), or disabled. Configuration problems, literal secrets in mercury.yaml, and tools skipped because their schema can't be used are listed too. The command exits with status 1 if any server fails, so it can be used in scripts.
Type these during a conversation with Mercury. Most work in both CLI and Telegram unless marked otherwise. They do not consume API tokens.

Command Description /help Show the full manual (Telegram gets a Telegram-specific version) /status Show agent name, provider, budget, and channels /progress Show live status for the current long-running task / or /menu CLI only: open the arrow-key command picker /permissions Change permission mode (Ask Me / Allow All) /models List configured models/providers for this session /models use <provider> Switch the current session model/provider /tools List all currently loaded tools /mcp Show MCP servers and whether they are connected /mcp tools <server> List an MCP server's tools and which ones the agent may use /skills List installed skills · see dedicated page for the full surface /skills search <query> Search the registry at skills.mercuryagent.sh /skills view <id> Show title, version, description, and registry URL for <category>/<slug> /skills install <id> Install a skill from the registry into ~/.mercury/skills/ /skills install <url> Install raw SKILL.md from a URL /skills remove <id> Uninstall a skill /memory View and manage second brain memory /tasks List scheduled tasks /stream Toggle Telegram text streaming (on/off) /stream on Enable streaming (live text updates) /stream off Disable streaming — responses arrive as single message

Command Description /budget Show token budget status /budget override Override budget for one request /budget reset Reset usage to zero /budget set <n> Change daily token budget (0 removes the ceiling: no limit)

A battery-saver-style mode that reduces token spend per request. When active, Mercury produces terser responses, runs fewer reasoning steps, and uses a shorter conversation history window. It also auto-engages at a configurable percentage of your daily budget. Command Description /saver Show saver status, today's savings, and lifetime savings /saver on Manually enable Token Saver Mode (persisted) /saver off Disable Token Saver Mode (also clears any auto-engagement) /saver toggle Toggle saver on/off /saver threshold <0-100> Set auto-engage threshold as a percentage of daily budget (default 75, 0 disables auto) /saver auto on|off Master switch for automatic engagement at threshold /saver routing on|off Opt-in: prefer cheaper providers while saver is active When saver auto-engages, Mercury sends a one-time notification so you know responses may be shorter. Disable manually with /saver off or /saver auto off. See Token Saver Mode reference for what changes when saver is active.

Command Description /code Show current programming mode /code plan Switch to plan mode (analyze and present options, no coding) /code execute Switch to execute mode (implement step by step) /code build Alias for execute mode /code off Exit programming mode /code toggle Cycle through: off → plan → execute → off /code agent <task> Delegate a coding task to a sub-agent in the background /code workspace CLI only: open current directory in workspace IDE mode

Command Description /ws Show workspace commands /ws open <path> Open a directory in workspace IDE mode /ws exit Exit workspace IDE mode back to general chat /ws refresh Refresh file tree and git status panel /ws stage <file|all> Stage a file or all changes /ws commit <message> Commit staged changes /ws undo <file> Revert file changes with git checkout /ws help Show workspace command list

Command Description /agents List all sub-agents and their status /agents stop <id|all> Stop a sub-agent or all sub-agents /agents pause <id> Pause a running sub-agent /agents resume <id> Resume a paused sub-agent /agents config Show sub-agent resource allocation /agents set max <n> Set max concurrent sub-agents

Persistent persona-scoped agents that run outside your conversation — each with its own persona, sandbox, skills, and durable queue. See the Mercury Bots guide for the full surface. Command Description /bots Roster with live fleet states /bots create <id> "Name" "Description" Onboard a bot /bots open <id> Open the bot's own thread /bot <id> <message> or @<id> <message> Dispatch a task to a bot (result lands in the bot's thread) /bots persona <id> <text> Set the bot's character /bots edit <id> Edit name, description, model, budget /bots delete <id> Delete the bot /bots promote <id> / demote <id> Fleet lead ↔ solo bot /bots stop <id> / start <id> Stop (holds jobs) / start (resumes subtree for leads) /bots enable <id> / disable <id> Reactivate a disabled (e.g. imported) bot /bots run <id> [routine] Fire a routine or bare wake now /bots journal <id> Recent runs for a bot /bots dlq Failed jobs (replayable) /bots replay <id> <jobId> Non-destructive DLQ replay /bots export <id> [path] Export a shareable bundle (leads carry their crew) /bots import <path> Recreate bots from a bundle (imports start disabled)

Command Description /bg <command> Run a shell command in the background /bg: <task> Run a natural-language sub-agent task in background /bg current Move the current in-flight task to background /bg list Show background tasks /bg <id> Show details/output for one background task /bg cancel <id> Cancel a running background task /bg stop <id> Alias for /bg cancel /bg killall Cancel all running background tasks /bg clear Prune completed background tasks

Command Description /spotify Show Spotify connection status /spotify auth Connect Spotify (browser or manual code flow) /spotify code <code> Complete auth with a pasted authorization code /spotify player CLI only: interactive music player with arrow-key controls /spotify devices List available Spotify devices /spotify device <id> Set active Spotify device /spotify now Show what is currently playing /spotify logout Disconnect Spotify and clear saved tokens

Command Description /halt Emergency: stop all agents and clear the task queue /stop Stop all agents, clear queue, release file locks, clear task board /reset Full reset: stop all + clear conversation context (requires confirmation) Fast-path commands /agents, /halt, /stop, /progress, /spotify, /code, /memory, and /bg all work even while Mercury is busy processing a task. They're processed immediately without waiting for the current task to finish.
Command Description /view Toggle progress view (balanced/detailed) /view balanced Show last 5 tool steps, compact format /view detailed Show last 20 tool steps, full format

Command Description /telegram Open Telegram management menu /telegram pending List pending Telegram access requests /telegram users List approved Telegram admins and members /telegram approve <code|id> Approve a pairing code or access request /telegram reject <id> Reject a pending Telegram access request /telegram remove <id> Revoke an approved Telegram user /telegram promote <id> Promote a Telegram member to admin /telegram demote <id> Demote a Telegram admin to member /telegram reset Clear all Telegram access and restart pairing
Command Description /start or /pair Request access (new users) or check status (approved users) /unpair Admin only: reset all Telegram access for this instance

These shortcuts work in the CLI terminal interface: Shortcut Description Ctrl+C Exit Mercury Ctrl+T Toggle progress view (balanced/detailed) Ctrl+B Show background tasks (or move current task to background if busy) Ctrl+N Insert newline (multi-line input) Ctrl+P Switch to code plan mode (in coding/workspace mode) Ctrl+X Switch to code execute mode (in coding/workspace mode)

When you type / in the CLI, an autocomplete popup appears with matching commands: Up/Down arrows — navigate through suggestions Tab or Enter — fill the selected suggestion into the input Enter (when input matches a command) — submit the command

Shortcut Description Esc / Ctrl+Q Exit workspace (from explorer) or return to explorer Ctrl+E Focus explorer panel Ctrl+G Focus git panel Ctrl+J Toggle chat panel Tab Cycle focus: explorer → code → right panel Arrow keys Navigate file tree / scroll panels Enter Open selected file Ctrl+U / Ctrl+D Scroll up/down by 8-10 lines PageUp / PageDown Scroll by 15 lines Telegram pairing and access Telegram stays private 1:1 only. The first user sends /start, receives a pairing code in Telegram, and you approve that code from the CLI during setup. Later Telegram users also send /start, appear as pending requests, and can then be approved or rejected from the CLI /telegram menu.

Plugins add features to Mercury that not everyone needs, without making the Mercury download bigger for everyone. You install the ones you want; the rest never touch your machine. A plugin can add tools the agent can use, a chat channel (such as WhatsApp) and, for some plugins, slash commands you can type. Every plugin can be turned off or removed at any time, and Mercury keeps running if a plugin breaks. Plugins are available from Mercury 1.4.0.

These are in the plugin catalog for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows x64 and Linux (x64 and arm64): Plugin Install What it does WhatsApp /plugins install whatsapp Chat with Mercury on WhatsApp from a spare number, and talk to it by voice call in both directions Optimus /plugins install optimus Mercury uses your computer: sees the screen, moves the pointer, types and opens apps, by chat or out loud The catalog is published at mercuryagent.sh/plugins/catalog.json. Each entry pins a version and a SHA-256 checksum, and Mercury checks the download against it before installing.

Where Example Any chat (terminal, Telegram, web, Discord, Slack) /plugins Shell mercury plugins list Web dashboard Configure → Plugins Telegram buttons /plugins, then tap Install, Disable or Uninstall They all do the same thing. If Mercury is running in the background, the shell commands ask it to make the change, so plugins start and stop right away without a restart.

Chat Shell What it does /plugins mercury plugins Installed and available plugins, with status /plugins ID mercury plugins open ID That plugin's menu: its settings, linking, test, turn off, uninstall. Reply with a number (or tap a button on Telegram) /plugins setup ID mercury plugins setup ID Walk through the plugin's setup again /plugins search weather mercury plugins search weather Find plugins in the catalog /plugins info ID mercury plugins info ID Tools, network access, secrets it reads, settings /plugins install ID mercury plugins install ID Install. Shows what the plugin needs first and asks you to confirm /plugins enable ID mercury plugins enable ID Turn it on /plugins disable ID mercury plugins disable ID Turn it off. Its data and settings are kept /plugins update mercury plugins update Update catalog plugins (or one: update ID) /plugins rollback ID mercury plugins rollback ID Go back to the version you had before /plugins uninstall ID mercury plugins uninstall ID Remove it. Add --purge to delete its data too /plugins set ID KEY VALUE mercury plugins set ID KEY VALUE Change a plugin setting /plugins pair ID PHONE mercury plugins pair ID (QR code) or --code PHONE Link a channel plugin's account, such as the spare WhatsApp number /plugins unlink ID mercury plugins unlink ID Log a channel plugin out of its account /plugins test ID mercury plugins test ID Send yourself a test message through a channel plugin After install, Mercury walks you through the plugin's setup, one question at a time, in the same chat. For WhatsApp that's your number, what Mercury may do in your chat, and linking the spare number. For Optimus it's whether it may control the computer, how you want to talk to it, and the talk key. Setup skips questions that don't apply: with an OpenAI provider already set up in Mercury, neither plugin asks which voice to use. mercury plugins install ID --no-setup installs without the walk-through.

You never need to remember a plugin's settings. /plugins ID (or mercury plugins open ID, or the dashboard) opens its menu: Every setting is listed on the menu with its current value. Pick one to change it. Related settings are grouped into sections, such as 🎙 Voice calls, each marked ✓ when it's ready or "needs setup" when it isn't. Choices say what they do. A yes/no setting shows, for example, "On: Mercury picks up when you call it" and "Off: your calls to Mercury ring out", and after you save, the reply repeats what your choice does. Follow-up settings come next. Change the voice engine to Gemini and Mercury asks for the Gemini key and model straight away, instead of leaving you to find them. No dead ends. Every question offers a way back with no change, and cancel closes the menu. The menu also has Link / Unlink and Send me a test message for channel plugins, Run setup again, Update, Turn off and Uninstall. In a chat, reply with the option's number (or tap a button on Telegram). Members see the status only.

A plugin that needs an AI provider (the voice engines in WhatsApp and Optimus use OpenAI or Grok) borrows the one you already set up in Mercury (dashboard → Providers, or mercury doctor). You set a key in one place. Keys a plugin asks for itself (a Gemini or Deepgram key, say) are stored with Mercury's own keys, shown only as "set", and readable only by plugins that declare them, so a key added for WhatsApp also works for Optimus. If a key is missing, Mercury tells you once what it turns off and how to fix it. install accepts a catalog id, a folder, a .tgz file, an https:// URL, or github:owner/repo (latest release). Only catalog plugins are verified by Mercury; install anything else only from people you trust. Only the owner (and admins on Telegram, Discord and Slack) can install or change plugins. In the web dashboard, changes are accepted only from the computer Mercury runs on.

Two kinds of plugin. Own process plugins run as a separate program: if they crash, Mercury restarts them, and after repeated crashes turns them off. In-process plugins run inside Mercury, with timeouts on everything they do. Only what it declared. A plugin can reach only the websites and read only the secrets listed in its manifest. /plugins info shows both, and install shows them before you confirm. A plugin that controls the computer (Optimus) is flagged with a warning. Tools ask first. A plugin tool that changes anything asks for your approval like any built-in tool. Bots never see plugin tools unless you allow them in the bot's tool list (weather__forecast, or weather__* for all of one plugin's tools). Automatic turn-off. A plugin is turned off, and you get a message saying why, when: it fails 5 times in a row; it crashes too often; its files changed since install; it isn't compatible with your Mercury version; Mercury failed to start twice right after it was installed or updated. Clean removal. Disable or uninstall stops its timers, network requests and tools straight away. No restart needed. Installing into a running Mercury starts the plugin straight away too. Updates you can undo. The previous version is kept, so /plugins rollback ID brings it back, with its settings.

documents.t: If Mercury won't start after a plugin change, start it with every plugin off: mercury start --safe-mode # or: MERCURY_PLUGINS=off mercury start mercury doctor --plugins # what's installed, what's off and why

~/.mercury/plugins/ state.json installed / enabled ID/versions/VERSION/ the plugin (current + previous) ID/data/ the plugin's own data (kept on uninstall unless --purge) ID/settings.json your settings for it Writing a plugin? See Reference → Writing plugins.

Mercury skills are Markdown-based extensions (SKILL.md files) that teach the agent how to do a specific task. The registry at skills.mercuryagent.sh hosts 126+ community-contributed skills across 23 categories, and Mercury can install them from four surfaces — they all share the same install path under the hood. Review before you ship. Skills run with elevated permissions when invoked. Open the registry page (mercury skills view <id> --web) and read the SKILL.md body before installing. For the file format, frontmatter spec, and runtime behavior, see Reference → Skills.

Surface Best for Entry point CLI subcommand (mercury skills …) Scripting, batch installs, JSON output mercury skills install <id> In-chat slash command (/skills …) Quick browse while chatting with the agent /skills search <q> Web dashboard Visual browse + activate/deactivate toggle http://127.0.0.1:6174/skills Telegram bot Browse and install while away from the machine /skills install <id> (admin-only) All four hit the same SkillStore.install(id) code path, write to the same ~/.mercury/skills/<category>/<slug>/SKILL.md location, and update the same ~/.mercury/skills/.index.json.
The fastest surface, available before or after starting the agent. No browser required.

mercury skills info # registry stats + reachability mercury skills categories # all 23 categories mercury skills browse finance-legal # paginated list mercury skills browse --page 2 --limit 20 mercury skills search "contract review" # full-text search mercury skills search --limit 3 prompt

mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review --web # opens registry page mercury skills view finance-legal/contract-review --raw # prints raw SKILL.md

# From the registry mercury skills install finance-legal/contract-review mercury skills install ai-ml/prompt-engineering finance-legal/contract-review # batch mercury skills install finance-legal/contract-review --force # reinstall same version # From a local file or arbitrary URL mercury skills install --from ./SKILL.md mercury skills install --from https://example.com/my-skill.md # Update mercury skills update # all installed mercury skills update finance-legal/contract-review # just one # Remove mercury skills remove finance-legal/contract-review # Observability mercury skills list # what's installed locally mercury skills doctor # install root + registry + cache

Flag Purpose --json Machine-readable output (useful for scripting / piping). --registry <url> Use a different registry; also accepts MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY. -q, --quiet Suppress progress output. -y, --yes Skip interactive confirmations. Environment variable Purpose MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY Default registry URL (overridden by --registry). MERCURY_SKILLS_INSTALL_ROOT Alternate install root (defaults to ~/.mercury/skills).

Available in every channel — the CLI TUI, the web dashboard chat, and Telegram (subject to the Telegram-specific gating below). The slash command list autocompletes when you type /skills and press Tab in the CLI. /skills # list installed skills /skills search <query> # top 5 registry matches with URLs /skills view <id> # title, version, description, registry URL /skills install <id> # install from the registry /skills install <url> # install raw SKILL.md from a URL /skills remove <id> # uninstall /skills help # subcommand list Every search hit and every view response prints the https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/<id> URL so you can review on the web before installing. Examples in a real chat session: > /skills search contract 🔍 Searching the registry for "contract"… Top 3 matches for "contract": • `finance-legal/contract-review` (v1.0.0) Review contracts and surface risky clauses. https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/finance-legal/contract-review • `finance-legal/saas-agreement` (v0.2.1) … > /skills install finance-legal/contract-review 📦 Installing `finance-legal/contract-review` from the registry… ✅ Installed `finance-legal/contract-review` (v1.0.0) 🔗 https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/finance-legal/contract-review Installs run without a confirmation prompt — same as the existing in-chat URL-install behavior. The view step (or the registry URL printed in search results) is where you should review before committing.

The Skills page in the web dashboard has two installers stacked in one card: Install from registry — paste a category/slug id and click Install. The toast reports the install status (installed, updated, reinstalled, already-installed) and the version. Install from URL — paste a URL pointing to a raw SKILL.md. Mercury fetches it, validates the frontmatter, and saves it to disk. The page header has a Browse skills.mercuryagent.sh link that opens the registry in a new tab. Each installed skill card has: A status badge (active / inactive). A toggle to activate or deactivate without deleting. A trash button to delete (with confirmation dialog). The dashboard talks to these endpoints: GET /api/skills # list installed with active state POST /api/skills/install # { url } — fetch and install from a URL POST /api/skills/install-from-registry # { id, force? } — install by registry id POST /api/skills/:name/activate POST /api/skills/:name/deactivate DELETE /api/skills/:name

Same subcommand surface as in-chat, with one extra rule: list, search, view are available to every approved user. install and remove are admin-only (same gate as /unpair). /skills # list installed /skills search <query> # registry search /skills view <id> # details + URL /skills install <id> # admin only /skills remove <id> # admin only /skills help The bot includes the https://skills.mercuryagent.sh/skills/<id> URL in every search result and every view response, so non-admin members can review a skill on a browser and then ask an admin to install it. /skills is registered in the Telegram command menu (between /spotify and /unpair), so it appears in autocomplete next to all the other bot commands.

SkillStore.install(id) calls GET /api/skills/<id> for the JSON detail, short-circuits with 'already-installed' if the local index already has the same version (unless --force), reconstructs the canonical SKILL.md from the JSON frontmatter + body fields, atomically writes it to ~/.mercury/skills/<category>/<slug>/SKILL.md (tmp file + rename), verification-reads the file back, then updates ~/.mercury/skills/.index.json. If either write fails, both the file and the index are rolled back so they never disagree. Skill ids must match ^[a-z0-9-]+/[a-z0-9-]+$ — that's the path-traversal guard. The agent picks up newly installed skills on its next discovery scan (next agent boot or /skills view in the dashboard).

Symptom Fix Invalid skill id The id must be <category>/<slug>, lowercase, hyphen-separated. Don't include the full URL. Registry 404 The id doesn't exist on the registry. Run mercury skills search <q> to find the right id. Registry timeout / unreachable Run mercury skills doctor to confirm reachability and cache state. Pass --registry or set MERCURY_SKILLS_REGISTRY if you self-host. Install succeeded but the agent doesn't see the new skill The skill loader scans on boot. Restart Mercury or open the dashboard's Skills page (it triggers a re-scan). Post-install verification failed The disk write didn't round-trip. Usually disk-full or a permission issue under ~/.mercury/skills/. The CLI rolls back automatically.
Reference → Skills — file format, frontmatter spec, runtime behavior, writing your own. CLI Commands — full mercury command reference. In-chat commands — all slash commands in chat.

Mercury Cloud is a hosted backend that turns a local Mercury install into a remotely managed, always-on agent. Pair once from the terminal, and Mercury maintains a persistent WebSocket to the cloud — no port forwarding, no reverse proxy, no certificate management.

mercury cloud connect This opens a browser-based pairing URL. Once paired, Mercury saves your credentials and starts a background daemon that keeps the Cloud WebSocket alive even after you exit the terminal.

Pair — mercury cloud connect opens a browser URL. Poll-based completion with structured failure codes (e.g. agent capacity reached). Authenticate — Mercury receives a JWT (short-lived), a refresh token (single-use), and an agent API key (long-lived). Connect — A background daemon maintains a persistent WSS connection to wss://backend.mercuryagent.sh/ws with 30-second heartbeats and automatic reconnect. Stay online — The daemon keeps the WebSocket alive even after you close the terminal. The agent API key enables headless self-recovery without browser re-pairing.

Mercury Cloud uses a three-tier token strategy: Token Lifetime Purpose JWT Short-lived API and WebSocket auth. Auto-refreshed before expiry. Refresh token Single-use Rotated on every refresh. Used to get a new JWT. Agent API key Long-lived Headless self-recovery. Never expires. If the JWT expires, Mercury tries the refresh token. If the refresh token is also dead, Mercury redeems the agent API key to get fresh tokens — no browser re-pairing needed. This means a server or Termux deployment stays online indefinitely.

Mercury Cloud agents can search a shared memory pool — cross-agent context that lives in the cloud. After local Second Brain retrieval, the agent calls searchPool() to fetch additional context from other agents in your fleet. Results are cached locally for 5 minutes per query.
Manage your agent from cloud.mercuryagent.sh — send messages, install skills, view memory, and monitor status. The dashboard communicates with your local agent over the Cloud WebSocket.

Mercury Cloud offers multiple models. At pairing time, Mercury fetches the available models and prompts you to choose: Available models: 1. Mercury Flash (mercury-flash) 2. Mercury Pro (mercury-pro) ... Choose a model [1-N, Enter for 1]: Switch models later with /cloud use <model-id> or mercury doctor.

Command Description mercury cloud connect Pair with Mercury Cloud via browser mercury cloud disconnect Clear Cloud credentials and stop the agent mercury cloud status Show Cloud connection status and usage mercury cloud login Refresh the JWT using the stored refresh token

Mercury Cloud config is stored in mercury.yaml under the cloud section: cloud: enabled: true apiUrl: https://backend.mercuryagent.sh wsUrl: wss://backend.mercuryagent.sh/ws agentId: your-agent-id tier: free The JWT, refresh token, and agent API key are also stored here (they auto-rotate). You don't need to manage them manually.

mercury cloud disconnect This stops the running agent, clears all Cloud credentials, switches the default provider back to your offline provider, and restarts Mercury in offline mode. The agent remains registered on the cloud dashboard — delete it there to revoke server-side credentials.
Mercury runs as a background daemon by default. Telegram and scheduled tasks keep working after you close the terminal.

mercury start Starts Mercury as a background daemon. Spawns a detached child process, writes a PID file to ~/.mercury/daemon.pid, and redirects output to ~/.mercury/daemon.log. Stale PID files are automatically cleaned up.
mercury start --foreground Runs Mercury attached to your terminal. Useful for debugging or when you want to see output directly. Shorthand: mercury start -f.
mercury up This one command does everything: installs the system service if needed, starts the background daemon, and confirms Mercury is running. If it's already running, it just shows you the PID.
mercury stop Sends SIGTERM (process.kill on Windows) to the background process and removes the PID file.
mercury restart Stops the running daemon (if any) and starts a fresh one. Useful when something isn't working right and you need a clean restart.
mercury logs Shows the last 100 lines of ~/.mercury/daemon.log.

mercury status Shows whether the daemon is running, its PID, and the log file path. Crash recovery Background mode includes a watchdog. If Mercury crashes, it restarts automatically with exponential backoff (1s, 1.25s, 1.56s...). After 10 crashes within 60 seconds, it exits to prevent crash loops. Stale PID files are auto-cleaned on startup to prevent "already running" false positives.

Don't want to manage a daemon, service, or updates yourself? Atomic Bot offers fully hosted Mercury Code instances — your agent runs 24/7 on their infrastructure with zero setup, starting at $19/mo. See Cloud Instance for details.
documents.s: No server? Run it in the cloud

documents.t: Daemon mode supports async background execution for both shell commands and delegated sub-agent work.

Background tasks use human-friendly IDs like swift-fox, calm-owl, or bright-heron instead of opaque timestamps. There are 2,304 unique combinations (48 adjectives × 48 nouns). If a collision occurs, a numeric suffix is appended.
Start with /bg <command> Inspect with /bg list and /bg <id> Cancel with /bg cancel <id> (or /bg stop <id>, /bg kill <id>) Cancel all running tasks with /bg killall (or /bg stopall)
Delegate coding with /code agent <task> or /bg: <task> Move active task to worker with /bg current Worker progress/completion is surfaced in the shared background task board (/bg list)

Background tasks are persisted to disk and survive daemon restarts. Running tasks that were interrupted by a restart are marked as failed. These workers are designed to keep Mercury responsive while long-running work continues.

macOS Linux Windows mercury service install creates a LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist. Auto-start: Loads on login via launchctl load Crash recovery: KeepAlive SuccessfulExit = false restarts on crash No sudo needed: User-level LaunchAgent, not system daemon Logs: ~/.mercury/daemon.log and ~/.mercury/daemon-error.log Manual management​ launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist mercury service install creates a systemd user unit at ~/.config/systemd/user/mercury.service. Auto-start: Enabled via systemctl --user enable mercury.service Crash recovery: Restart=on-failure with 5s delay No sudo needed: User-level service Boot without login: Run sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER once Logs: ~/.mercury/daemon.log or journalctl --user -u mercury Manual management​ systemctl --user start mercury systemctl --user status mercury systemctl --user stop mercury mercury service install creates a Windows Task Scheduler task named MercuryAgent. Auto-start: Triggers on user logon via schtasks Crash recovery: Built-in watchdog with exponential backoff No admin needed: Runs with limited privileges (/rl limited) Logs: %USERPROFILE%\.mercury\daemon.log Manual management​ schtasks /query /tn "MercuryAgent" /fo list schtasks /run /tn "MercuryAgent" schtasks /delete /tn "MercuryAgent" /f
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.cosmicstack.mercury.plist
systemctl --user start mercury systemctl --user status mercury systemctl --user stop mercury
schtasks /query /tn "MercuryAgent" /fo list schtasks /run /tn "MercuryAgent" schtasks /delete /tn "MercuryAgent" /f

Mercury does not currently ship first-party Docker assets in this repository (no Dockerfile or docker-compose.yml by default). If you run Mercury in a container, treat it as an advanced/custom deployment: Prefer foreground mode (mercury start --foreground) inside the container Let the container runtime handle restart policy Mount ~/.mercury as persistent storage Validate terminal/TTY behavior separately for interactive CLI usage

Install Mercury as a system service so it starts automatically on boot and restarts on crash. mercury service install This detects your platform and generates the appropriate service config. Platform Method Requires Admin Auto-Start Crash Recovery macOS LaunchAgent plist No On login KeepAlive (restart on crash) Linux systemd user unit No* On login Restart=on-failure, 5s delay Windows Task Scheduler (schtasks) No On logon Built-in watchdog *Linux boot-without-login requires loginctl enable-linger $USER (one-time, needs sudo).
mercury service status mercury service uninstall

Everything about Mercury Desktop on a Mac in one place: installing it, opening it the first time, and what to do when macOS gets in the way. If someone sent you this link, jump to Fixing problems. You need macOS 11 (Big Sur) or newer, on an Apple Silicon (M1 and newer) or an Intel Mac.

Open Terminal (press ⌘ Space, type Terminal, press Return), paste this and press Return: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install-desktop.sh | sh That's all. In about a minute Mercury is in Applications and opens by itself, with no security prompt. What the command does, in order: Picks the build for your Mac (Apple Silicon or Intel, also when Terminal runs under Rosetta). Downloads Mercury from the GitHub release. Checks the download's SHA-256 against the one GitHub recorded for it, and checks the app's code signature is intact. If anything doesn't match, it installs nothing. Closes Mercury Desktop if it's open (Mercury itself keeps running, so no chat or bot stops), replaces the app, and keeps the old one until the new one is in place. Opens it. You can read the script before running it. Run the same command again any time to reinstall or repair the app. Why there's no prompt this way: macOS checks apps that a browser downloaded, because the browser marks them as coming from the internet. Mercury Desktop isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID yet, so that check stops it. A download made with curl isn't marked, so the check doesn't run. Options, if you need them: Variable What it does MERCURY_VERSION=1.5.0 Install that version instead of the latest MERCURY_APP_DIR=~/Applications Install somewhere else (default: /Applications, or ~/Applications if you can't write there) MERCURY_NO_OPEN=1 Don't open the app afterwards For example: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install-desktop.sh | MERCURY_VERSION=1.5.0 sh

If you'd rather not use Terminal: On the download page, choose macOS → Apple Silicon or Intel. Not sure which Mac you have? Open the Apple menu → About This Mac: "Chip: Apple M…" is Apple Silicon, "Processor: Intel" is Intel. Open the .dmg and drag Mercury onto Applications. Open Mercury from Applications. The first time, macOS stops it. Follow Opening it the first time.

Only needed for the .dmg. Installed with the command above? Skip this. Open Mercury. macOS says "Apple could not verify 'Mercury' is free of malware that may harm your Mac or compromise your privacy." Click Done (not Move to Trash). Open the Apple menu → System Settings → Privacy & Security. Scroll down to Security. You'll see "Mercury" was blocked to protect your Mac. Click Open Anyway. Enter your Mac's password (or use Touch ID), then click Open Anyway once more. Mercury opens, and macOS won't ask again for this copy. Updates install from inside the app without asking either. The Open Anyway button appears only for about an hour after you tried to open the app. If you don't see it, open Mercury once more, click Done, and go back to Privacy & Security. On macOS 14 (Sonoma) and older there's a shortcut: in Applications, right-click (or Control-click) Mercury, choose Open, then Open again. macOS 15 and newer removed this shortcut.

The first screen asks where Mercury should run: Install Mercury here sets up Mercury on this Mac: it downloads the release, checks it against the release's checksums, and runs it as a login item so it starts when you log in. No terminal, no Node.js. Connect elsewhere connects to a Mercury on another machine. The owner of that Mercury approves this Mac with a 5-character code. The rest is in Install & first run.

This is the expected first-launch message for a downloaded .dmg. Allow it once: Opening it the first time. Or skip the whole thing by installing with the one command, which replaces the copy you have.
documents.s: "Apple could not verify 'Mercury' is free of malware"

documents.t: The app isn't damaged; macOS says this about some unsigned apps that came from a browser. Install with the one command, or clear the browser's mark on the copy you have: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Mercury.app Then open Mercury again. If you installed it in your own Applications folder, use ~/Applications/Mercury.app instead.
documents.s: "Mercury is damaged and can't be opened. You should move it to the Trash."

documents.t: Open Mercury first and click Done on the warning; the button appears after that, for about an hour. Still nothing? Your Mac may be managed by an organisation that only allows App Store or identified developers' apps. Ask your administrator, or install with the one command.

documents.t: You probably have the build for the other chip. Check the Apple menu → About This Mac, then reinstall with the one command, which picks the right one. Mercury Desktop needs macOS 11 or newer.

documents.t: That's the Optimus plugin asking for what it needs to use your computer: Accessibility (mouse and keyboard), Screen Recording (seeing the screen) and the Microphone (if you talk to it). Turn them on in System Settings → Privacy & Security. macOS asks you to confirm Screen Recording again about once a month.
