documents.t: Mercury Desktop updates itself: an Update button appears in the top right when a new version is out. The download is signed with Mercury's update key and checked before it installs, so macOS doesn't stop it. See Updating Mercury. To reinstall or go back to a specific version, run the install command again (with MERCURY_VERSION for a specific one).

Quit Mercury Desktop and drag Mercury from Applications to the Trash. Optional, the app's own settings and caches: rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/sh.mercuryagent.desktop \ ~/Library/Caches/sh.mercuryagent.desktop \ ~/Library/Logs/sh.mercuryagent.desktop Saved logins to remote Mercurys are in Keychain Access under sh.mercuryagent.desktop. Removing the app doesn't remove Mercury itself (the runtime, your memory and chats in ~/.mercury). To remove that too, run mercury uninstall. It asks before deleting your data (--keep-data keeps it, --purge-data deletes it).

Mercury Desktop is the app for Mercury. It can install Mercury on your computer for you, or connect to a Mercury you already run on a server, a home machine or Mercury Cloud. One app can hold several connections at once. It runs on macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel, macOS 11 or newer), Windows 10 and 11 (x64) and Linux (x64).

The macOS guide has every step and every fix in one page. Paste this into Terminal: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install-desktop.sh | sh It picks the build for your Mac (Apple Silicon or Intel), downloads it from the GitHub release, checks its SHA-256 against the one GitHub recorded and checks its code signature, puts Mercury in Applications and opens it. If anything doesn't match, it installs nothing. Run it again any time to reinstall; a running Mercury Desktop is closed first, while Mercury itself keeps running. Read the script before you run it if you like. Installed this way, Mercury opens on the first try with no security prompt: macOS only asks about apps a browser downloaded, and the app isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID yet. Options: MERCURY_VERSION=1.5.0 installs a specific version, MERCURY_APP_DIR=~/Applications installs somewhere else, and MERCURY_NO_OPEN=1 doesn't open it afterwards.

Get it from the download page. It picks the right build for your computer. Every build is also on GitHub Releases. Computer File Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 and newer) Mercury_<version>_aarch64.dmg Mac with an Intel chip Mercury_<version>_x64.dmg Windows Mercury_<version>_x64-setup.exe (or the .msi for managed installs) Linux Mercury_<version>_amd64.AppImage, .deb or .rpm

Mercury Desktop 1.5.0 isn't code-signed with an Apple or Windows certificate yet, so your computer asks once before it opens it. Signing is coming in a later release. Updates are different: every update is signed with Mercury's update key and checked before it installs (see Updating Mercury).

Installed with the Terminal command above? There's nothing to do. With the .dmg: Open the .dmg and drag Mercury to Applications. Open Mercury. macOS says "Apple could not verify Mercury is free of malware". Click Done. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security. Under Security, click Open Anyway next to Mercury, then confirm with your password. On older macOS versions you can right-click Mercury in Applications and choose Open instead. If macOS says Mercury "is damaged and can't be opened", clear the download flag and open it again: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Mercury.app
Run Mercury_<version>_x64-setup.exe. If Microsoft Defender SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway.

# AppImage: any distribution chmod +x Mercury_*_amd64.AppImage ./Mercury_*_amd64.AppImage # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install ./Mercury_*_amd64.deb # Fedora / openSUSE sudo dnf install ./Mercury-*.x86_64.rpm

The first screen checks this computer for a running Mercury and offers three ways in. Use the Mercury here. Mercury is already installed on this computer. If it's running, the app connects. If it's stopped, Start Mercury starts it. If it's too old for the app, Update Mercury updates it first. Install Mercury here. The app downloads the Mercury release for your computer, checks its SHA-256 against the release's checksums.txt, installs it to ~/.mercury/bin and runs it as a service. You don't need a terminal. Then it walks you through choosing a model. Connect elsewhere. Mercury runs on another machine: a server, a home computer, a phone on Termux, or Mercury Cloud. On this computer the app signs in with Mercury's local attach token, so there is nothing to type.
documents.s: First run: where should Mercury run?

documents.t: You need the address the other Mercury is reachable at, usually through a tunnel such as Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel (Mercury itself only listens on 127.0.0.1). Then choose one of two ways to sign in: Sign in with that Mercury's dashboard username and password. The owner of that Mercury has to approve this device. The app shows "Waiting for the owner to approve this device" and a 5-character code. The owner approves it from Telegram or WhatsApp (approve K7Q2M), from /server or mercury server approve K7Q2M on that computer, or in Mercury Desktop on that computer. Nobody answering within 10 minutes means no. Device token. The owner makes a token on that computer with /server token <name> (or mercury devices add "<name>") and gives it to you. It starts with mdt_ and is shown once. The app keeps each connection's credentials in your system keychain. Removing a connection in Settings → Connections also revokes its token on that Mercury. See Remote access & security for what an approved device can and can't do, and how the owner controls it.

Add as many connections as you like and switch between them from the top bar. The app checks every connection for updates, not just the one you're using, and shows each in its updates panel (see Updating Mercury).

Chat and Code. Conversations, and a coding workspace per project. Research. A research bar with live progress, sources read and failed with reasons, and a report you can export as PDF or Word. Bots. Create and run bots, and read their results in one inbox. Notifications when a reply, a research run or a bot needs you. Settings → About shows the app's and every server's version and has Check for updates.
documents.s: What else is in the app

documents.t: Mercury only listens on 127.0.0.1. To use it from another device (Mercury Desktop on your laptop, the web dashboard from your phone), you put a tunnel or proxy in front of it, such as Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel. Mercury treats anything that arrives that way as remote, even when the tunnel runs on the same machine. You stay in control: a new device needs your approval, and a remote device has to ask you before it does anything that could take over your Mercury.

A request is from this computer only when it comes from 127.0.0.1 and carries no proxy or tunnel header (Forwarded, X-Forwarded-*, X-Real-IP, CF-Connecting-IP, Tailscale-* and similar) and names localhost as its host. Mercury Desktop and the terminal on this computer use Mercury's local attach token, which is never accepted through a tunnel. A request straight to this machine that names some other host is refused, which blocks DNS-rebinding attacks. If you run Mercury behind your own proxy on another name, add that name to web.allowedHosts in mercury.yaml.

When a remote device needs your permission, Mercury asks you with a 5-character code. You answer once, from any of these: Telegram, WhatsApp or another connected chat: reply approve K7Q2M or deny K7Q2M. Only an admin of that chat can answer. The terminal on this computer: /server approve K7Q2M in chat, or mercury server approve K7Q2M in a shell. Mercury Desktop on this computer: Approve or Deny on the card it shows. The device that asked can never answer its own question. Nobody answering within 10 minutes means no.

Signing in from another device with the dashboard password doesn't give it access straight away. The device shows "Waiting for the owner to approve this device" and the code, and gets its token once you approve. Signing in from this computer needs no approval.

An approved device can chat, run things under your current permission mode and read results. These need your approval each time: the terminal (and it's off entirely for remote devices unless you turn it on); changing the workspace folder, turning Allow All on, or changing the permissions file; operator or full-access bots, raw bot permissions and bot imports; installing skills from a URL, and plugins; channel settings and tokens, letting someone into a channel or making them an admin, Signal linking; Mercury Cloud sign-in, and changing a provider's server address without a new key; restarting Mercury, changing the password or username, and revoking another device; a board's working folder; starting a server update. Mercury Cloud asks you the same way before it turns Allow All on or installs a skill. If a device repeats a request while your answer is pending, Mercury doesn't ask you again.

Each approved device gets a device token (mdt_…) that Mercury Desktop keeps in the system keychain. Expiry. A device not used for 30 days is signed out and needs your approval again. Limit. 10 devices at most. Mercury checks the limit before it asks you. New location. When a known device connects from an address it hasn't used before, Mercury tells you. Revoke. Revoking a device cuts its open connections at once. Password change. Changing the dashboard password signs out every other browser, and can sign out all devices too. To make a token by hand for a device that can't sign in itself, run /server token <name> (or mercury devices add "<name>") on this computer. It's shown once.

/server in the terminal chat opens a menu for remote access. It works only on the computer Mercury runs on: in the terminal, an attached terminal, or Mercury Desktop there. mercury server gives the same commands from a shell. /server open the menu /server status what can connect, and how /server on | off allow or refuse other devices /server approve <code> let a waiting device or action through (deny <code> to refuse) /server devices paired devices · /server revoke <id|name> · /server revoke-all /server token <name> make a token for a device by hand (shown once) /server allow-ip <ip|range> · remove-ip <ip|range> · allow-any /server shell on|off the terminal for remote devices (each command still asks you) /server expire <days>|never · /server limit <n> /server check the security check · /server log the security log The settings live in ~/.mercury/remote.json and apply at once: Setting Default Meaning enabled true Other devices may connect. /server off refuses them all. allowIps empty (any) Addresses or CIDR ranges allowed to connect. allowShell false Whether remote devices get a terminal. Each command still asks you. maxDevices 10 How many devices can be paired. idleDays 30 Days unused before a device is signed out.

With an address list set, Mercury refuses any client whose address isn't on it. It needs a tunnel that passes the real client address (Tailscale and Cloudflare do). If the tunnel hides it, Mercury refuses the client rather than guessing, and /server warns you.

mercury doctor --security It checks the dashboard password, devices, file permissions on Mercury's secrets and how your tunnel forwards requests. Every mercury doctor run shows a one-line summary of it, and /server check shows the same findings. The security log, ~/.mercury/security/audit.jsonl, records failed and locked sign-ins, pairings, approvals and refusals, revocations, expired devices, new locations, blocked requests, password and setting changes, and started updates. /server log shows the latest entries.

A proxy without forwarding headers looks local. If you put Mercury behind your own proxy (plain nginx, for example), make it send X-Forwarded-For and keep the original host. A proxy that sends neither and rewrites the host to localhost makes remote requests look local. The attach token still protects the most sensitive operations, and the security check flags it. An approved device is trusted like you while it's paired. It answers its own Ask Me prompts and runs things under your permission mode. Revoke a device you no longer use. Keep the tunnel private if you can. A Tailscale tailnet, or Cloudflare Access in front of a Cloudflare Tunnel, means only your devices can reach the sign-in page at all.

There are two things to keep current: Mercury Desktop (the app) and Mercury itself (the runtime, on this computer or on a server). Both update the same careful way: download in the background, check the download, install, and confirm the new version works. If it doesn't, they put the old version back. Nothing pops up uninvited. The one exception is an update marked as required, described below.

Mercury publishes one update notice at https://mercuryagent.sh/updates/manifest.json. It lists the newest versions with their release notes, the oldest version still supported, and any message for people running Mercury. The notice is signed. Mercury and Mercury Desktop ignore a notice whose signature doesn't check out, and an older notice than one they've already seen. If the notice can't be fetched (you're offline, a firewall blocks it), nothing is blocked. Mercury falls back to asking GitHub or npm for the newest version and keeps working. Mercury checks at most every 6 hours. Check for updates asks right away.

When something can be updated, an Update button appears at the top right of the window, like Chrome's. It covers the app and every server the app connects to. Its colour rises the longer an update waits: Waiting Colour Under 2 days Grey 2 to 4 days Accent 4 to 7 days Amber 7 days or more Red A security update is red from the start. A required update reads Update required and can't be hidden.

Click the button to open the panel. It has a row for Mercury Desktop and one for each server with an update: the version you have and the new one, with What's new to read the notes before you update; the action: Download, Restart to update, or Update server; live progress: bytes, speed, time left and the current step; Later, which hides that update for 24 hours. When more than one thing can be updated, Update all updates them together.

With Download updates automatically on (the default), the app downloads a new version in the background. Nothing installs until you restart. A dropped connection doesn't start the download over. The app resumes from the bytes it has, even after you quit and reopen it. The app waits up to 30 seconds for data before it reconnects, and tries up to 5 times. Cancel stops a download and keeps what it has. Resume download continues from there. A download only counts as ready after its signature checks out. One that doesn't match is deleted, so the next try starts clean.

Restart to update installs the update and reopens the app. If a reply is still coming in, the app asks first. The reply keeps running on the server and is there when the app is back. Install a downloaded update when I quit (on by default) installs it the next time you quit, so the next start is the new version. If an update fails 3 times, the app stops retrying that version and offers Download from website instead.

Settings → About has Check for updates. It checks Mercury Desktop and every server you connect to in one go, then says either "Everything is up to date" or what it found. Update everything then updates each server that can update itself and restarts the app last, once the servers are done. The tray menu has Check for Updates… too.

A server's row in the updates panel has Update server. From a device other than that server's own computer, the owner approves the update first (the same 5-character code as new devices). The panel follows the update through the server's restart and reconnects when it's back.

mercury update # what's new, and whether an update is required mercury update check # ask again now mercury upgrade --check # the same, from upgrade mercury upgrade # update to the newest version mercury upgrade --now # don't wait for running work mercury upgrade --force # reinstall even when already on the newest version With Mercury running, mercury upgrade asks the running Mercury to do the update, so it can wait for running work and come back as the new version. With Mercury stopped, the command does every step itself and leaves Mercury stopped.

Waits for running work. A reply, a queued message or a bot run finishes first, for up to 10 minutes. Update now without waiting in the app (or --now) skips the wait. Downloads the new version, resuming if the connection drops, and checks it against the release's SHA-256 checksums. An npm install fetches the exact version into npm's cache. Backs up the current program and Mercury's settings files in ~/.mercury. Stops Mercury, installs the new version and starts it. Checks it works. The new version must answer as the new version within 90 seconds. If it doesn't, rolls back. Mercury puts the old program and settings back and starts the old version. If the new version crashes on start, this happens in about 15 seconds. Mercury is offline only between steps 4 and 6, usually a few seconds. If a release is announced but its files aren't published yet, the update stops before anything changes and says to try again later. That doesn't count as a failure. If an update to one version really fails 3 times, Mercury stops offering it on its own. mercury upgrade still tries, and shows what went wrong. A Mercury running from a source checkout doesn't update itself. Update it with git pull and a build.

Sometimes a version has to go, usually for a security fix. The update notice then names the oldest supported version and says why. Mercury Desktop shows a full-screen notice that Escape and clicking outside don't close. It explains the reason and has Update now with live progress. You can still minimise the window. Continue without updating asks you to tick every box first: I understand this version has a known problem that the update fixes. Mercury may stop working with my servers or some features until I update. I'm responsible for anything exposed while I stay on this version. I'll update as soon as I can. That lasts until the app restarts or for 24 hours, whichever comes first, and the top-right button stays red meanwhile. The same screen appears when the server the window is connected to is below its required version. If you can't update that server yourself, it says what the owner has to run. On a server, a required update shows in the terminal every time Mercury starts, in mercury doctor and in mercury update, and /update ignore can't silence it.

After Mercury Desktop or a server you connect to moves to a newer version, the app shows a toast once: "Mercury Desktop updated to 1.5.0 · What's new". It opens the release notes. Settings → About → What's new opens them again. In the terminal, /whatsnew shows the notes for the version you run.

The update notice can carry a short message for people on certain versions. Mercury Desktop shows an information message once as a toast, and a warning or critical one as a banner under the top bar. You can dismiss a message, except a critical one marked as permanent. The terminal shows each message once when Mercury starts.

Mercury can be built from source two ways: Standard build — produces the regular ESM bundle in dist/, the same artifact published to npm. Good for local development, contributions, and npm link. Standalone executable — produces a single self-contained binary that embeds the JS runtime and the entire Mercury bundle. End-users do not need Node.js installed.
Node.js ≥ 20 — required for the build toolchain. Bun ≥ 1.3 — only needed if you're building standalone binaries. Install Bun: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash

git clone https://github.com/cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent.git cd mercury-agent npm install npm run build # tsup + post-build (UI, static assets, wasm) npm start # runs node dist/index.js To use your local build as the global mercury command: npm link mercury --help
Mercury uses bun build --compile to embed the entire bundle into a single platform-native binary. The resulting file runs on machines with no Node.js, no Bun, and no dependencies installed.
npm install npm run build:bin # builds the binary for your current OS/arch ./release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 --help

Command Targets Behavior on existing build npm run build:bin host only skip if already built npm run build:bin:all all 5 platforms skip per-target npm run build:bin:force host only overwrite npm run build:bin:all:force all 5 platforms overwrite Supported targets for --all: macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon) macOS x64 (Intel) Linux x64 Linux arm64 Windows x64

The build script reads the version from package.json and writes binaries into a versioned subfolder. Older builds are never overwritten — you can keep many versions side-by-side. release/ ├── latest → symlink to the most-recent version ├── v1.1.9/ │ ├── mercury-macos-arm64 │ ├── mercury-macos-x64 │ ├── mercury-linux-x64 │ ├── mercury-linux-arm64 │ ├── mercury-win-x64.exe │ └── checksums.txt (SHA-256 for every binary in the folder) └── v1.2.0/ └── ... Bump version in package.json before building and the script automatically creates a new folder. If a binary for the current version+target already exists, the script skips it (printing ↷ skip (already built)) unless you pass --force. Verify integrity with the generated checksums: cd release/v1.1.9 shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt # mercury-macos-arm64: OK

Bun ships its own runtime per target, so you can build all five platforms from any one host (e.g. produce a Windows .exe from your Mac): npm run build:bin:all Native node modules can't cross-compile, but Mercury's only native dep (better-sqlite3) is optional — at runtime the binary falls back to sql.js (pure JS + wasm). Cross-compiled binaries are fully functional.

Unsigned binaries trigger Gatekeeper on first launch. For local use, right-click → Open once and macOS will remember the choice. For distribution: codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: Your Name" release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 xcrun notarytool submit release/v1.1.9/mercury-macos-arm64 --apple-id ... --wait Why Bun and not pkg / Node SEA? Mercury's dependency graph includes ESM modules with top-level await (ink, yoga-layout). Both pkg and Node.js Single Executable Applications require CommonJS entry points and can't transform top-level await. Bun runs ESM natively and embeds its own runtime, so it sidesteps the whole problem.

bun: command not found — install Bun with curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash, then either restart your shell or use the explicit path ~/.bun/bin/bun. ERROR: dist/index.js not found — the bin script depends on the standard build. The build:bin npm script chains both; if you ran the bin script directly, prefix with npm run build. Binary silently exits with code 0 — usually means the package.json version lookup failed. The build pipeline injects the version at compile time via tsup --define. If you've modified the entry file, make sure the pkgVersion fallback path remains intact (see src/index.ts). Stale release/latest symlink — re-running any build:bin command repairs the symlink to point at the current package.json version.

Mercury runs on any modern Linux distro with glibc ≥ 2.31 (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, Fedora 34+, Arch, etc.) on x86_64 or arm64.

curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh The installer picks the right binary for your CPU, verifies the SHA-256 checksum, places it at ~/.mercury/bin/mercury, and adds that directory to your shell PATH (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.config/fish/config.fish). After install: exec $SHELL -l mercury --version :::note Older x86-64 CPUs The default Linux x64 build uses AVX2. On a CPU without it (Intel before 2013, some VMs) the installer picks the baseline build automatically — from /proc/cpuinfo, or by switching after an Illegal instruction crash. To force it: MERCURY_ASSET=mercury-linux-x64-baseline curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh. :::
npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent Requires Node.js 22+. Recommended via nvm so you avoid sudo for global packages.
documents.s: Via npm (if you already have Node)

documents.t: CPU Asset x86_64 mercury-linux-x64 aarch64 / arm64 (Raspberry Pi 4/5 64-bit, AWS Graviton, etc.) mercury-linux-arm64 Check yours: uname -m # x86_64 or aarch64 For armv7 (32-bit Pi, older boards), use the npm route — there's no prebuilt 32-bit ARM binary yet.
curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | MERCURY_VERSION=1.1.9 sh
curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | \ sudo MERCURY_INSTALL=/usr/local MERCURY_NO_PATH=1 sh This puts mercury at /usr/local/bin/mercury (already on most users' PATH).
To run Mercury as a long-lived daemon under systemd, see the Daemon Mode → System Service guide.
Mercury's TUI works fine over SSH. For long sessions, run it inside tmux or screen: tmux new -s mercury mercury # detach: Ctrl-b d # reattach: tmux attach -t mercury
rm -rf ~/.mercury # remove the PATH line from your shell rc npm uninstall -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

Mercury supports macOS 11 (Big Sur) and later, on both Apple Silicon (arm64) and Intel (x64).

curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh This downloads the latest binary for your CPU, verifies its SHA-256 against the published checksums.txt, and installs to ~/.mercury/bin/mercury. Your shell PATH is updated in ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc if you use bash). After install: exec $SHELL -l # reload PATH mercury --version
npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury Requires Node.js 22+. Install Node via nvm, Homebrew (brew install node@22), or the official installer.
documents.s: Via npm (if you already have Node)

documents.t: The installer auto-selects: CPU Asset Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) mercury-macos-arm64 Intel mercury-macos-x64 To verify which architecture your Mac uses: uname -m # arm64 or x86_64
curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | MERCURY_VERSION=1.1.9 sh
curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | \ MERCURY_INSTALL=/opt/mercury MERCURY_NO_PATH=1 sh Add /opt/mercury/bin to your PATH manually.

The binary is currently unsigned. On first run macOS may quarantine it. Either: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.mercury/bin/mercury …or right-click the binary in Finder and choose Open to whitelist it once. A signed/notarized build is on the roadmap.
rm -rf ~/.mercury # then remove the PATH line added to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc For npm installs: npm uninstall -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

Mercury runs on Android via Termux, giving you a real coding agent in your pocket. It also works in other minimal environments like iSH (iOS), Alpine containers, and Raspberry Pi.

Android 7.0+ Termux installed from F-Droid or GitHub Releases (the Play Store build is unmaintained — do not use it) ~500 MB free storage for Node.js, Mercury, and native module compilation Network access

Termux is the recommended path on Android because the prebuilt Linux binaries target glibc, while Termux uses bionic libc. Use the npm route: pkg update && pkg upgrade -y pkg install nodejs-lts git python make clang pkg-config -y npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury nodejs-lts provides Node 22+ (required since 1.3.1) and npm. Python, Make, Clang, and pkg-config are required when npm needs to build native dependencies such as better-sqlite3 for Android's bionic libc. Do not use Mercury's standalone Linux binary on Termux.

Let Mercury read/write files in your Android storage: termux-setup-storage # grants ~/storage/ symlinks: ~/storage/shared, ~/storage/downloads, etc. Now you can point Mercury at projects in ~/storage/shared/Projects/....

Android may stop Termux processes when the app is swiped away or the device sleeps. For the best available background behavior: Install Termux:API and Termux:Boot from the same source as Termux (F-Droid or GitHub), then install the API commands: pkg install termux-api termux-wake-lock Disable battery optimization for Termux in Settings → Apps → Termux → Battery. Start Mercury with its supported daemon command: mercury start Termux does not run systemd, so mercury service install is intentionally unsupported. To request startup after reboot, create ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury: mkdir -p ~/.termux/boot cat > ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury <<'EOF' #!/data/data/com.termux/files/usr/bin/sh termux-wake-lock mercury start EOF chmod +x ~/.termux/boot/start-mercury Termux:Boot only runs after the user has opened its app once, and Android/OEM background restrictions can still stop Mercury. A wakelock reduces suspension but increases battery use; release it with termux-wake-unlock when Mercury is stopped. This setup cannot guarantee server-like 24/7 availability. See Daemon Mode for mercury start, mercury status, and mercury stop details.
documents.s: Keep Mercury running in the background

documents.t: A common Termux setup: run Mercury's Telegram integration on your phone so you can chat with it from any device. mercury doctor # enable Telegram, paste bot token mercury start

No prebuilt binary — must use npm. The standalone installer (install.sh) won't work on Termux because of glibc/bionic differences. No system service manager — systemd service install/status/uninstall is unavailable. Use Mercury's daemon commands and optionally Termux:Boot. No guaranteed background uptime — wakelocks and Termux:Boot cannot override every Android or OEM process-killing policy. TUI rendering — Mercury's interface assumes a wide terminal. Rotate landscape or pair Termux with an external keyboard for the best experience. Background limits — Aggressive OEMs (Xiaomi, Oppo, Huawei) need extra battery-optimization tweaks beyond the standard Android settings. Storage permission — Required for accessing project files outside $HOME.
mercury upgrade …or: npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@latest

iSH runs an Alpine Linux user-space on iOS. Mercury works there via npm: apk add nodejs npm npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury Performance is limited — iSH emulates x86 via usermode, so expect slow startup. Best used for read-only / chat-style sessions.

Alpine uses musl libc, so the standalone Linux binary won't load. Use npm: apk add --no-cache nodejs npm git npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent This applies to Docker images based on alpine:* as well.

64-bit Pi OS (Pi 3/4/5): the standard Linux installer works — pulls mercury-linux-arm64. 32-bit Pi OS or armv6 (Pi Zero, Pi 1): no prebuilt binary; install via npm: curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_20.x | sudo -E bash - sudo apt install -y nodejs npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent

If your platform isn't listed and the binary doesn't run (Exec format error, missing libc), the npm route always works as long as Node.js 20+ is available. If Node isn't packaged for your OS, see Build From Source.
Setup Telegram integration — control Mercury from anywhere Daemon Mode — keep it running 24/7
Mercury runs natively on Windows 10 (build 1809+) and Windows 11, on x64. Native arm64 binaries are not yet published — on Windows on ARM, use WSL or the npm route.

Open PowerShell (any version) and run: irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex This downloads mercury-win-x64.exe, verifies its SHA-256, installs it to %USERPROFILE%\.mercury\bin\mercury.exe, and prepends that directory to your user PATH. No admin required. After install, open a new terminal window and run: mercury --version Execution policy If PowerShell blocks the script, allow user scripts for the current session: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex
npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent mercury Requires Node.js 22+ (since 1.3.1). Install from nodejs.org or via winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS.
documents.s: Via npm (if you already have Node)

documents.t: $env:MERCURY_VERSION = '1.1.9' irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex

$env:MERCURY_INSTALL = 'C:\Tools\mercury' $env:MERCURY_NO_PATH = '1' irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex Then add C:\Tools\mercury\bin to your PATH manually via System Properties → Environment Variables.

Mercury's TUI uses Unicode, true color, and ANSI escapes. For best results, use Windows Terminal (default on Windows 11, free from the Store on Windows 10). The legacy cmd.exe window may render box-drawing characters incorrectly.
If you prefer a Linux environment, install Mercury inside WSL2: wsl --install -d Ubuntu # inside WSL: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh Follow the Linux guide from there.
The .exe is unsigned today. SmartScreen may show "Windows protected your PC" on first run — click More info → Run anyway. A code-signed build is on the roadmap.

Remove-Item -Recurse -Force $env:USERPROFILE\.mercury Then remove the entry from your user PATH (System Properties → Environment Variables). For npm installs: npm uninstall -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent
Setup Daemon Mode → System Service for running Mercury as a Windows service

Run mercury for the first time. The onboarding wizard asks for: Your name — used by the agent to address you Agent name — defaults to "Mercury", customize it LLM providers — choose one or more: DeepSeek, OpenAI, Anthropic, Grok, Ollama Cloud, Ollama Local, Atomic Chat, or OpenAI Compatible Model selection — after each valid key, Mercury fetches recommended chat models and lets you choose a default Telegram bot token — optional, for remote access in private 1:1 chats Provider keys are validated by format and then by fetching available models. If model discovery fails, Mercury asks you to re-enter the key instead of accepting random text. If you enable Telegram during first-time setup, Mercury starts a temporary pairing flow: send /start to your bot in Telegram, copy the pairing code you receive there, then paste that code into the CLI to finish setup. All config is stored in ~/.mercury/ — nothing in your project directory. Masked keys When reconfiguring with mercury doctor, existing API keys are shown masked like sk-x••••4f2a. Press Enter to keep the current value, or paste a new key to replace it.

Recommended: mercury up The easiest way to run Mercury persistently. Installs the system service if needed, starts the daemon, and ensures it's running. mercury up If Mercury is already running, mercury up just confirms it and shows the PID. If the service isn't installed yet, it installs it first, then starts the daemon.

mercury start Starts Mercury as a background daemon by default. Telegram becomes your primary interface. Logs go to ~/.mercury/daemon.log. Stale PID files are auto-cleaned. Includes crash recovery with exponential backoff.

mercury start --foreground Runs Mercury attached to your terminal with the Ink TUI interface. Press Ctrl+C to exit. The CLI supports chat, coding workspace mode, progress views, and interactive permission prompts. Shorthand: mercury start -f. When running in background mode, you can stop it with: mercury stop
Add --verbose to any start command to see debug logs on stderr: mercury start --verbose

Mercury offers two ways to work on a repository: a CLI workspace (terminal-based IDE with keyboard navigation) and a Web Workspace IDE (full graphical editor in the browser). Both share the same backend tools and Git operations.
Open http://127.0.0.1:6174/workspace in the dashboard to launch the browser-based editor.

Click Change Folder at the top to pick the repository you want to work on. The path is persisted to web-chat-settings.json in your Mercury home directory, so the workspace remembers it across restarts.

A collapsible tree of the current workspace folder. Click a folder to expand/collapse; click a file to open it in a new tab. The refresh icon rescans the tree. The left panel is resizable — drag the right edge to grow or shrink it.

Multi-tab — every file you open becomes a tab. A dot next to the filename means unsaved changes. Syntax highlighting for TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go, Ruby, Swift, Java, C/C++, JSON, YAML, Markdown, and more (powered by react-syntax-highlighter). Editable overlay — click anywhere in the code to start editing. Cmd/Ctrl+S saves the active file. The bottom info bar shows the file path, language, and a Save button for dirty files.

Terminal tab — runs shell commands in the workspace root using /api/terminal/exec. Includes command history (↑/↓ to recall). Chat tab — a focused conversation thread scoped to this workspace. The agent sees the open file and can apply edits directly. Maximize / Minimize — click the Maximize icon in the top-right of the panel header to expand the bottom panel to fill the whole workspace area. Click again to restore. The panel is resizable — drag the top border to set its height.

The Git panel mirrors the most useful parts of VS Code's Source Control view. Pull, Push, Refresh icons across the top. The refresh icon spins while it loads and shows a brief Refreshed confirmation. Status — staged and unstaged files are listed separately. Hover a file to stage / unstage it. Click to view a unified diff. Branches — see the current branch and switch to another (with optional create to make a new branch). Commit log — the last 15 commits with author and message. Commit message box with two helpers: The sparkle icon runs AI Commit Message Generation (POST /api/git/generate-commit-message). Mercury auto-stages any unstaged changes first, then asks the configured default provider to draft a conventional-commit message from the diff. The generated message is inserted into the box for you to review or edit before committing. Commit button — commits the staged files with the message. The right panel's resizer sits on its left edge — drag it left to grow the panel, right to shrink.
All three panels (Explorer, Bottom, Source Control) are independently resizable. Drag the divider between any two panels to adjust.
If you prefer staying in the terminal, Mercury includes a CLI IDE-style workspace mode for repository-focused coding.

You can enter workspace mode in multiple ways: /code and choose workspace /code workspace /ws open <path> Once active, Mercury switches to coding context for that repository. Agent responses appear in the normal scrollable chat view so you can always see full output.
Use programming modes to control behavior: /code plan — analysis/planning first, minimal code changes /code execute — implementation mode /code off — return to normal conversation behavior

Shortcut Action Ctrl+P Plan mode Ctrl+X Execute mode Ctrl+E Focus explorer pane Ctrl+G Focus git pane Ctrl+J Toggle right panel between chat and git Tab Cycle focus: explorer → code → right panel Esc Return to explorer (or exit workspace from explorer) Ctrl+Q Exit workspace Shift+Enter Insert newline (multi-line input) Alt+Enter Insert newline (fallback for terminals that don't distinguish Shift+Enter)

Focus Keys Action Explorer ↑ ↓ Move selection Explorer ← → Collapse / expand folder Explorer Enter Open selected file Code ↑ ↓ Scroll code ±1 line Code PgUp PgDn Scroll code ±15 lines Code Ctrl+U Ctrl+D Scroll code ±10 lines (vim-style) Chat ↑ ↓ Scroll agent output ±1 line Chat PgUp PgDn Scroll agent output ±10 lines Chat Ctrl+U Ctrl+D Scroll agent output ±8 lines Git ↑ ↓ Move through changed files Git Enter Stage selected file

Command Description /ws open <path> Open a directory in workspace mode /ws refresh Refresh file tree + git status /ws focus <area> Focus a panel: explorer, code, git, or chat /ws stage <file|all> Stage one file or all changes /ws commit <message> Commit staged changes /ws undo <file> Revert file changes /ws toggle-chat Toggle right panel between chat and git /ws chat-scroll <n> Scroll agent output by n lines /ws exit Exit workspace mode back to general chat

Workspace mode (CLI and web) supports explicit delegation and backgrounding: /code agent <task> — delegate coding work to a sub-agent /bg current — move active in-flight work to background /bg list — inspect all background tasks (shell + sub-agent) /bg <id> — view task details/output (IDs use friendly names like swift-fox) /bg cancel <id> — cancel running background work /bg stop <id> / /bg kill <id> — aliases for cancel /bg killall / /bg stopall — cancel all running background tasks This lets you continue coding/chatting while long operations run asynchronously.

During long-running tasks, Mercury shows real-time progress: The status bar displays the current tool/action (e.g., ● step 5 · ✂️ Editing App.tsx) Heartbeat messages escalate timing (20s → 30s → 45s → 60s) to reduce noise Use /progress to see the last 10 completed steps with timing Consecutive identical tool calls are collapsed (e.g., "Read 3 files")

The Source Control panel calls these endpoints under the hood. They are useful if you want to script against the local instance. Method Path Purpose GET /api/git/status Staged + unstaged file list GET /api/git/branches All branches with current + upstream POST /api/git/checkout Switch branch ({ branch, create? }) GET /api/git/diff?path=...&staged=... Unified diff GET /api/git/log?limit=15 Commit log POST /api/git/stage Stage files ({ files: [...] } or ["."] for all) POST /api/git/unstage Unstage files POST /api/git/commit Commit ({ message }) POST /api/git/push Push ({ remote?, branch?, setUpstream? }) POST /api/git/pull Pull from upstream POST /api/git/generate-commit-message AI-generated conventional commit from staged diff

Mercury connects to Discord as a bot, providing a real-time conversational interface with slash commands, streaming responses, rich embeds, and an organization-style access model with admin roles and pairing codes.

A Discord account with permission to manage a server (or create one). A Discord Bot Token from the Discord Developer Portal. A server (guild) where you have admin privileges to invite the bot. Platform note Discord integration requires Node.js 18 or later (the discord.js v14 dependency). The standalone binary includes all necessary dependencies automatically.

Go to Discord Developer Portal and click New Application. Give it a name (e.g. "Mercury") and click Create. Navigate to Bot in the left sidebar and click Reset Token to generate a bot token. Copy it — you'll need it in Step 4. Under Privileged Gateway Intents, enable: Message Content Intent — required for Mercury to read your messages. Server Members Intent — required for the access control system. Click Save Changes.

Navigate to OAuth2 → URL Generator in the left sidebar. Under Scopes, select: bot, applications.commands. Under Bot Permissions, select: Send Messages Read Message History Use Slash Commands Attach Files Embed Links Copy the generated URL and open it in your browser to invite the bot to your server.
documents.s: Step 2: Invite the Bot to Your Server

documents.t: In your Discord server, go to Server Settings → Roles. Create a role named Mercury Admin (or any name you prefer). Assign this role to yourself and anyone else who should have admin control over Mercury.

Run mercury doctor and select Discord when prompted, or set these environment variables: # Required DISCORD_ENABLED=true DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN=your-bot-token-here # Optional — restrict to a specific server DISCORD_GUILD_ID= # Optional — restrict to a specific channel DISCORD_CHANNEL_ID= # Optional — admin role name (default: "Mercury Admin") DISCORD_ADMIN_ROLE_NAME=Mercury Admin # Optional — enable streaming (edit-in-place) responses (default: true) DISCORD_STREAMING=true Or add them to ~/.mercury/.env.

Start Mercury: mercury up In Discord, type /start in any channel where the bot is present. Mercury will display a pairing code. Enter it in the CLI: mercury discord pair <code> You are now the Discord admin. Other users can request access with /start, and you can approve them.

Mercury Discord uses an organization access model with admins and members. Role Description Can approve requests? Admin First user to pair (or anyone with the configured admin role). Can approve/reject access requests, promote/demote users. Yes Member Approved by an admin. Can send messages and receive responses. No Pending Sent /start but not yet approved. No

Command Description mercury discord list Show approved admins, members, and pending requests mercury discord approve <userId> Approve a pending request by Discord user ID mercury discord reject <userId> Reject a pending request mercury discord remove <userId> Remove an approved admin or member mercury discord promote <userId> Promote a member to admin mercury discord demote <userId> Demote an admin to member mercury discord reset Clear all Discord access (start fresh)

Feature Description Slash commands Built-in /start, /status, /progress, /permissions, /models, and more Streaming responses Messages are edited in place as tokens arrive (toggle with DISCORD_STREAMING) Rich embeds Task progress and completion banners use Discord embeds for visual clarity DM support Private conversations work alongside server channels Admin role integration Discord server roles can be used for access control Rate limiting Built-in busy detection and rate limiting for shared servers File handling Send and receive file attachments

Variable Description Default DISCORD_ENABLED Enable/disable Discord channel false DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN Bot token from Discord Developer Portal — DISCORD_GUILD_ID Restrict to a specific server. Leave empty for all servers. — DISCORD_CHANNEL_ID Restrict to a specific channel. Leave empty for all channels. — DISCORD_ADMIN_ROLE_NAME Discord role name that grants admin access Mercury Admin DISCORD_STREAMING Enable real-time streaming (edit-in-place) true

Bot doesn't respond to messages Make sure Message Content Intent is enabled in the Discord Developer Portal. Check that DISCORD_ENABLED=true and DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN is set correctly. Run mercury logs to check for connection errors. Bot joins servers it shouldn't Set DISCORD_GUILD_ID to restrict the bot to your server only. If the bot joins an unconfigured guild, it will automatically leave and log a warning. Slash commands not showing up Slash commands are registered when the bot starts. Restart Mercury (mercury restart) if commands don't appear immediately. Discord caches slash commands — it may take up to an hour for changes to propagate globally. Streaming not working Ensure DISCORD_STREAMING=true (default). Discord rate-limits message edits — Mercury handles this automatically by falling back to new messages when rate-limited.

Mercury can act as your GitHub companion — creating pull requests, reviewing PRs, managing issues, and making co-authored commits — all through natural conversation. When configured, five GitHub tools are registered alongside Mercury's built-in toolset, letting you manage repositories without leaving the terminal or Telegram. Conditional availability GitHub tools only appear when GITHUB_TOKEN is configured via mercury doctor. Without a token, these tools are not registered and won't be available in conversation.

Co-authored commits — Mercury's avatar appears alongside yours on every commit it helps with Pull requests — "Create a PR for this change" and Mercury stages, commits, pushes, and opens the PR Issue management — "Check open issues" or "File a bug for the login crash" Code review — "Review PR #5" and Mercury reads the diff and posts a summary Full API access — The github_api tool lets Mercury hit any GitHub endpoint
Run mercury doctor and fill in the four GitHub fields: mercury doctor
Your GitHub username. This is used for commit attribution and identifying you in API calls. Example: hotheadhacker

Every Mercury-assisted commit automatically includes a Co-authored-by: Mercury <mercury@cosmicstack.org> trailer. No configuration needed — this is the default. Mercury's avatar will appear alongside yours on GitHub. You can customize the email in ~/.mercury/.env by setting GITHUB_EMAIL if you prefer a different co-author address.

You need a token so Mercury can authenticate with the GitHub API. Never share this token. It's stored locally in ~/.mercury/.env and never sent anywhere except GitHub's API. Where to create your token Fine-grained PAT (recommended): Go to github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new Give it a name (e.g. mercury-agent) and set an expiration Under Repository access, select All repositories or choose specific repos Under Permissions → Repository permissions, grant: Contents — Read and write Pull requests — Read and write Issues — Read and write Click Generate token and copy it immediately Classic PAT: Go to github.com/settings/tokens/new Give it a name (e.g. mercury-agent) and set an expiration Select the repo scope (full control of private repositories) Click Generate token and copy it immediately

Set a default repository so you can say "create an issue" without specifying the repo every time. You can enter it in any of these formats: hotheadhacker/mercury-agent https://github.com/hotheadhacker/mercury-agent Mercury will parse the owner and repo name automatically from either format. Press Enter on any field to keep its current value. When the PAT is set, you'll see: ✓ GitHub tools registered (5)

Tool What it does create_pr Create a pull request with title, body, head branch, and base branch review_pr Fetch a PR diff, review the changes, and post review comments list_issues List and filter issues in a repository (open, closed, by label, by assignee) create_issue Create a new issue with title, body, labels, and assignees github_api Raw GitHub API access — an escape hatch for any endpoint not covered above

When Mercury commits code using git_commit, it automatically appends a Co-authored-by: Mercury <mercury@cosmicstack.org> trailer. This means Mercury's avatar appears alongside yours in GitHub's commit history — giving credit where it's due.

PAT storage Your GitHub PAT is stored in ~/.mercury/mercury.yaml alongside your other configuration. It is never sent to any external service — only to the GitHub API directly from your machine. Treat this file like any other credential: don't commit it, don't share it, and rotate the token if you suspect it's compromised.

:::caution Beta Kanban Boards are a beta feature in v1.1.9. The data model and API surface are stable, but expect UI refinements in subsequent releases. The web dashboard labels this section "Kanban Boards (Beta mode)". ::: Mercury's Kanban system provides persistent task management with agent-driven execution. Boards are stored in SQLite (with JSON fallback) and accessible via the Web Dashboard (/board) or the REST/SSE API.

Property Description Title Card name Description Markdown-rendered task description Status pending, running, paused, done, failed, question Priority critical, high, normal, low Labels Arbitrary tags for categorization Comments Threaded comments with author tracking Attachments Linked files (stored on disk, downloadable) Dependencies Blocks/blocked-by relationships Parent–child Hierarchical card grouping

Status Meaning pending Not yet picked up — waiting to be run running The agent is actively working on it paused Execution paused (often after token-budget exhaustion or manual halt) done Completed successfully failed The agent could not complete the card question The agent has a clarifying question and is awaiting human feedback The question status is what powers the Feedback loop — when the agent needs input, it parks the card in question and waits for you to respond from the UI or via POST /api/boards/:id/feedback/:feedbackId/respond.
Header reads "Kanban Boards (Beta mode)". Create new boards, generate boards from a natural-language description, archive, delete, activate / deactivate.

Columns — one per status, each scrollable independently (Trello-style). The whole row scrolls horizontally if you have many statuses. Cards — drag and drop a card between columns to change status. The drag handler calls PATCH /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId with the new status. Description rendering — card descriptions are full Markdown (lists, code, headings). Descriptions longer than 280 characters are truncated with a "See more" link. Clicking the truncated text (or "See more") opens the full description in a modal with scrolling and full Markdown. The pencil icon next to the description is the only way to enter edit mode — clicking the description body itself just opens the read-only modal. This prevents accidental edits. AI Plan — click Plan on a card and Mercury drafts an execution plan (GET /api/boards/:id/execution-plan) you can review before running. Smart execution runs the plan card-by-card respecting dependencies. Run / Halt — per-card Run (▶) and Halt (■) buttons. Board-level Run all and Halt all buttons in the toolbar. Feedback — when a card is in question status, a callout appears at the top with the question text and a response field.

When a card is run, the agent autonomously processes the task: Card status moves to running. Agent executes the described task within a configurable token budget. On completion the status moves to done and a comment is appended with results. If the token budget is exhausted, execution auto-pauses (paused). If the agent needs human input, status moves to question and a feedback record is created.
POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/cascade runs the selected card and recursively all of its dependents in dependency order.
POST /api/boards/:id/smart-execute walks the whole board, picking up pending cards whose dependencies are done, until either the board is fully done or it hits an unresolved blocker.

Each board can define context that is injected into every card's prompt: Working directory — where file operations execute (POST /api/boards/:id/context/directory) Custom variables — key-value pairs (/context/variables) Instructions — system-level guidance (/context/instructions) Structure definition — expected project layout (/context/structure) Knowledge base — reference material (/context/knowledge)

GET /api/boards POST /api/boards GET /api/boards/:id PATCH /api/boards/:id DELETE /api/boards/:id POST /api/boards/:id/activate POST /api/boards/:id/deactivate POST /api/boards/:id/generate # natural-language board generation GET /api/boards/:id/execution-plan POST /api/boards/:id/smart-execute POST /api/boards/:id/run-all POST /api/boards/:id/halt-all

POST /api/boards/:id/cards POST /api/boards/:id/cards/bulk PATCH /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId DELETE /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId POST /api/boards/:id/cards/reorder POST /api/boards/:id/cards/clear-done POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/run POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/halt POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/cascade

GET /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/comments POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/comments DELETE /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/comments/:commentId GET /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/attachments POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/attachments DELETE /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/attachments/:attachmentId GET /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/attachments/:attachmentId/content GET /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/attachments/:attachmentId/download POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/labels DELETE /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/labels/:labelId POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/parent POST /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/dependencies DELETE /api/boards/:boardId/cards/:cardId/dependencies/:depId

GET /api/boards/:id/context POST /api/boards/:id/context/directory POST /api/boards/:id/context/variables POST /api/boards/:id/context/instructions POST /api/boards/:id/context/structure POST /api/boards/:id/context/knowledge
GET /api/boards/:id/feedback POST /api/boards/:boardId/feedback/:feedbackId/respond
GET /api/boards/:id/events Subscribe to a Server-Sent Events stream for live status updates as cards are processed (status changes, comments added, feedback raised).

Mercury is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. Connect it to MCP servers — local programs or remote endpoints — and their tools become available to the agent next to Mercury's built-in tools: your issue tracker, a database, internal company tools, a browser, anything that ships as an MCP server. You stay in control. A server's tools are hidden until you allow them, every call asks you first in Ask Me mode, and Allow All does not cover MCP tools — only tools you name in autoApprove run without a prompt. What is supported MCP tools over stdio (a local command Mercury starts) and Streamable HTTP (a remote URL), with static headers for authentication. MCP resources, prompts, sampling, OAuth sign-in and legacy SSE servers are not supported yet. Mercury Bots do not get MCP tools.

Put tokens in ~/.mercury/.env, never in mercury.yaml: # ~/.mercury/.env DOCS_MCP_TOKEN=your-token-here Configuration refers to them as ${env:DOCS_MCP_TOKEN}. Mercury resolves the reference only when it connects, so the value is never written back into mercury.yaml.

A local stdio server — Mercury shows you the exact command and asks before saving: mercury mcp add files --stdio npx -- -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ~/Documents A remote HTTP server with a bearer token: mercury mcp add docs --http https://mcp.example.com/mcp --header 'Authorization: Bearer ${env:DOCS_MCP_TOKEN}' Use single quotes around ${env:…} so your shell doesn't expand it. add connects once to test the server and lists its tools before saving.

Nothing is enabled until you say so: mercury mcp test files # see every tool the server offers mercury mcp allow files list_directory search_files Allowed tools appear to the agent as mcp__files__list_directory, mcp__files__search_files, and so on. If the daemon is running, Mercury restarts it to apply the change.

Ask Mercury something that needs the tool. In Ask Me mode you'll see: MCP tool call Server: files Tool: list_directory Arguments: { "path": "/Users/you/Documents" } Answer Yes (this call), Always (this tool, in this chat, until Mercury restarts) or No.

Command Description mercury mcp list Configured servers, their tool filters, and env/header settings (secrets masked) mercury mcp add <id> --stdio <command> [-- args...] Add a local server mercury mcp add <id> --http <url> Add a remote Streamable HTTP server mercury mcp test <id> Connect once and list every tool as allowed, hidden or skipped mercury mcp allow <id> <tools...> Show these tools to the agent ('*' for all) mercury mcp disallow <id> <tools...> Hide these tools again mercury mcp enable <id> / disable <id> Turn a server on or off without removing it mercury mcp remove <id> Remove a server mercury doctor --mcp Connect to every enabled server and report its health Options for add: Option Applies to Meaning --env KEY=VALUE stdio Environment variable for the server process (repeatable). Use ${env:NAME} for secrets. --cwd <dir> stdio Working directory for the server process --header 'Name: value' http HTTP header (repeatable). Use ${env:NAME} for secrets. --allow-private http Allow a private or loopback address (see Security) --allow a,b both Tools to show to the agent ('*' for all) --auto-approve a,b both Tools that run without asking — also in scheduled runs --disabled both Save without enabling -y, --yes both Skip confirmations In any chat, /mcp shows each server's status and /mcp tools <server> lists its tools. These are read-only: servers can only be added or enabled from the terminal. The web dashboard has a read-only MCP page with the same information.

Servers live under mcp.servers in ~/.mercury/mercury.yaml. The mercury mcp commands edit this for you; you can also edit it by hand and restart Mercury. mcp: servers: files: transport: stdio command: npx args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/Documents"] tools: allow: [list_directory, search_files] docs: transport: http url: https://mcp.example.com/mcp headers: Authorization: "Bearer ${env:DOCS_MCP_TOKEN}" tools: allow: ["*"] deny: [delete_page] autoApprove: [search] enabled: true Field Transport Description server id (the key) both Lowercase letters, digits and -, starting with a letter, up to 24 characters transport both stdio or http command, args stdio The program to start and its arguments. ${env:NAME} works in args. env stdio Extra environment variables for the server process. ${env:NAME} works here. cwd stdio Working directory url http The server's Streamable HTTP endpoint (http or https) headers http Static request headers. ${env:NAME} works here. allowPrivate http true to allow private, loopback and .local/.internal addresses enabled both false to keep the server configured but not connected timeoutMs both Per-call timeout (default 60000) tools.allow both Tool names the agent may see; "*" means all. Default: none. tools.deny both Tool names that are always hidden; wins over allow tools.autoApprove both Exact tool names that run without asking (no wildcards) An invalid server entry is skipped with a warning in the log and in mercury doctor --mcp; the rest still load. A missing ${env:NAME} variable marks that server as failed with env NAME is not set.

When. Enabled servers connect in the background when Mercury starts. A slow or broken server never delays startup or blocks other tools. Servers reconnect with backoff (1s doubling to 5 minutes, up to 10 attempts) if a connection drops. Where. The process that runs the agent owns the connections — normally the background daemon. The attach terminal, and mercury code while the daemon runs, do not start servers themselves. Tool changes. If a server announces that its tool list changed (tools/list_changed), Mercury refreshes it. New tools are hidden unless your allow list covers them, and run without asking only if their exact name is in autoApprove. Tool names. Tools are exposed as mcp__<server>__<tool>. Characters outside A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - become _, and names are capped at 64 characters (some model providers reject longer names); a shortened or clashing name gets a short hash suffix. mercury mcp test shows the exact names. Unusable tools. A tool whose input schema can't be passed to the model (not an object, larger than 16 KB, or referencing a remote $ref) is skipped and reported with the reason. Descriptions inside a schema are shortened to 300 characters, since the model reads them on every turn. Results. Text is passed to the model, capped at 32 KB per call. Images and audio are replaced by a short placeholder such as [image/png, 12.3 KB — not shown]. An error result from the server reaches the agent as Error: ….

MCP tools have their own rules, separate from the shell and file tools: Situation What happens Tool not in allow (or in deny) The agent can't see it Ask Me mode You're asked before every call, with server, tool and arguments (shown whole up to 4,000 characters; longer ones show the start and the end) You answer Always That tool runs without asking in that chat until Mercury restarts Allow All mode You're still asked — Allow All never covers MCP tools Tool in autoApprove Runs without asking, in chats and in unattended runs Scheduled tasks and sub-agents They ask on the chat they came from, like a normal call; nothing is approved for them. A run with no one to ask (fail-closed, internal) only runs autoApprove tools Plan mode MCP tools are not available Telegram/Signal members (non-admins) MCP tools are not available Mercury Bots MCP tools are not available autoApprove takes exact tool names only, so a tool a server adds later can never slip in through a wildcard. Hints that a server sends about its own tools (such as "read-only") never change these rules.

MCP servers are third-party code and third-party text. Mercury treats them that way: Untrusted text. Tool descriptions and results come from the server and can contain prompt-injection attempts ("ignore your instructions and…"). They reach the model like any web page would, and they can never change permissions. Only allow tools from servers you trust, and prefer Ask Me for anything that writes or sends. Process isolation. A stdio server does not inherit Mercury's environment, so your model provider API keys and other .env values never reach it. It gets only a minimal set of variables (HOME, LOGNAME, PATH, SHELL, TERM, USER on macOS/Linux; APPDATA, COMSPEC, HOMEDRIVE, HOMEPATH, LOCALAPPDATA, PATH, PATHEXT, PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE, PROGRAMDATA, PROGRAMFILES, PROGRAMFILES(X86), PROGRAMW6432, SYSTEMDRIVE, SYSTEMROOT, TEMP, USERNAME, USERPROFILE, WINDIR on Windows) plus the env you configure for it. Network. HTTP servers go through Mercury's SSRF protection: private, loopback and .local/.internal addresses are refused unless you set allowPrivate: true for that server, and redirects to other origins are not followed. allowPrivate opens loopback and your LAN only: link-local addresses such as the cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254) stay blocked. Secrets. Values you reference with ${env:NAME} are resolved at connect time and masked as **** wherever they could surface — logs, tool results, server stderr, mercury mcp list, /mcp, mercury doctor --mcp, the dashboard and /api/mcp. A literal token typed into mercury.yaml triggers a warning, and so does handing a server one of Mercury's own keys (for example ${env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}): that server would see it. Owner-only setup. Adding or enabling a server is done from the terminal; the agent has no MCP tool for it. When the agent uses its file tools (write_file, edit_file, create_file, delete_file) on mercury.yaml, permissions.yaml or .env, Mercury always asks first — even under Allow All — and refuses in unattended runs. Shell commands that change MCP setup (mercury mcp add, enable, allow… or anything that names mercury.yaml) also always ask, even under Allow All, and are refused in unattended runs. Other shell edits to permissions.yaml or .env follow your permission mode.

mercury mcp test <id> # one server, with its tool list and stderr on failure mercury doctor --mcp # every enabled server; exits 1 if any fails MCP servers ✓ files: connected, 14 tools, 2 allowed — npx ✗ docs: failed — env DOCS_MCP_TOKEN is not set — https://mcp.example.com - old: disabled — uvx In chat, /mcp shows the live status of the running Mercury; the dashboard's MCP page shows the same.

Symptom Fix env NAME is not set Add NAME=… to ~/.mercury/.env and restart Mercury Blocked: … is a private/internal address The server is on your machine or network. Set allowPrivate: true (or add it with --allow-private) if you trust it Connection closed right after start The command failed. mercury mcp test <id> prints the server's stderr — often a missing package, a wrong path, or a missing token connect timed out after 15000 ms The server didn't answer the MCP handshake. Check it speaks MCP over stdio (not HTTP), or that the URL is the MCP endpoint HTTP 401 / 403 Check the token in .env and the header name the server expects Tool missing for the agent It isn't in tools.allow — mercury mcp test <id> shows hidden and skipped tools skipped: input schema … The server's schema for that tool can't be sent to the model; nothing to configure MCP tool … needs approval in a scheduled task Add the tool to tools.autoApprove if it should run unattended Command works in your shell but not in the daemon The background service runs with a fixed PATH. Use the full path to the program (for example /opt/homebrew/bin/uvx)

Windows. Commands such as npx that are .cmd shims work as command: npx. Standalone binaries. MCP is built into the standalone binaries (verified on the Windows binary; macOS and Linux run the same bundled code). Stdio servers still need their own runtime installed — Node.js for npx, Python for uvx. Termux. MCP is untested on Termux. Install Mercury with npm there; stdio servers that only need Node.js are expected to work.

Mercury Bots are persistent, persona-scoped agents that run outside your conversation. Unlike sub-agents (which die with their task) or channels (which answer as one persona), bots are long-lived specialists: each has a name, a character, its own private workspace, its own skill library and permission scopes, a per-bot token budget, and a durable job queue. Dispatch work and keep talking — the bot works in the background and delivers results in its own thread.

Concept What it is Bot A persistent persona agent: bot.yaml manifest + permissions.yaml, sandbox at ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/, journal-backed history Wake Turning a bot on for a turn (/bots run <id> [routine] or a dispatched task) Thread The bot's own chat — results, thinking streams, and journal history land here, never in your active chat Fleet lead A bot promoted to organize its own crew (/bots promote <id>) — tell it what, it decides how and who Crew The bots under a lead; results bubble up through the lead; multi-level hierarchies supported Bundle Shareable export of a bot (or whole fleet): manifests + personas + permissions + skills DLQ Dead-letter queue for failed/timed-out jobs, replayable non-destructively Needs-you alert Escalation to your active channel when a bot is blocked (failed job, permission wall, stopped bot)

Sub-agent Mercury Bot Lifetime dies with its task persists across restarts Identity anonymous named persona with editable character Workspace session workspace private sandbox ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ + shared folder Results your chat the bot's own thread Memory none journal history hydrates on reopen Skills session skills native library + per-bot libraries Schedule — bot_schedule — bots own their routines

/bots # roster with live states /bots create researcher "Researcher" "Web research specialist" /bots persona researcher "Meticulous researcher who cites sources." /bots promote researcher # make it a fleet lead (optional) /dispatch_bot bot=researcher task="Compare X vs Y, cite sources" /bots open researcher # open its thread The result lands in the researcher's thread — your chat stays clean. Check on it with /bots or open its thread and reply directly.

Run these inside a conversation with Mercury (CLI, Telegram, Discord, Slack, or Web): Command Description /bots Roster with live states — on Telegram with tappable Stop/Start/Run/Runs buttons per bot and a fleet row (Cost, Outputs, Doctor, Stop all) /bots create <id> "Name" "Description" Onboard a bot (persona, permission tier, fleet, budget size, and where results land) /bots open <id> Open the bot's own thread (TUI) /bot <id> <message> or @<id> <message> Dispatch a task; the result (and any delivered files) come back to the chat that asked /bots cost [days] Token spend per bot and fleet, today against the caps /bots outputs [id] · /bots folder <id> · /bots fetch <id> [name] What was delivered; open the folder; send a file to this chat /bots show <id> [runId] · /bots journal <id> What a run did (tools, deliveries, reply) · recent runs /bots tasks <leadId> A lead's delegated tasks and their results /bots budget <id> <tokens|suggest|none> Daily token cap (default 5M; none = unlimited) /bots persona <id> <text> · /bots edit <id> <field> <value> Character · any config field /bots permissions <id> [readonly|builder|operator|full] Capability tier /bots promote <id> / demote · /bots crew <leadId> · /bots add-crew / remove-crew Fleet structure /bots stop <id> / start <id> · /bots stop all / start all Hold and resume one bot (and its crew) · the whole fleet /bots enable <id> / disable <id> Suspend/reactivate (imported bots start disabled) /bots run <id> [routine] Fire a routine now, or a bare wake /bots dlq [clear [id]] · /bots replay <id> <jobId> Failed jobs; drop them; re-run one /bots doctor · /bots storage Fleet health · disk usage /bots export <id> [path] · /bots import <path> Bundles (a lead's carries its crew; imports start disabled) /bots help This list, inside any chat CLI mirrors the read-only surface — mercury bots doctor (fleet health check, exit 1 when actionable), mercury bots list, mercury bots storage.

Every bot gets a private sandbox: ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/. Work stays isolated; other bots can't wander into it. The fleet-shared folder ~/.mercury/bots/_shared/ is for cross-bot files — implicit grants for crew members, explicit for leads. Access scopes (read / write / execute per directory) are declared in the bot's permissions.yaml; hand-edits apply live; malformed entries skip + warn rather than crash. Shell approval follows the bot's own allow-list (permissions.yaml autoApproveCommands). Finished results exit via bot_deliver into a folder you can actually find: ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot name>/ (Windows: Documents; Termux: shared storage; bots.deliverablesDir in mercury.yaml overrides). Finals sit on top, crew work under work/, with a README index and files named 2026-10-10 Oxide Series D explained.md. The path is shown when you onboard a bot and in /bots; /bots outputs lists deliveries and /bots folder <id> opens the folder. Writes to the shared folder are budgeted per run — it is for data other bots consume, not for notes. Bots never write to the deliverables folder by hand. The retention janitor enforces per-bot disk caps (journal rotation, DLQ cap), so a forgotten fleet can't fill your disk.

Bots own routines through bot_schedule — schedule their own future runs and recurring jobs, visible in /tasks and the fleet doctor. Leads additionally self-organize: give a lead a goal and it recruits crew, splits work, and synthesizes results upward. Every unattended run is governed: A turn is capped at 300k tokens and 20 minutes (autonomy.maxTokensPerTurn, maxTurnMinutes in bot.yaml); long context is compacted automatically. Every bot has a daily token cap — 5M unless you set one with /bots budget <id> <tokens|suggest|none> — and the fleet has one (bots.fleetDailyTokenBudget). You are warned at 80%; at 100% the bot pauses until tomorrow. A routine tick is skipped, never queued, while the bot is still busy or within its routine's minimum interval (schedules[].minIntervalMinutes). A cadence you declare in bot.yaml is honoured as written; routines a bot creates for itself run at most every 30 minutes, at most three per bot. Bots stay online. A bot is idle between runs, never dead: a routine that keeps producing nothing is cooled down (6 hours, doubling to a day) and resumes by itself; budget pauses lift at midnight and queued work is pumped then; /bots doctor flags a bot whose routine has not fired in twice its cadence (stale). Bots run in their own lane — they never touch your main chat or code session. Leads delegate typed tasks with fleet_delegate — several at once, each with a goal and what "done" means — and are woken once with a digest when the batch finishes or its deadline passes. A lead's standard job can be declared as a pipeline in bot.yaml (pipeline.stages), and fleet_pipeline runs it end to end with no lead turn between stages: pipeline: name: article stages: - { name: research, bot: source-researcher, goal: "Build a sourced dossier on {{input}}" } - { name: draft, bot: article-writer-draft, goal: "Write the 800–1000 word piece from {{previous}}" } - { name: check, bot: fact-checker, goal: "Fact-check {{previous}} and fix what fails" } - { name: package, bot: delivery-packager, goal: "Finalise {{previous}} for delivery", final: true } Bots remember. After a productive run, durable facts (sources, decisions, where things are) go into the bot's own memory, and every turn starts with a digest of its last five runs plus its own working-state note (bot_state). bots.fleets.crewProvider puts crew work on a cheaper provider. A run is judged by what it did, not by what it says: delivered a file, took an action, delegated, or nothing. A routine that only writes notes gets one nudge to deliver; three empty runs in a row cool it down (6h, doubling to 24h; it resumes by itself, or /bots start resumes it now). Monitoring routines can declare expects: check to be allowed to find nothing.

Everything above works from your phone: /bots and /bot are in Telegram's command menu, and the roster comes with buttons — Stop / Start, Run and Runs per bot, and a fleet row with Cost, Outputs, Doctor and Stop all. A tap runs the same slash command you would have typed (same permissions, same reply). Creating a bot works there too: /bots create <id> "Name" "Description", then your next message is its persona, and the template, permissions, fleet and budget steps arrive as buttons. When a bot finishes a task you asked for from Telegram, the reply comes back to that chat with the delivered files attached, not a path on your Mac; /bots outputs <id> lists what a bot has delivered with a 📎 button per file, and /bots fetch <id> [name|latest] sends one.

/bots export <id> # single bot (or whole crew if lead / whole fleet) /bots import <path> # recreate bots — starts disabled by design Bundles contain manifests, personas, permissions, and skill libraries so a recreated fleet works identically. What never travels: ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ sandbox state, journals, and .env secrets. Import locally, review, /bots enable.

The local dashboard ('Mercury Bots' section) shows the live roster, per-bot threads with streamed thinking, needs-you badges, and a fleet step view that mirrors the TUI (solo / lead auto-build / lead manual).

/bots roster — live per-bot states (running / waiting / stopped / needs-you). /bots cost [days] — token spend per bot and fleet against the caps; /bots show <id> [runId] — the tool trace, deliveries and reply of a run; /bots stop all — the kill switch; /bots dlq clear — drop dead-lettered jobs. Journals — per-bot run history with real timings, steps, tool calls, the outcome (deliverable, action, delegated, message, none) and delivered paths; a compact transcript per run is kept (last 50). DLQ + replay — failures classify honestly (failed, timed out) and replay non-destructively. /bots doctor (in any chat) and mercury bots doctor — storage health, stale routines, whole-home write grants, outcome ratio, queue depth, journal rotation, and scheduler linkage (routines registered but never wired are flagged before they silently never fire).

Bots are persona-scoped: tools, skills, and scopes come from the bot's own manifests, not from your session. Permission tiers (ask / allow) are chosen explicitly at onboarding — nothing defaults silently. Bots stopped with /bots stop hold their queued jobs; nothing sneaks back in via the due-sweep until you /bots start. Imported bundles start disabled — inspect before enabling.

Optimus is a plugin that lets Mercury use your computer. It looks at the screen, then moves the pointer, scrolls and types the way a person does, and opens apps, URLs and files. Ask in any Mercury chat ("look at my screen", "open Safari and search for…"), or press a talk key, say what you want, and hear Mercury answer while it works. It's an optional plugin, version 0.4.8, from the official plugin catalog. It needs Mercury 1.4.0 or newer.

Platform Support macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) Full. You grant Accessibility, Screen Recording and Microphone once. Windows x64 Full. Nothing to grant. Windows running as administrator (Task Manager, installers) can't be controlled. Linux x64 and arm64, X11 Full. Linux, Wayland Limited. Screenshots go through the desktop's screen-sharing prompt. Mouse, keyboard and the talk key only reach X11 (XWayland) apps for now, and the "Mercury is driving" overlay isn't shown. Use chat, or ask Mercury to start listening. An X11 session gives Optimus full control.

In any Mercury chat: /plugins install optimus Or from a shell: mercury plugins install optimus Install shows a warning that this plugin controls the computer, lists what it needs, and asks you to confirm.
