Release 1.1.6 focuses on a major CLI/TUI upgrade, workspace IDE flow, background execution reliability, and docs coverage.

New Ink-based interactive TUI with improved startup, status, and activity views. Workspace IDE mode with explorer, preview, git panel, coding chat, and keyboard navigation. Background task system for long-running shell and agent work (/bg ...) with live status. Sub-agent lifecycle integration with background tracking and coding delegation (/code agent <task>). Spotify UX revamp (Spotify Deck), shortcuts, volume up/down, and optional inline album art. New runtime model switching commands (/models, /models use <provider>). New platform diagnostics command (mercury doctor --platform). Default seeded web-search skill for fresh installs.

Added minimal/detailed activity views and updated controls. Improved streaming responsiveness and markdown rendering stability. Added coding shortcuts: Ctrl+P plan Ctrl+X execute Esc / Ctrl+Q exit workspace Improved startup permission picker behavior and one-step confirm flow. Added raw-mode watchdog to improve terminal input reliability across environments.

Introduced /ws command family with open/refresh/stage/commit/undo/exit. Added dedicated coding workspace docs page and updated command references. Added automatic handoff of interrupted long tasks to background workers.

Added BackgroundTaskManager integration into agent lifecycle. Added /bg current to move active work to background. Added /bg list, /bg <id>, /bg cancel <id>, /bg clear for operational control. Added supervisor lifecycle hooks so agent progress/completion is reflected in background board.

Added Spotify Deck-style panel and clearer action feedback. Added keyboard shortcuts in player mode (N, P, +, -, Z, Esc). Added separate volume up/down controls. Added safe-gated inline album art support (MERCURY_SPOTIFY_ART=1, iTerm local sessions).

Expanded Docusaurus docs for: coding workspace mode sub-agents + background tasks platform diagnostics Spotify player shortcuts and album art gating default web-search skill Docker status guidance (no first-party Docker assets shipped in repo)
This release includes broad UX/system changes across TUI, background execution, and docs. For provider/model management, use mercury doctor to configure and /models to switch session model.

Release 1.1.7 brings two new providers (ChatGPT Web and GitHub Copilot), a redesigned real-time progress system, Mercury Autopilot with intelligent loop detection, major Telegram improvements, and a full landing page redesign with the interactive Killipi mascot.

ChatGPT Web provider — use your ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscription directly, with OAuth device flow authentication. GitHub Copilot provider — authenticate via GitHub OAuth and use Copilot models as a Mercury provider. Mercury Autopilot — AI-based loop detection that analyzes parameter diversity and success rates to distinguish productive work from stuck loops, with auto-abort capability. Real-time progress system — live status cards with step tracking, elapsed timers, and collapsed tool execution history. Completion banners — task summaries with elapsed time, step count, model used, and token usage/budget metrics. Interactive Killipi mascot — hero centerpiece on the landing page with cursor tracking, expressions, and ambient glow effects.

Added ChatGPT Web provider with full OAuth device flow. Authenticate with your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription and use it as a Mercury backend. Added GitHub Copilot provider with OAuth device flow and Copilot token exchange. Moved ChatGPT Plus/Pro OAuth option under the OpenAI provider group during onboarding. Fixed ChatGPT Web inclusion in the configured providers list and default selector.

Implemented AI-based loop detection with auto-abort capability. Replaced inline tool loop detection with a dedicated ToolCallLoopDetector module. Smart repetition analysis evaluates parameter diversity and success rate to classify work as productive, suspicious, or stuck. Added strict tool usage guidelines to the system prompt to reduce unnecessary repetition. Increased tool loop tolerance thresholds to avoid false positives on legitimate multi-step tasks.

New progress tracking system with /progress command and foreground heartbeat alerts. Live status bar displays a "processing" label before the first tool step occurs. Tool steps are hidden while the agent is in thinking state, shown only when actively executing. Collapsed tool execution history tracked and displayed in agent progress notifications. Completion banners now include elapsed time, step count, and token usage/budget metrics. Completion banners are constrained to substantial tasks — minor step-based interactions no longer trigger them.

Slash command suggestions — type / and get autocomplete suggestions with arrow-key navigation and Enter selection. Multi-line input — Shift+Enter for new lines (later rebound to Ctrl+N). Input cursor support — proper cursor positioning in the TUI input field. Choice prompt selection — interactive prompts for CLI agent interactions. Scrollable Agent Output panel — replaces the old static chat view in the workspace. Workspace focus management — keyboard navigation between panels with scrolling and chat toggling. View toggle rebound to Ctrl+T with improved input sanitization. Dynamic thinking status indicators in the UI header.

Implemented Telegram-specific task lifecycle with message deferral and structured help documentation. Ephemeral message tracking and cleanup — permission prompts and transient messages auto-delete after handling. Telegram help command now shows a clean, Telegram-formatted reference with only Telegram-relevant commands.

Interactive write approval — file write operations now prompt with a clear approval flow. Safe read-only allowlist — shell commands like ls, cat, find, grep, git status, git log, and git diff are auto-approved without prompting. Persistent plan tracking and read-only tool restrictions for programming mode.
Human-readable background task IDs (e.g., task-alpha, task-bravo) replace opaque numeric IDs. Mass task termination support via /bg cancel all.

Full visual redesign of the landing page with updated color palette and refined layout. Interactive Killipi mascot added to the hero section — eyes follow cursor, click for expressions, ambient particle effects. Fixed Docusaurus admonition rendering — updated all :::tip, :::info, :::warning blocks to use the v3 directive label syntax (:::type[Title]). Fixed mobile sidebar visibility in dark mode with explicit background and text color overrides. Expanded documentation for sub-agents, Spotify integration, autopilot, and provider configuration.

This release includes 35 commits with +3,829 lines of new source code across 25 files. New keyboard shortcut for multi-line input: Ctrl+N (changed from Shift+Enter). View toggle shortcut changed to Ctrl+T.

Release 1.1.9 introduces the Mercury Web Dashboard — a full React SPA at localhost:6174 — alongside a persistent Kanban board system, an in-browser Workspace IDE with Git and AI commit messages, a dual-layer (conscious + subconscious) Second Brain, intelligent skill batching, and a cross-platform build pipeline. Note: Version 1.1.8 was published briefly and then unpublished before reaching wide distribution due to a dependency-tree issue (a transitive next dependency inflating install size by ~285 MB). 1.1.9 ships the same feature set with a leaner dependency graph — install footprint dropped from ~429 MB to ~87 MB (−80%).
documents.s: v1.1.9 — Mercury Web, Kanban & Subconscious Memory

documents.t: Mercury Web Dashboard — React SPA with PWA install, login, dark/light theme, multi-thread chat with SSE streaming. Workspace IDE — file tree, multi-tab editor, integrated terminal, Source Control panel with AI-generated conventional commit messages, and a maximizable bottom panel. Kanban Boards (Beta) — persistent SQLite-backed task boards with Markdown descriptions, AI execution plans, cascade & smart execution, board context, attachments, comments, dependencies, and a question-status feedback loop. Second Brain — Conscious + Subconscious — dual-tier memory model, person tracking with aliases & relationships, goals view, and graph visualization. Skill Batching & Intent Router — automatic grouping for multi-skill invocations, plus a web UI to install skills from URL, activate/deactivate, and delete. Cross-platform build — a Node-based post-build.cjs replaces the old shell pipeline; runs identically on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

The dashboard is opt-in: enable it via mercury doctor or by setting web.enabled: true in mercury.yaml. It binds to 127.0.0.1:6174 only and is never exposed to the network. Authentication — username/password login with HTTP-only session cookies. Default credentials: mercury / Mercury@123. Editable from Settings → Account. PWA install — install Mercury from the browser address bar to launch it in its own window. Pages — Status, Chat, Tasks, Board, Workspace, Second Brain (Memory / Persons / Goals / Graph), Providers, Permissions, Skills, Schedules, Usage, Profit Sharing, Settings. Multi-thread Chat — every conversation lives at /chat/:threadId. Threads have a deletable sidebar, a per-thread model switcher, and a Code Mode toggle that flips the agent into coding context for that thread. Real-time updates — Server-Sent Events stream agent activity, tool calls, and Kanban status changes. Theme — light / dark / system toggle in Settings → Appearance. Settings cleanup — agent personality is no longer editable from the web UI; the new Defaults card holds default provider and daily token budget.

A full in-browser editor at /workspace. Folder picker — choose any directory on your machine; the choice is persisted across restarts. File Explorer — collapsible tree with refresh, resizable left panel. Multi-tab editor — syntax highlighting for 20+ languages; per-tab dirty state; Cmd/Ctrl+S to save. Bottom panel — split between Terminal (with command history) and a Chat thread scoped to the workspace. A new Maximize / Minimize button expands the panel to fill the workspace area. Source Control panel — staged / unstaged file list, per-file diff viewer, branch switcher with create-new-branch, last 15 commits, pull/push/refresh buttons (with spinning indicator and a "Refreshed" toast on manual refresh). AI Commit Message Generation — click the sparkle icon and Mercury auto-stages unstaged changes and drafts a conventional-commit message from the diff using the default provider. Resizable layout — Explorer, Bottom panel, and Source Control panel all resize independently, including correct inverted-direction resizing on the right edge.

Persistent task boards backed by SQLite (with JSON fallback). Labelled "Kanban Boards (Beta mode)" in the UI. Real status set — pending, running, paused, done, failed, question. Drag-and-drop between columns updates status. Per-column scrolling — Trello-style: each column scrolls independently inside a horizontally-scrolling board. Markdown descriptions with "See more" truncation at 280 chars; click the description to open a full-screen modal, click the pencil to edit. AI Execution Plan — preview what the agent will do before running a card. Cascade execution — run a card and recursively all of its dependents in dependency order. Smart execution — board-wide walk that picks up pending cards whose dependencies are done. Token-budget aware — long-running cards auto-pause when their token budget is exhausted. question feedback loop — when the agent needs human input, the card moves to question and surfaces a feedback callout for you to respond. Board context — per-board working directory, custom variables, instructions, structure definition, and knowledge base, all injected into card prompts. Collaboration — comments, attachments (with download), labels, parent–child hierarchy, and blocks/blocked-by dependencies. SSE event stream — /api/boards/:id/events for live status updates.

A two-tier memory model inspired by how human memory actually behaves. Conscious tier (durable, active scopes) — top-of-mind, always available for retrieval. Subconscious tier (subconscious scope) — out of active recall, no further confidence decay, recalled automatically when contextually relevant. After 30 days without being referenced, an active memory moves to the subconscious instead of being deleted. When a subconscious memory is recalled into a relevant conversation, it is promoted back to conscious. Hard deletion happens only on explicit dismissal — otherwise memories live forever in the subconscious. Other Second Brain improvements: Persons — alias resolution, relationship mapping, and dedicated detail pages with last-seen and related memories. Goals & Projects — filtered views over type: goal and type: project memories with inline add. Graph view — force-directed visualization of memories, persons, and goals. Better extraction — persons are now extracted from identity, project, and episode memories (not just relationship); multi-type extraction in a single pass; dedup rules; resilient fallbacks for malformed LLM output. The Telegram /memory menu gained a 💤 Subconscious button mirroring the web view.

Skill batching — related skills are automatically grouped for efficient multi-skill execution. Intent router — classifies natural-language input and dispatches to the matching skill or batch using intents, categories, and tags from each skill's frontmatter. Web UI — install skills from a SKILL.md URL, toggle active/inactive, and delete from /skills. Progressive disclosure — only frontmatter is held in context until a skill is invoked, keeping token usage low.

Friendly background task IDs (e.g. swift-fox) carried forward with stability fixes. Token-counter recovery: if dailyUsed becomes corrupted, Mercury rebuilds it from the request log on startup. Improved interrupt handling — in-flight work auto-backgrounds on interrupt and continues asynchronously.
The TUI dashboard now displays web server status so you can see at a glance whether the dashboard is live and on which port.

Cleaner canvas — the always-on text labels were causing severe overlap and unreadability on dense graphs. Labels now appear only on the hovered / selected node, with a rounded background pill for legibility. Smarter tooltip — shows the full, untruncated memory summary (was previously trimmed to ~60 chars), wraps onto multiple lines, and flips to the left of the cursor when near the right edge so it's never clipped. Click-to-open detail dialog — single-click on any node now opens a Radix dialog that fetches the full memory record (GET /api/brain/memory/:id) and shows summary, detail body, scope, importance, confidence, evidence count, source, and timestamps. Drag / pan still work — a 4 px / 500 ms threshold distinguishes a click from a drag. Graceful fallback — nodes without a backing memory record (e.g. synthesized aggregates) still render their data inside the dialog.

Cross-platform scripts/post-build.cjs replaces shell-only build steps — runs identically on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Calls npx vite build, copies ui/dist to dist/web/ui, and writes a kill-switch service worker. PWA cache kill-switch — older versions of Mercury Web could serve stale bundles from the PWA cache. The new build writes a self-unregistering service worker that clears caches and reloads clients on first load after upgrade, guaranteeing users see the new UI. Clean production build output with reduced artifact size and clearer logs.

Three runtime dependencies were declared in package.json but never imported by src/: geist — Vercel font wrapper. Fonts are vendored directly in src/web/static/vendor/geist/; the npm package transitively dragged in next and @next/* (~285 MB). js-tiktoken — no usages anywhere in source. react-dom — only used by ui/ (which has its own package.json); ink does not require it. Removing all three reduces the end-user install footprint dramatically: Metric Before After node_modules size ~429 MB ~87 MB Package count 114 95 No functional change — typecheck, tsup bundle, and Vite UI build all pass unchanged.

The web dashboard is opt-in — Mercury still runs CLI-only by default; the web server starts only when web.enabled: true. All data (boards, memory, threads, skills) lives in ~/.mercury/. Nothing leaves your machine. The Kanban board is a beta feature in this release — the data model and API are stable, but expect UI refinements in subsequent versions. Web channel feedback is welcome via /feedback or GitHub issues.

Mercury meets the cloud. Pair from the terminal, authenticate with auto-rotating JWTs, stay online over a Cloud WebSocket, and search a shared memory pool across all your agents. 1.2.0 is the cloud release. Mercury Cloud is a hosted backend that turns a local Mercury install into a remotely managed, always-on agent — no port forwarding, no reverse proxy, no manual certificate management. Pair once from the terminal, and Mercury maintains a persistent WebSocket to the cloud, relaying commands, streaming responses, and syncing memory in real time. This release ships as a patch set: 1.2.0 (the launch), 1.2.1 (runtime activation hardening), and 1.2.2 (cross-platform CI and packaging fixes). All three are covered on this page. Why "Cloudy Mercury"? The Mercury planet (☿) has always been the messenger. Cloudy Mercury gives that messenger a cloud — a persistent connection that keeps it reachable, synced, and self-healing even when your terminal is closed.

Area What changed Mercury Cloud Hosted backend with terminal pairing, JWT + refresh token auth, long-lived agent API key, Cloud WebSocket, and remote dashboard Pairing flow mercury cloud connect opens a browser-based pairing URL; poll-based completion with structured failure codes Auth & recovery Auto-rotating JWTs via single-use refresh tokens; long-lived agent API key for headless self-recovery without re-pairing Cloud WebSocket Persistent WSS connection with 30s heartbeat, exponential reconnect, and real-time message relay Runtime activation activateCloudRuntime guards foreground/daemon state, waits for WebSocket online, and propagates failures Shared memory pool searchPool() fetches cross-agent context from the cloud, cached in SQLite for 5 minutes per query Token store Shared in-memory token store keeps the WS client and provider in sync during rotation Termux (Android) better-sqlite3 is now optional — --help and --version work without the native addon Windows File-mode and posix-path fixes for work-ledger and platform.ts Provider Mercury Cloud is a first-class provider with model selection at pairing time

Run mercury cloud connect and Mercury opens a browser-based pairing URL. The flow is poll-based with a 5-minute timeout and structured failure codes (e.g. AGENT_LIMIT_REACHED with upgrade guidance): mercury cloud connect Once paired, Mercury saves: A JWT (short-lived, auto-rotated) A refresh token (single-use, rotated on every refresh) An agent API key (long-lived, for headless self-recovery) The agent ID and tier

Mercury Cloud uses a three-tier token strategy: JWT — used for API and WebSocket auth. Auto-refreshed before expiry. Refresh token — single-use, rotated on every refresh. If the JWT expires, Mercury tries the refresh token first. Agent API key — long-lived, never expires. If both JWT and refresh token are dead, Mercury redeems the agent API key to get fresh tokens without a browser re-pair. This means a remotely-deployed agent on a server or Termux can stay online indefinitely without manual intervention — the agent API key is the self-healing path.

After pairing, Mercury maintains a persistent WSS connection to wss://backend.mercuryagent.sh/ws with: 30-second heartbeat to detect dead connections Exponential backoff reconnect (up to 50 attempts) Pre-connect token rotation — never handshakes with an expired JWT Message relay — remote commands, streaming responses, skill installs, memory operations, and conversation sync The WebSocket stays alive even after you exit the foreground TUI — the background daemon keeps it open.

Mercury Cloud agents can search a shared memory pool — cross-agent context that lives in the cloud. After local Second Brain retrieval, the agent calls searchPool() to fetch additional context from other agents in your fleet. Results are cached in a local SQLite DB for 5 minutes per query to kill per-turn network cost.
Manage your agent from the cloud dashboard at cloud.mercuryagent.sh — send messages, install skills, view memory, and monitor status. The dashboard talks to your local agent over the Cloud WebSocket.

The activateCloudRuntime function is the single entry point for starting or restarting a managed runtime after Cloud credentials land. It: Checks foreground state — rejects if Mercury is running only in the foreground (can't activate Cloud without a managed runtime) Accepts already-online foreground — if credentials didn't change and the foreground WebSocket is already online, returns without restarting Stops a running daemon — graceful SIGTERM before starting a fresh one Starts a managed runtime — restartService() if a system service is installed, otherwise startBackground() Waits for WebSocket online — up to 20 seconds; throws if the Cloud WebSocket doesn't come up Propagates failures — throws if stopDaemon fails, so the caller knows credentials were saved but the runtime is stale

Mercury Cloud is a first-class provider (mercuryCloud) backed by an OpenAI-compatible API at https://backend.mercuryagent.sh/v1. At pairing time, Mercury fetches the available models and prompts you to choose: Available models: 1. Mercury Flash (mercury-flash) 2. Mercury Pro (mercury-pro) 3. ... Choose a model [1-N, Enter for 1]: The provider's JWT is automatically swapped when the shared token store rotates — no race conditions, no burned refresh tokens.

Restored activateCloudRuntime as the single activation path for cloud connect and cloud login, replacing a simpler ensureDaemonRunning that had dropped foreground checks, WebSocket verification, and failure propagation. This fixed 8 failing pairing-flow tests.

Windows: resolveShell now uses posix.join for the Termux shell path (was backslash-joined on Windows). work-ledger.test.ts skips the 0o600 mode assertion on Windows (chmod is a no-op for owner bits). Termux: better-sqlite3 is now lazy-loaded via createRequire in pool-search.ts, so --help and --version work without the native addon (it doesn't compile on Android). CI: The Termux CI job treats better-sqlite3 as optional (the runtime already falls back gracefully).

Command Description mercury cloud connect Pair with Mercury Cloud via browser mercury cloud disconnect Clear Cloud credentials and stop the agent mercury cloud status Show Cloud connection status and usage mercury cloud login Refresh the JWT using the stored refresh token

Mercury Cloud is opt-in — run mercury cloud connect to pair. Existing configs, providers, threads, kanban boards, and Second Brain data carry over unchanged.

Same five targets as v1.1.13: OS Architecture Binary macOS Apple Silicon mercury-macos-arm64 macOS Intel mercury-macos-x64 Linux x86-64 mercury-linux-x64 Linux ARM64 mercury-linux-arm64 Windows x86-64 mercury-win-x64.exe Direct downloads: mercury-macos-arm64 mercury-macos-x64 mercury-linux-x64 mercury-linux-arm64 mercury-win-x64.exe checksums.txt Full changelog: v1.1.13 → v1.2.2

Mercury Code stops dying and starts telling the truth. 1.2.3 rebuilds Mercury Code's completion pipeline around one contract: every task ends in a verdict — a verified completion, or an honest pause that names its blocker and resumes. Before this release, step-budget exhaustion produced green "Task complete" banners over half-done work, big file writes were severed mid-argument by the output cap, narration-locked models looped forever, and long builds died at memory pressure. Now every failure mode routes to a named recovery path, and no task can claim success without evidence. Why "Unstoppable Mercury"? This is the release where the agent stopped being a chat wrapper around an LLM and became an orchestrator with guarantees. When a model narrates instead of building, the agent grounds the work itself, mechanically forces the first tool call, rotates to another model, and issues a wake-up call — ten enforced rounds before it ever pauses. And when it pauses, it tells you exactly what blocked it.

Area What changed Completion contract Turn-end verdicts (text-stop / steps-exhausted / interrupted / truncated / aborted) — budget exhaustion is a pause, never a fake completion AUTO mode Mercury Code's new default: plan + build in one flow; one confirmation only for large changes Escalation harness Grounding → forced mutating tool call → provider rotation → wake-up call; narration is mechanically impossible on forced steps Verification gate Build/test/typecheck evidence required before "Task complete" in execute/AUTO mode Compact-on-pressure Memory pressure compacts the conversation in place and continues (OpenCode practice) Output size No Mercury-imposed cap — the model's native limit governs; adaptive halving for providers that reject it Honest verdicts Pauses carry the blocker ("write_file: permission denied") and resume via "continue"; work-ledger paused state persists across restarts Live TUI Plan checklist, ask_user choice picker (now visible in Mercury Code), thinking preview, wheel scrolling, file-change previews Security SSRF guard on fetch_url/install_skill, credential files 0600, random initial web password, secret redaction in logs

The heart of the release. Previously, the agent loop had one optimistic pass — and every ending, including half-done work, was celebrated as complete. Now: Every turn end is classified — text-stop, steps-exhausted, interrupted, truncated, aborted (src/core/completion-verdict.ts). Budget exhaustion is a pause, never a completion. The task pauses with a resumable work-ledger entry and a message that names the blocker — including the last failed tool result (e.g. write_file: permission denied). Evidence-gated completion — implementation tasks must run a build/test/typecheck command before the completion banner is allowed. No evidence → one forced verification round. Honest banners — "Response delivered · no file changes" (git-verified), first-person pause messages, and a change summary with per-file +/− stats and verification evidence at completion.

Mercury Code now starts in AUTO by default: read first, plan silently, implement immediately. Small and medium changes proceed without asking; large or consequential changes present a concise plan with a single ask_user confirmation (recommended option default-selected), then build without re-asking. Manual plan/execute modes remain available (/code plan, /code execute, /code toggle), and /code chat (new) exits to regular chat instantly.
documents.s: AUTO mode — no more mode switching

documents.t: When a model narrates instead of building, Mercury Code escalates mechanically — none of it depends on the model's goodwill: Grounding — the agent executes a deterministic directory listing itself (no LLM) and injects it as verified state. Forced action — via prepareStep, the first step of a guard round runs with toolChoice: 'required' and mutating tools only. Narration is impossible on that step. Provider rotation — guard rounds walk the fallback chain; a narration-locked model isn't the only worker. Wake-up call — after a full failed cycle, the bound doubles with a blunt directive ("your next response MUST begin with a mutating tool call, ZERO prose"). Ten mechanical rounds total across providers before any pause.
documents.s: The escalation harness — the agent makes things happen

documents.t: OpenCode's session-pipeline practices were adopted where they make Mercury harder to kill — and extended with guarantees neither OpenCode nor Claude Code expose: Practice OpenCode Mercury 1.2.3 Memory/context pressure Compact and continue Compact and continue (compactConversation), abort only if pressure persists Doom-loop protection Threshold 3 → intervention Loop detector → abort attempt → provider fallback Provider failures Exponential backoff, retry-after, max 5 Fallback chain + durable retries + named per-provider failure ledger Completion guarantees None documented Completion contract: forced action, wake-up calls, evidence-gated completion Plus: a stall watchdog (3-min silence → visible pulse, 8-min → abort into resume machinery), automatic continuation (six fresh step budgets, provider hard-deadlines count as one attempt), and write-truncation recovery (sectioned writes with full-budget resume rounds).

Live plan checklist — the update_plan tool maintains pending / ▶ active / ☑ done steps in the transcript, so you always see which step is being implemented. ask_user choice picker — now renders inside Mercury Code (previously the tool blocked on a prompt that never rendered — an invisible hang) and owns the keyboard while pending. Live thinking preview — model reasoning streams as a quoted preview instead of dead air. Wheel scrolling — full-screen transcripts scroll with the trackpad via a filtered stdin proxy; mouse sequences never leak into input. File-change previews — bounded, syntax-highlighted excerpts of every created/edited file, with per-file stats at completion. Developer status line — repo state, mode, token budget (⚡ %), and only the keys that matter.

SSRF guard: fetch_url and install_skill validate scheme and private ranges (DNS-resolved) on every redirect hop; 512 KB payload caps. MERCURY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_FETCH=1 to opt out for local testing. Credential files (web-config.json, web-sessions.json) written 0600 and repaired on load; the initial web password is now random per install. Secret redaction: API keys masked in logs and command-output echoes; shell blocklist gains swapped-flag rm -fr variants. Mercury Cloud: credential rotation failures now say run "mercury cloud connect" instead of an opaque 401 loop.

Yoga WASM "memory access out of bounds" crashes — ink patched (freed-node reference hygiene + <Static> identity dedup), shipped via patch-package. Duplicate-message render loop (~30 s cadence) from still-mounted static children. Scroll repair after long-session trims (/mc scroll-set was parsed as a NaN delta — dead code). Prose questions no longer fight the narration guard; not-a-git-repo no longer false-claims "no file changes". /chat from Mercury Code tears down state properly instead of half-exiting.

npm install -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.2.3 No config changes required. New optional environment variables: MERCURY_STALL_SOFT_MS, MERCURY_STALL_HARD_MS, MERCURY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_FETCH, MERCURY_MAX_STEPS (testing). patch-package ships as a runtime dependency — the bundled ink patch applies automatically on install.

Mercury stops being one agent and becomes a fleet. 1.3.0 is the biggest capability shift since the Second Brain: Mercury Bots — persistent, persona-scoped agents that live outside your conversation. Each bot has its own persona (bot.yaml + permissions.yaml), a private sandbox workspace under ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/, its own skill library and permission scopes, a per-bot token budget, and a journal-backed thread history that survives restarts. Dispatch work and keep talking to Mercury — the bot works in the background and delivers results in its own thread, never in the middle of your chat. And because one bot is never enough: promote a bot to fleet lead and it recruits and organizes its own crew — multi-level hierarchies with results bubbling up through the lead. Ship the whole fleet to a teammate as a single bundle. Watch it all live from the web cockpit. Why "Mercury Bots"? Sub-agents die with their task; channels answer one persona at a time. Bots are neither: they are persistent specialists with identities, workspaces, and queues — the difference between hiring a contractor for the afternoon and employing a small team.

Area What changed Persistent runtime Persona manifests (bot.yaml/permissions.yaml), private sandbox per bot, journal-hydrated threads, wakes + durable queue Fleet hierarchy Fleet leads recruit/manage their own crew (imperative self-organization); multi-level fleets; results bubble up through leads Durable queue + DLQ Jobs survive restarts; lease-heartbeat; timed out classification; non-destructive /bots replay Web cockpit Mercury Bots section on the local dashboard: live roster, per-bot threads, needs-you badges, fleet step view mirroring the TUI Sandbox + bot_deliver Isolated per-bot workspaces; final artifacts via bot_deliver; retention janitor caps disk; _shared folder for cross-bot files Bundles /bots export / /bots import — portable fleets; imported bots start disabled; sandbox/journals/.env never travel Permissions Explicit tiers at onboarding (ask/allow), per-bot shell allow-lists, malformed scopes warn instead of crashing CLI mercury bots doctor / list / storage mirroring the in-chat surface

A bot is not a sub-agent and not a channel — it's a third way to run intelligence: Sub-agent Bot Lifetime dies with its task persistent across restarts Identity anonymous worker named persona (name, description, character) Workspace inherits your session private sandbox at ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ (+ fleet-shared folder) Results land in your chat land in the bot's own thread Continuity none journal history hydrates on reopen Permissions your session's its own scopes, declared in the persona The wake lifecycle: dispatch a task → the bot's thread shows live state and streamed thinking → it works through the durable queue → results land in its thread → if something genuinely needs you (failed job, blocked permission, stopped bot), a needs-you alert reaches your active channel.

Any bot can be promoted to a fleet lead (/bots promote <id>). Leads are different: Imperative self-organization — tell the lead what to achieve, not how; it recruits crew, delegates, and synthesizes results (multi-level hierarchies supported). Crew management — fleet-delegation, fleet-layout, and fleet-stop/start semantics: stopping a lead holds its whole subtree; /bots start on the lead resumes it. Onboarding tiers — solo bot → lead auto-build (lead designs its own crew from your brief) → lead manual (you hand-pick every member). Bundle portability — exporting a lead ships the whole crew as one bundle.

The fleet runs on a durable job queue (SQLite-backed with a JSON fallback), hardened through eight Windows/teardown cycles: Jobs survive restarts; workers take leases with heartbeats. Deaths classify honestly: timed out (worker died), failed (permanent) — both land in the DLQ, replayable non-destructively via /bots replay <id> <jobId>. Post-close queue operations degrade to no-ops, never crashes; traversal guards are separator-agnostic. mercury bots doctor cross-checks schedules: routines that exist in the scheduler but never got registered (the silently never fires failure) are flagged before they bite.

The local web dashboard now has a Mercury Bots section: Live fleet roster with per-bot states (running / waiting / stopped / needs-you). Per-bot thread view — chat with any bot from the browser, thinking streamed live. Fleet step view mirroring Mercury Code TUI steps — solo, lead auto-build, lead manual tiers all render identically. Needs-you escalation badges surface bots that are blocked and waiting on you.

Every bot works inside ~/.mercury/bots/<id>/ — its own workspace with per-directory read/write/execute scopes declared in the persona. Final artifacts exit through bot_deliver (platform or download format), so nothing lives only inside a sandbox. The retention janitor enforces per-bot disk caps (journal rotation, DLQ cap) — a forgotten fleet can't eat your disk. ~/.mercury/bots/_shared/ is the fleet-shared folder: implicit grants between crew members, explicit grants for leads.

/bots export <id> [path] # manifest + persona + permissions + skills (+ crew if lead) /bots import <path> # recreate bots — imported bots start disabled A lead's bundle carries its entire crew. Whole-fleet export is supported. Imported bots start disabled by design — you inspect them, then /bots enable when you trust them. Sandboxed state, journals, and .env secrets never travel.

Onboarding walks through capability tiers (ask / allow) — nothing defaults silently in the dark. Hand-edited bot.yaml / permissions.yaml apply live; malformed scope entries skip with a warning instead of crashing turns. Telegram member installs no longer surface install_skill.

Live thinking streams — bot reasoning streams into its thread as a quoted preview; fleet speedups from a single-provider lease wait and batched roster fetches. mercury bots CLI — doctor (exit 1 = actionable), list, storage for disk usage. Windows/teardown hardening — eight cycles of EBUSY/EINVAL/traversal fixes across the queue, heartbeat tests, and retention backdating. v1.2.4 → v1.2.7 carried in — dynamic status verbs, "Did you know?" tips, slash-autocomplete coverage everywhere, smart-conditional completion stats, and the RevShare integration (#117). See the changelog for the full per-version detail.

npm install -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.3.0 mercury restart Standalone-binary users: re-run the one-line installer from mercuryagent.sh, then mercury restart. No config migrations. Bots are opt-in — nothing changes until you create one: /bots create researcher "Researcher" "Web research specialist" /bots persona researcher "You are a meticulous researcher who cites sources." Full Changelog: https://github.com/cosmicstack-labs/mercury-agent/compare/v1.2.7...v1.3.0

The release where Mercury stays out of your way. 1.3.1 is about the shape of the thing: one process runs your bots and your channels, and the terminal is a window onto it — open in under a second, closed without consequence. Bots now do work instead of writing notes about work, deliver files where you can find them, stay online without burning tokens, and can be run from your phone. Underneath, Node 22 and a patched Ink 8 renderer; alongside, everything from the earlier, unpublished "Honest Mercury" work — chat that answers, "done" that means verified, and six security fixes.

One runtime (ADR-024) The daemon owns channels, bots and the web port; mercury attaches to it. No second copy of the fleet in your terminal. Instant attach Listener binds first at boot; /api/health answers with pid/version; a foreign process on the port is named, not restarted around. Bots that do work (ADR-020) Per-turn caps, outcome judged from the tool trace, daily budgets on by default, deliverables in ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot>/. Fleets that coordinate (ADR-021) Typed tasks with one digest wake, pipelines as data, bots that remember. Operate the fleet (ADR-022) /bots cost, /bots show, /bots stop all, DLQ clear, budget presets. Bots in your pocket (ADR-023) Telegram command menu, tappable roster, files pushed to the chat, onboarding with native buttons. Bots stay online No-outcome routines cool down and auto-resume; declared cadence honoured; doctor flags stale bots. Node 22 + Ink 8 Required for npm installs; binaries unaffected. Four Mercury hunks on Ink 8, upstreaming.

Launching mercury with no daemon used to spawn one and boot a second full runtime in the terminal. Both ran the fleet on one queue, both polled Telegram (409 conflicts), and the terminal copy ran every bot turn on the thread that paints your keystrokes. Now the terminal spawns the daemon and attaches; a foreground runtime beside a live daemon (mercury code) is a terminal for the main agent only. The event loop is measured: /api/health.loopLag, and stalls ≥250 ms are logged. Your login service follows the install: after a reinstall (npm → binary, stable → dev, new Node) the old LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Task used to keep resurrecting the old daemon. Mercury now re-points it on launch, on macOS, Linux and Windows. mercury doctor → Login service: points at this install.

Caps and compaction — 300k tokens / 20 min per turn; context compacted automatically. Judged by the trace — a run is deliverable, action, delegated, message or none; a reply that claims more than the trace shows is flagged. Budgets by default — 5M tokens/day per bot, 20M per fleet; warned at 80%, paused until tomorrow at 100%. Deliverables you can find — bot_deliver files land in ~/Documents/Mercury/<Bot name>/, finals on top, crew work under work/, README index. Legacy outputs migrate on first start. Routines honoured — a bot.yaml cadence runs as written; bot-created routines ≥30 min; three empty runs cool a routine down (6 h → 24 h) and it resumes by itself.

fleet_delegate hands several typed tasks to the crew and wakes the lead once with a digest. Pipelines are data in bot.yaml (research → draft → check → package), stages chain themselves, finals are promoted. Every turn starts with a digest of the last five runs and the bot's own working-state note; durable facts go into the bot's memory.

/bots cost [days], /bots show <id> [runId], /bots stop all / start all, /bots dlq clear, /bots doctor, /bots outputs, /bots fetch. On Telegram: /bots and /bot in the command menu; the roster arrives with Stop/Start · Run · Runs per bot and Cost · Outputs · Doctor · Stop all — a tap runs the real command. Delivered files come back to the chat as attachments. /bots create on Telegram runs the full onboarding — persona, permissions tier, solo/fleet, budget — as native buttons that settle in place.
documents.s: Operate it — from the terminal or a phone

documents.t: Never published on its own; everything from it ships here: chat no longer forced through tool rounds, "done" means a check actually passed, one feedback contract on every channel, /trace, /new everywhere, context window v2, memory bounds, Telegram prompt timeouts that say what they defaulted to, per-agent permission contexts, the replay eval harness, and six published security advisories (GHSA-hj5j-2689-x8r2, -xc4h-859q-mq79, -gc84-h2g2-h54w, -h2c6-h3vx-mqwh, -qjx7-rw28-6hxq, -r27w-9m8h-qwg8).
documents.s: Honest Mercury — the earlier 1.3.1 work, folded in

documents.t: Mercury's terminal renderer moves to Ink 8 + React 19, which needs Node 22. Stock Ink's <Static> is positional — a bounded transcript remounted the whole subtree every frame — and tall frames stamped copies into scrollback on every repaint. Mercury vendors Ink 8 with four hunks (keyed static, scrollback guard, freeze gate, IME cursor anchor), verified in CI as tarball + hunks, and is proposing them upstream from cosmicstack-labs/ink.

The attach TUI (what mercury now opens) does not yet have bot threads (/bots open) or the /telegram / /discord / /slack menus. Use /bots send <id> <message>, mercury telegram … from the shell, or mercury code for the in-process TUI. First item of the next release. Bots share the daemon's thread with the main agent — bounded, not isolated. loopLag will tell you if it ever matters.

Standalone binaries — nothing to think about: curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh # macOS / Linux irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex # Windows npm — check Node first: node -v # must be 22+ nvm install 22 && nvm alias default 22 # if it is not npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.3.1 mercury # re-points your login service, migrates bot outputs, attaches mercury upgrade checks the Node requirement before it removes anything; the package refuses to install on an older Node with a readable message. ~/.mercury carries over untouched.

Mercury picks up the phone, and picks up the mouse. 1.4.0 is the first stable release since 1.3.8. Its headline is the plugin system: optional features you install only if you want them, each running in its own process so a bad plugin can't take Mercury down. Two official plugins ship with it. WhatsApp lets you chat with Mercury and talk to it by voice call, and Mercury can call you. Optimus lets Mercury use your computer: it sees the screen, moves the pointer and types like a person, by chat or out loud with a talk key. Both are in the stable plugin catalog for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows x64 and Linux (x64 and arm64). 1.3.9 only shipped on the dev channel; its fix is folded in here.

Plugins (#203, ADR-025) /plugins install, enable, disable, update, rollback, uninstall, from a checksum-verified catalog. Out-of-process plugins can't crash Mercury. Plugin API 1.2 Tools can return images to the model (kept out of chat history), permissions.desktop, and whatsapp and desktop channel types. One place for keys Plugins use Mercury's own providers. Set an OpenAI key once and voice works everywhere. Guided setup, flatter menus Setup on install. /plugins <id> lists every setting, explains what each choice does, and asks for follow-up settings right after you save. WhatsApp 0.1.1 (#202) Chat from a spare number, voice calls in both directions, scheduled calls, approvals by voice or chat, access levels. Optimus 0.4.7 (new) Mercury uses your computer: sees, points, scrolls and types like a person, with a talk key, a mute key, "stop", and an honest "done". Built-in web_search Free and keyless. News and current events get looked up, not guessed. Photos, PDFs, voice notes Mercury sees photos and PDFs you send in chat, and listens to voice notes.

Features only some people want were heading into the single binary, making it bigger and riskier for everyone. Now they're plugins (ADR-025): Install from the catalog. /plugins install whatsapp in any chat, mercury plugins install whatsapp in a shell, or Configure → Plugins in the dashboard. The catalog at https://mercuryagent.sh/plugins/catalog.json pins each version to a SHA-256 checksum. Isolated. An out-of-process plugin is a separate program speaking MCP over stdio. If it crashes, Mercury restarts it; after repeated crashes or 5 failures in a row it's turned off and you're told why. A plugin reaches only the network hosts and reads only the secrets it declared, and install shows them before you confirm. Hot-plugged and reversible. Install, enable, disable and uninstall take effect without a restart. Installing into a running Mercury now starts the plugin immediately. /plugins rollback <id> brings back the previous version with its settings. mercury start --safe-mode starts with every plugin off. Guided setup and a flatter menu. Setup runs right after install, one question at a time, and skips questions that don't apply. /plugins <id> lists every setting with its current value. Yes/no options say what each answer does ("On: Mercury picks up when you call it"), follow-up settings appear right after you save (pick Gemini, then the Gemini key), and every question has a way back. Mercury's own providers. A plugin that needs OpenAI or Grok uses the provider you already set up in Mercury. Keys a plugin asks for itself are stored with Mercury's keys and shared with other plugins that declare them. A missing key is explained once, with what it turns off. Plugin API 1.2. Tools can return images to the model, sent with that tool result only and never stored in history, logs or memory. permissions.desktop flags a plugin that controls the computer. Channel types are whatsapp and desktop. See Writing plugins. Docs: Plugins.

Chat with Mercury on WhatsApp, with Mercury running on a spare number as a linked device. It uses an unofficial protocol, so don't link your main number. Voice calls both ways. Call the spare number and talk to Mercury, or let Mercury call you when something matters. Only your number can call. Scheduled calls. "Call me at 9pm about the deploy", "call me back in 20 minutes", from chat, the terminal or a call. Also /call and /calls. Times are worked out in code and confirmed exactly; one retry if you miss it; calls survive restarts. "Call me when it's done" does the work, then calls. Mercury works during the call. It looks things up with web_search, uses its tools and memory, and keeps you posted while it works. Approvals are asked by voice and posted in the chat at once; the first answer wins, and a spoken yes only counts in your own words. Links and files during a call. Mercury sends links and details to the chat instead of reading them out, and can see photos and documents you send while you talk. Voice engine choice. OpenAI Realtime by default (your Mercury OpenAI provider), or Gemini Live, Grok Voice, ElevenLabs, Azure, Qwen-Omni, or your own Mercury model with a speech-to-text and a text-to-speech provider. Access levels. General (chat only) or Extended (memory, files, tools). Members never get more than you. Link, check and unlink from the dashboard, with a QR code or a pairing code. Voice notes, photos and PDFs you send are understood. Docs: WhatsApp.

Mercury uses your computer. Ask in any chat, or press the talk key and say it. Sees and acts like a person. Screenshots of the display the mouse is on; the pointer glides, scrolling is smooth, and text is typed key by key, so it works in every editor. A "Mercury is driving" ring and label follow the pointer, and never appear in its own screenshots. Listening mode. The talk key (default ctrl+alt+m, Control+Option+M on a Mac) starts a voice session with spoken replies and live narration of each step. Press it while Optimus works and everything stops. Mute key (default ctrl+alt+shift+m): stop listening, keep working. Nothing you say is sent while muted. "Stop" stops. Saying "stop" halts every screen action and the task at once. Silence (60 seconds by default) ends a session, so the mic never streams for nothing. A soft tick-tock while it works, and the TUI status bar shows when Optimus is listening, working or muted. Honest about "done". Steps report Sent, not done; Mercury checks the screen before saying a task is finished, and failed steps are reported as failed. You stay in control. Off until you allow it. Anything that submits, sends, pays, deletes or installs needs your approval. Move the mouse and it hands control back. It never types passwords or card numbers. Voice settings shared with WhatsApp: the same engines, and a key added for one works for the other. No signing hassle. Installs locally with no Apple Developer ID. On macOS, Optimus builds Optimus.app signed with a certificate made on your Mac, and you grant Accessibility, Screen Recording and Microphone once. Docs: Optimus.

Built-in web_search, free and keyless (web and news), through the SSRF guard. The built-in web-search skill uses it. Photos and PDFs from chat are attached to the turn for models that accept them, and voice notes are transcribed with your OpenAI provider. Mercury always knows it comes from Cosmic Stack. Model picker in the web dashboard: plain-language model names, renaming, a reasoning picker, every local Ollama model, and ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan models. Blog "Listen to article" player, using the reader's built-in voices.

mercury doctor applies what you changed (from 1.3.9). Doctor restarts the running daemon when the configuration actually changed, and dashboard saves say "restart to apply" with a Restart button. The web dashboard works on the Windows standalone binary. Mercury didn't recognise the Windows marker for its embedded files and reported "web UI not found". Found and fixed by @farena-ai in #189. ChatGPT OAuth turns no longer fail after a tool call. Long messages no longer fail memory search ("Expression tree is too large"). New dashboard chats no longer land in the previous conversation; dashboard permission prompts render and resolve. One failing alert no longer fans out into hundreds of repeated messages on a plugin channel. Plugin installs work with GNU tar on Windows.

WhatsApp uses an unofficial protocol. A WhatsApp update can break it, and automated use can get the number restricted. Use a spare number. Optimus on Linux Wayland is limited: screenshots go through the desktop's screen-sharing prompt, and mouse, keyboard and the talk key only reach X11 (XWayland) apps. X11 sessions get full control. Optimus on Windows can't control windows running as administrator (Task Manager, installers). Out-of-process plugins can't add slash commands yet.

npm: npm install -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.4.0 mercury restart Standalone binaries: rerun the installer from mercuryagent.sh, or run mercury upgrade. curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install.sh | sh # macOS / Linux irm https://mercuryagent.sh/install.ps1 | iex # Windows Then add the plugins you want: /plugins install whatsapp /plugins install optimus ~/.mercury carries over untouched. Plugins live in ~/.mercury/plugins/.
Mercury learns how you work, saves its own skills, and searches again. Released 2026-10-24. Install or update: mercury upgrade, npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.4.1, or the GitHub release.
documents.s: v1.4.1 — Mercury learns how you work

documents.t: Memory became beliefs with evidence. Every claim about you now carries support and counter-evidence, a confidence that fades unless it is seen again, the context it applies in, and a status: candidate → held → confirmed by you; contested; retired; forgotten. What you say outright beats what Mercury inferred and never fades. Nothing is deleted behind your back. It learns working traits, not personality types: reply length, when to ask before acting (per project or domain), options vs a recommendation, tone, your expertise and risk appetite per domain, when you are usually around, how you give feedback. It never infers health, religion, politics, sexuality or personality types, never stores credentials, and never generalises about other people beyond what you said. Two loops. After each turn a strict extractor turns the turn into belief operations (or nothing; Mercury's own replies are never evidence about you). Every hour of activity, and at shutdown, a reflection pass reads your messages and behaviour across sessions, infers traits, merges duplicates, flags contradictions and rewrites the owner brief. The model finally sees it: "About you" and "How to work with you" sit in every prompt, plus the beliefs relevant to each message. Beliefs it acted on without objection gain support; a correction retires the old belief and holds the new one. You hear about it. Behaviour-changing learning ends the reply with one line: ☿ Noted: … Say "forget that" to undo. Contradictions are asked about once. /memory learned|beliefs|contested|confirm|correct|forget|settle, /forget <text>, "forget that", the forget_memory / confirm_belief / correct_belief tools, a dashboard view with Confirm/Forget, and an editable ~/.mercury/soul/owner.md whose notes are read back. Hygiene: the old extractor saved Mercury's own replies as your preferences (about half of a typical store). Those rows are quarantined, not deleted (dashboard → Quarantined, with Restore); real memories became beliefs. The prose fallback is gone, merging works, conflicts no longer delete at random, and soul files you edited are never overwritten by migration. One source. /memory, the dashboard, the save_memory / search_memory tools, the bots and cloud sync all read and write the belief store now; the old memories table is a read-only archive. Your name, email and handles stay in identity.owner in mercury.yaml and are never stored as beliefs. Chat can actually use what it read. Per-message recall shows held beliefs first and fills with unverified candidates (labelled as hunches), so what Mercury learned today and what the upgrade migrated is visible now, not after a second session. "What do you know about me?" injects the strongest beliefs directly. Stopwords and channel scaffolding no longer pollute the search, and the "About you" section pads with hedged candidates until enough is held. Two extractor leaks closed. A correction that opens like an acknowledgement ("No no, I said British spelling…") is no longer skipped as trivial, and an operation the model emits without an excerpt now cites your message instead of being thrown away (that alone dropped whole turns on Haiku). Pick the model that learns. memory.learning.provider: anthropic (or LEARNING_PROVIDER) runs extraction and reflection on a capable provider while chat keeps its own; unset falls back to the default. Safe upgrade. The first boot after upgrading backs second-brain.db up to second-brain.pre-owner-model.db before migrating, the migration runs once and never crashes the boot, every memory you could see before is still listed (or waits in Quarantined), and "☿ Noted" lines are limited to one per channel every few minutes.
documents.s: Owner Model: Mercury learns how to work with you (ADR-026)

documents.t: Mercury turns long work into skills. After a multi-step task it would do again (a recurring report, a conversion pipeline, a deploy, a site or device it operates) has worked end-to-end, Mercury saves the procedure with the new create_skill tool — exact commands, paths, checks and pitfalls — and tells you in one line. Next time it is one use_skill away. Kept apart from your skills. Self-made skills live in ~/.mercury/skills/self-made/, carry origin: mercury, are listed under their own "Self-made" label and count as unverified until used again. Drafts are rejected unless they are a real, verified, credential-free procedure; a self-made skill never shadows an installed one. Skill categories and intents work again. Discovery registered each skill's category, intents and tags and then rebuilt the index, wiping them; the prompt fell back to a flat list and intent routing matched on names only. Fixed by building the index first. No junk shelf. /skills self-made shows each one with use counts; unused ones go dormant after 30 days (disabled, never deleted) and the shelf is capped at 40. /skills self-made enable|disable|remove <name>. Bots and channel members cannot create skills.

Search returns real results again, still free and keyless. Bing's web RSS feed, the main engine, now answers automated requests with pages unrelated to the query (train timetables for a TypeScript question), and DuckDuckGo, Mojeek and Startpage answer with bot challenges. web_search now asks Brave Search first, then Wikipedia, Hacker News, Bing News and Google News, and keeps only results that mention the query, so a source serving junk counts as empty and the next one is tried. A thin answer is topped up from Wikipedia, the same page is never listed twice, and Brave rests for a minute after rate-limiting instead of being retried every query. No new dependency. Old DuckDuckGo skills stop failing. fetch_url on a search-engine results page (DuckDuckGo, Google, Bing, Yahoo, Brave, Startpage, Mojeek) runs the query through web_search instead of returning the challenge page. An installed web-search skill that scrapes such a page and never mentions web_search is replaced by the built-in one on start, with the original kept as SKILL.md.replaced.bak; skills you edited that already use web_search are left alone. The built-in web-search skill (1.2.0) tells the model to rephrase once before giving up and never to fetch search pages directly.

Regular chat works like an agent again. Its instructions forbade helper scripts and batching ("call write_file for each one individually"), so a task like converting an EPUB to Markdown was done file by file by hand. Chat now reaches for the strongest existing tool (pandoc, ffmpeg, a Python library) or one script, does a quick web search when it isn't sure what the best tool is, and checks the output before saying it is done. It also gets a short working contract like Mercury Code's: do the work, plan multi-step tasks, report what was checked. /model and /cloud offer the arrow-key picker in the attached terminal again. The picker was only wired to the foreground terminal; since the default launch attaches, /model printed a list and left you typing /models use <name>. Both now open the same ↑↓ picker on your own screens (attached terminal and dashboard), and Esc keeps the current model instead of silently taking the first option. A model switch says what it does. /model used to answer "Saved for future sessions", which read as "takes effect next session". It now says ✓ Switched to <model> (<provider>). In effect from your next message, and kept as the default., and the status row shows the new model at once. Pickers answered in the attached terminal reach the runtime. The answer endpoint only resolved permission prompts, so choosing in /permissions, /model or a question picker did nothing: the command waited out its 2-minute timeout behind a "Thinking" spinner. Choices and Esc now resolve at once, and the spinner is hidden while a picker waits on you. /new no longer leaves the attached terminal "Thinking" forever. After /new or /session <ref> the runtime re-bound your screen to the new session, but the terminal kept listening on the old one, so every reply went where nobody was looking and /stop seemed ignored. The runtime now tells the screen to follow, and the terminal also follows whenever a message is routed to another session. Yes-or-no and "which one?" questions come as a picker, not prose. Chat now asks decisions through its question tool (↑↓ and Enter) and keeps prose for questions that need free text (a name, a path).

Every new session asks for its permission mode again. Since 1.3.1 the default mercury launch attaches to the background runtime, which never showed the "Ask Me / Allow All" prompt, so everyone was silently in Ask Me. The prompt is back wherever a session starts: the foreground terminal and Mercury Code at launch, the attached terminal when you start a new session or type /new. Your current mode is listed first, so Enter keeps it and ↓ Enter switches; the pick is remembered as the default for next time and applied to every screen. Resuming an existing session prints one dim line with the mode in effect instead. /permissions works everywhere you are the owner (attached terminal and dashboard too, not just the foreground terminal), including /permissions allow-all and /permissions ask-me. "Always" on a command prompt now covers that command for the rest of the chat (every pandoc …, git commit …), not just the exact string. Installs, wrappers like sudo/sh -c, and remote Mercury Cloud requests stay exact-match. Telegram and Signal can switch back from Allow All to Ask Me (the switch used to be ignored until restart).

The session picker fits the screen, new session first. mercury used to list up to six sessions under the launch pad regardless of the terminal height, so on a 24-row terminal Ink dropped the wordmark off the top. The list is now budgeted to the height (the tip goes first, then sessions fold into … N more · /sessions in the chat), and "Start a new session" is the first, pre-selected row instead of the last. One useful row, not a dump. The row under the input is status only. Left: the session (⚿ copper-mint-thd · hi). Right: permission mode, today's budget meter, model, Code mode, Optimus, an update — fitted to the terminal width in priority order with compact forms (claude-haiku-4-5 not claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, ⚡12% when narrow), so a long model or session name never crowds out the rest; what does not fit is dropped, lowest priority first, never cut mid-word. Optimus wins the row. While Optimus is listening or working, its activity is the first segment on the right and the last one the fit ever drops; the session on the left shrinks to its alias to make room. Model only on the row. The provider name is gone from the status row (claude-sonnet-4-5, not Anthropic · claude-sonnet-4-5); the model name already says who serves it. The budget meter is back on the row. ⚡ ██████░░ 76% shows today's token use as a bar that goes green → yellow (70 %) → red (90 %), the colours the completion footer has always used. It outranks the model when the row is narrow, so it stays visible as ⚡76% down to very small terminals. The attached terminal and the foreground TUI share one builder. The bar updates live. The attached terminal (what mercury opens) read the model once on connect and never again; model switches, Code mode, permission changes and Optimus activity never reached it. The runtime now pushes a status update on every model switch and checks every 2 seconds for anything else. The bar shows the thread, model, Code mode, Ask Me / Allow All, today's token use and Optimus activity; the foreground and Mercury Code bars show the permission mode too. The launch pad's budget row works again (it read field names the runtime never sent). Said once, in the chat. While a turn runs, one line above the input shows the spinner, the phase (Thinking, the running tool, Writing) and the elapsed time, cyan then yellow at 30 s and red at 90 s, under the finished steps' ✓ marks. The status row under the input never repeats it. Choosing a permission mode no longer prints a confirmation line either: the row shows the mode. No key hints on the row. ↵ send · /help · ctrl+c detach is gone; Enter sends, /help lists the commands, and the row keeps its width for status. The right half is a single truncating line now, so it can no longer wrap onto a hidden second line and end in Anthropic · .

Search that finds things, and a research prompt that asks only when you mean it. Released 2026-10-25. Install or update: mercury upgrade, npm i -g @cosmicstack/mercury-agent@1.4.2, or the GitHub release.

Three web sources, the ones that work. web_search asks Parallel's public search first (keyless MCP built for agents, about a second, with excerpts and dates), then DuckDuckGo's html page, then its lite page. Brave, Wikipedia, Hacker News and Bing's web feed are gone from web search: Brave refuses automated requests and the others answered general questions badly. News keeps Parallel (article links only, section fronts dropped), then Bing News, Google News and Hacker News. DuckDuckGo parsed exactly. Both pages are read from their real markup: each result's title, the real address behind DuckDuckGo's redirect, and the snippet; ads (result--ad, sponsored rows) are dropped. A challenge is retried once after a short pause, and a page that is neither results nor "No results" is reported as "page not recognised" instead of silently empty. Tests run against saved copies of both real pages. News links open the article. News search used Google News first, whose links are Google redirects (news.google.com/rss/articles/…) that can't be turned into the publisher's address. Bing News now comes first and its links are unwrapped to the real article; Google News is the fallback, and its links are marked as redirects. Search never depends on the model. Results come only from Mercury's own search tools, never from a provider's built-in web search, so search works the same with every model. The web-search skill (1.3.0) explains the sources and tells the model to report which ones failed and why when a search comes back empty. You can see what happened. Every result ends with the trail, for example Searched: Parallel: timed out → DuckDuckGo: 8 results, so "nothing found" and "everything was blocked" read differently.

The research prompt asks only when you want research. It used to fire on words ("latest", "recent", "explain", "today's news"), so "convert the latest epub" or "explain how my build works and fix it" got a research question. The words now only decide whether to check; one short model call decides whether you asked for an in-depth, multi-source write-up. Instructions, quick questions and today's news never get the prompt, and a failed or slow check means no prompt. Quick answer comes first. The picker starts on "Quick answer", so an accidental Enter never starts a long research run.

Mercury gets an app. 1.5.0 ships Mercury Desktop for macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows and Linux, at the same version as the runtime. It installs Mercury on your computer without a terminal, or connects to Mercury on a server, and it keeps both up to date. Download it.

Install or connect. The first screen finds a Mercury on this computer, installs one (the release is checked against its SHA-256 checksums and runs as a service), or connects to Mercury elsewhere. Several connections at once. See Install & first run. Not code-signed yet. A downloaded installer asks once before the first launch; the download page has the steps. On a Mac, curl -fsSL https://mercuryagent.sh/install-desktop.sh | sh installs it with no prompt (it checks the download's SHA-256 first). Updates are signed and checked before they install.

Tunnels are remote. Requests through Tailscale, Cloudflare or a proxy are no longer treated as coming from this computer, even when the tunnel runs on the same machine. New devices need your approval, with a 5-character code you answer from Telegram, WhatsApp, the terminal or Mercury Desktop on this computer. Sensitive actions from a remote device ask you first: the terminal (off for remote devices by default), Allow All, the workspace folder, powerful bots, plugins and skills from a URL, channel tokens, Cloud sign-in, restarts and the password. Device lifecycle: devices unused for 30 days are signed out, 10 devices at most, a new address tells you, revoking cuts open connections. /server, mercury server and mercury doctor --security. Plus a sign-in attempt limit, CSRF and DNS-rebinding protection, and a security log. See Remote access & security.

One signed update notice says what's new, what's required and anything Mercury needs to tell you. An unsigned or older notice is ignored, and being offline never blocks anything. Server updates wait for running work, download with checksums, back up, install, confirm the new version answers, and roll back on their own if it doesn't. mercury upgrade uses the same steps. Mercury Desktop has a Chrome-style Update button, an updates panel for the app and every server, resumable signed downloads, Check for updates and Update everything. Required updates get a full-screen notice that only a ticked checklist gets past, for a while. See Updating Mercury.
documents.s: Updates that never leave you broken

documents.t: Research is one visible run: a plan you can edit, live progress, every source read or failed with the reason, and a report even when a run is cut short. Reports are saved to ~/mercury-artifacts/Research and export as PDF or Word.
What Mercury makes goes in ~/mercury-artifacts, one folder per chat, instead of loose files in your home folder.
Mercury can use tools from Model Context Protocol servers. Add one with mercury mcp add, allow the tools you want, and every MCP call asks first in Ask Me mode. See MCP Servers.

Every bot run ends by reporting, saying there was nothing new, or saying it failed. Results wait in an inbox until you read them. Waste is capped by rule: a minimum gap between routine runs, tools by group, and a routine that keeps failing switches itself off.
mercury upgrade Or download Mercury Desktop and choose Use the Mercury here: it offers to update an older Mercury first.
